diseases.name: Anthrax

agents.name: Bacillus anthracis
agents.notes: Gram-positive, spore-forming, non-motile rod. Spores survive in soil for decades and concentrate in alkaline, calcium-rich ground — the classic 'anthrax triangle' of soil pH above 6.0, high organic matter and alternating wet/dry cycles.
agents.reservoir: Soil spore bank; carcases of infected animals

hosts.notes: Herbivores are highly susceptible. Carnivores and pigs are comparatively resistant. Susceptibility is set by exposure and dose, not by age or sex.

notifiable.note: A confirmed animal case is a public health event. Human infection is almost always occupational — hide, wool, bone-meal and carcase handling.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide, but spore persistence makes it endemic in defined soil foci. In southern Africa, recognised foci exist across Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa, and outbreaks track rainfall: spores are brought to the surface by flooding and then concentrated in grazing swards as water recedes.

aetiology.summary: Infection follows ingestion, inhalation or cutaneous inoculation of spores from a contaminated environment rather than animal-to-animal contact. The bacterium does not spread from a live animal to its neighbours; the environment is the source, and the carcase is the amplifier.
determinants: Presence of a viable soil spore bank in the grazing area
Soil pH above about 6.0 with adequate calcium — alkaline soils preserve spores, acid soils destroy them
Bruising or skin damage allowing cutaneous entry during handling
Concentrated feed or forage contaminated with bone meal, hides or wool
Failure to incinerate or deep-bury a carcase, which seeds the site for decades
risk_factors: Grazing recently flooded or newly opened pasture in a known endemic focus
Unvaccinated herds in endemic districts
Opening a carcase at pasture for post-mortem without precautions
Occupational contact with hides, wool, hair or bone products
Seasonal: outbreak peaks at the end of the rainy season and in the dry season that follows
aetiology.epidemiology: Morbidity and mortality are highest in cattle and can reach 80% or more in an affected group; sheep and goats are also severely affected. Transmission is environmental, so cases cluster by paddock and by grazing history rather than by contact. The spore form is the maintenance strategy: the vegetative bacterium dies readily, but the spore is resistant to heat, desiccation, UV and most disinfectants, and defines the recurrence interval of outbreaks at a site.

pathophysiology.summary: Spores germinate in macrophages and regional lymph nodes, then the vegetative bacteria multiply in the bloodstream and release a tripartite toxin that simultaneously disables phagocytosis, causes tissue oedema and triggers fatal systemic shock. The result is a rapidly rising bacteraemia with splenic engorgement and haemorrhage rather than a localised inflammatory lesion.

cascade.title: Spore uptake and germination
cascade.detail: Spores are phagocytosed by macrophages and dendritic cells at the entry site and carried to regional lymph nodes, where they germinate into vegetative bacilli within hours.

cascade.title: Encapsulation and immune evasion
cascade.detail: The poly-gamma-D-glutamic acid capsule blocks opsonisation and phagocytosis, so the bacterium multiplies unchecked in the lymph node and spills into the efferent lymph.

cascade.title: Toxaemia
cascade.detail: Vegetative bacilli release protective antigen, which assembles with lethal factor and oedema factor. Oedema factor is an adenylate cyclase that raises intracellular cAMP and produces massive fluid accumulation; lethal factor cleaves MAP kinase kinases and drives macrophage apoptosis.

cascade.title: Bacteraemia and capillary injury
cascade.detail: Bacteria multiply to very high numbers in blood — up to 10^7 organisms per millilitre — and the toxins injure capillary endothelium, increasing permeability and causing widespread petechial and ecchymotic haemorrhage.

cascade.title: Shock and death
cascade.detail: Loss of vascular integrity, reduced effective circulating volume and a systemic inflammatory response produce rapid shock. Death can occur within hours of the first sign, which is why peracute anthrax is usually found rather than seen.

lesions: Incomplete rigor mortis and rapid decomposition with bloating
Dark, tarry, incompletely clotted blood oozing from the natural orifices
Markedly enlarged, soft, dark-red 'blackberry jam' spleen
Serosanguinous fluid in thoracic and abdominal cavities
Petechial to ecchymotic haemorrhages on serosa, epicardium and mucosa
Oedematous, haemorrhagic mesenteric and regional lymph nodes
clinical_signs: Sudden death, often the only observed event
High fever (41-42 degrees Celsius) in the brief period before collapse
Trembling, staggering and dyspnoea
Blood-stained discharge from nose, mouth, anus or vulva
Subcutaneous oedema, particularly of the neck, brisket or perineum in less acute cases

antemortem: Blood smear from an ear vein or tail tip: Gram-positive square-ended rods in chains, often with capsule visible on polychrome stain
Rectal temperature and clinical examination, though the window is short and handling risk is high
postmortem: Do not open the carcase. A field post-mortem on suspected anthrax releases spores and endangers everyone present and the site itself.
If a carcase has been opened, a blood smear from an ear or a swab of peripheral blood is the only safe sample
laboratory: Gram stain and M'Fadyean polychrome methylene blue stain of peripheral blood showing capsulated rods
Bacterial culture on blood agar — non-haemolytic, ground-glass colonies
Bacteriophage lysis (gamma phage) for confirmation
PCR targeting pag, capC or chromosomal markers
Ascoli thermoprecipitin test for contaminated hides and animal products
differentials: Blackleg (Clostridium chauvoei) — crepitant muscle lesions, no splenic enlargement
Malignant oedema (Clostridium septicum) — wound-associated, gas in tissues
Lightning strike or electrocution — no fever, no bacteraemia, no spleen change
Haemorrhagic septicaemia (Pasteurella multocida) — septicaemia but no spores and no soil focus
Babesiosis or other acute haemolytic disease — anaemia and haemoglobinuria rather than splenic engorgement

prevention: Annual vaccination with a live spore vaccine in endemic districts, timed to precede the risk season
Never open a suspected carcase; incinerate or deep-bury with quicklime and mark the site
Restrict grazing of known spore foci, especially in the weeks after flooding
Source feed and bone meal only from certified suppliers
Wear gloves and cover wounds when handling hides, wool or suspect carcases
control.vaccination: Live attenuated spore vaccines (Sterne strain) give solid immunity for about a year in cattle and sheep; annual revaccination is required. Vaccinate before the risk season, not during an outbreak, and never vaccinate an animal already incubating the disease.
treatment: Penicillin G (procaine or potassium) is the drug of choice; oxytetracycline is an acceptable alternative
Treat early and aggressively — survival is possible only if treatment starts before severe toxaemia
Supportive care: fluids, and avoid stressing the animal further
Animals that die of anthrax must not be treated or butchered post-mortem
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority immediately — anthrax is notifiable in almost every jurisdiction
Quarantine the affected paddock and stop all movement
Incinerate carcases in situ or bury at least 2 metres deep with quicklime; do not move a carcase before it is burned
Disinfect equipment, boots and vehicles with 5% formalin or 2% glutaraldehyde; spores resist most common disinfectants
Vaccinate in-contact animals and identify the source of exposure
Trace hides, wool and feed that may have left the premises
public_health: Human cases are usually cutaneous, occupational or by inhalation of spores during hide and wool processing
Report human exposures to the public health authority and document occupational groups at risk
Post-exposure prophylaxis for high-exposure contacts under medical direction
Do not allow dogs or scavengers near a carcase — they smear spores across the site
control.notes: The single most important control measure is not opening the carcase. Most contemporary anthrax outbreaks are amplified by well-intentioned curiosity.

diseases.prognosis: Peracute cases die within hours with no realistic chance of treatment. Acute cases treated early with penicillin can recover. For the herd, the prognosis depends on how quickly vaccination and carcase disposal are completed.

diseases.name: Blackleg

agents.name: Clostridium chauvoei
agents.notes: Gram-positive, spore-forming, strictly anaerobic rod. The organism is a normal inhabitant of the intestinal tract and its spores contaminate soil and pasture, where they survive for years. Unlike anthrax, blackleg is not primarily a soil-borne ingestion disease in adults — it is a latent-muscle disease.
agents.reservoir: Soil spore bank; intestinal carriage in healthy ruminants

hosts.notes: Occurs mainly in well-conditioned calves and young cattle aged 6 months to 2 years. Sheep are affected at any age, often after shearing or vaccination — the so-called 'blackleg of sheep' syndrome.

notifiable.note: Not WOAH-listed and not generally notifiable, but it is routinely confused with anthrax, and that confusion is the practical reason to know it well.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in grazing livestock areas. Endemic wherever cattle graze spore-contaminated pasture, which includes most of southern Africa.

aetiology.summary: Blackleg is an endogenous infection in which spores ingested during grazing are deposited in muscle and liver, remain dormant, and then germinate when local conditions turn anaerobic — after blunt trauma, exertion or a growth spurt with rapid muscle development. It is not usually spread from animal to animal.
determinants: Ingestion of spores from contaminated soil or pasture, usually in the first weeks of life
Deposition of spores in muscle tissue during the bacteraemic phase of ingestion
A trigger that creates local anaerobic conditions in muscle — bruising, trauma, exertion or rapid growth
Susceptibility of young, rapidly growing, well-conditioned animals
risk_factors: Grazing recently disturbed or flooded pasture that has brought spores to the surface
Blunt trauma from handling, transport, fighting or rough terrain
Rapid weight gain in well-fed calves
Vaccination or injection sites that create local tissue damage and anaerobic conditions
A history of blackleg on the property — the spore bank persists for years
aetiology.epidemiology: Typically affects a small number of animals, not the whole herd, and cases are often clustered in a cohort of similarly aged calves. Morbidity is usually 1-5%, but case fatality in untreated animals approaches 100%. The disease is non-contagious in the epidemiological sense: the environment and latent spores are the source, so outbreaks recur at the same property rather than spreading between properties.

pathophysiology.summary: Dormant spores in muscle germinate when the local redox potential falls, and the vegetative bacteria multiply rapidly in the anaerobic environment, releasing toxins that cause coagulative necrosis of muscle fibres and a spreading, gas-producing myositis with profound toxaemia.

cascade.title: Latent spore colonisation
cascade.detail: Spores ingested during grazing enter the bloodstream and are deposited in skeletal muscle, heart and liver, where they remain dormant for months without causing disease.

cascade.title: Germination trigger
cascade.detail: Local tissue damage from trauma or exertion reduces oxygen tension and pH, creating the anaerobic, reducing environment that triggers spore germination.

cascade.title: Toxin-mediated myonecrosis
cascade.detail: Vegetative bacteria multiply in the damaged muscle and release alpha toxin, a phospholipase that lyses cell membranes, and hyaluronidase, which breaks down connective tissue and lets the infection spread along fascial planes.

cascade.title: Gas production and crepitus
cascade.detail: Fermentation by the multiplying anaerobes produces gas within the muscle, giving the characteristic crepitant swelling when the lesion is palpated.

cascade.title: Toxaemia and death
cascade.detail: Absorbed toxins produce a rapidly progressive systemic toxaemia with fever, cardiovascular collapse and death, usually within 12-48 hours of the first sign.

lesions: Dark red to black, dry, spongy muscle with a rancid odour, typically in the hindlimb or shoulder
Gas bubbles and crepitus in affected muscle
Extensive subcutaneous and interfascial oedema
Fibrinous pericarditis and myocarditis in some cases
Liver with areas of necrosis
Blood-stained fluid in body cavities; rapid decomposition
clinical_signs: Sudden onset of severe lameness in one limb, with a hot, painful, pitting swelling
High fever (41 degrees Celsius or above) early in the course
Crepitus on palpation of the affected muscle
Rapid deterioration, recumbency and death within 12-48 hours
In sheep, often a wound-associated form after shearing or injection, with local swelling and toxaemia

antemortem: Clinical examination showing acute lameness with a hot, painful, crepitant muscle swelling
Differentiate from anthrax before opening anything — the consequences of error are asymmetric
postmortem: Affected muscle is dark, dry and spongy with a characteristic rancid smell and gas bubbles
Lesions are usually confined to one or two muscle groups, unlike anthrax where the whole carcase is altered
Spleen is not markedly enlarged, which is the key differentiator from anthrax
laboratory: Gram stain of affected muscle or exudate showing large Gram-positive rods, often with subterminal spores
Anaerobic culture on blood agar, incubated anaerobically
PCR or fluorescent antibody testing for C. chauvoei
Note that C. septicum and C. novyi cause overlapping syndromes and require differentiation
differentials: Anthrax — the critical differential; spleen is enlarged and bloody, blood does not clot, and there is no crepitant muscle lesion
Malignant oedema (C. septicum) — usually wound-associated and more rapidly spreading
Bacillary haemoglobinuria (C. novyi type D) — jaundice and haemoglobinuria
Bruising or fracture from trauma — no fever, no toxaemia
Snake bite — local swelling but no crepitus or characteristic muscle colour
Nutritional myopathy (white muscle disease) — bilateral, no fever or gas

prevention: Vaccinate calves from 2-3 months of age with a clostridial vaccine, with a booster 4-6 weeks later
Vaccinate dams in late pregnancy so colostral antibody protects calves until their own response develops
Avoid rough handling, transport injury and unnecessary trauma in young stock
Maintain good nutrition without forcing extremely rapid growth in susceptible calves
control.vaccination: Formalised or toxoid clostridial vaccines covering C. chauvoei are effective and widely used, usually combined with C. septicum, C. novyi, C. haemolyticum and C. perfringens. Two doses are required for primary immunisation, then annual boosters.
treatment: High-dose penicillin is the treatment of choice if started very early, before extensive toxaemia
Oxytetracycline is an alternative
Supportive care: NSAIDs, fluids and rest
Surgical drainage and debridement of affected muscle is sometimes attempted but rarely practical in field conditions
Most animals are found dead or are beyond treatment by the time they are seen
outbreak: Vaccinate all in-contact calves immediately and give a booster in 4-6 weeks
Remove surviving animals from the affected paddock where practical
Dispose of carcases by deep burial or incineration to avoid further soil contamination
Do not open a suspect carcase until anthrax has been excluded
control.notes: The most important practical point is the anthrax differential. Blackleg and anthrax present similarly as sudden death in cattle, and the handling of the carcase is completely different.

diseases.prognosis: Poor once clinical signs are established; case fatality approaches 100% in untreated animals. With very early penicillin treatment, survival is possible but uncommon in practice. Vaccinated animals are well protected.

diseases.name: Bovine tuberculosis

agents.name: Mycobacterium bovis
agents.notes: A slow-growing, acid-fast, lipid-rich bacillus closely related to M. tuberculosis. The waxy cell wall resists desiccation, phagosome fusion and many disinfectants, which explains both its environmental persistence and the chronicity of disease.
agents.reservoir: Infected cattle; badgers in the UK and Ireland; African buffalo and other wildlife in southern Africa; humans with M. bovis infection

hosts.notes: Cattle are the principal maintenance host in managed herds. Pigs and cats are usually infected by drinking infected milk and develop alimentary or oropharyngeal lesions.

notifiable.note: Test-and-slaughter programmes are the standard control approach and impose substantial cost on producers. Unpasteurised milk is the main route of human exposure.

diseases.distribution: Present worldwide where cattle are farmed, though many high-income countries have achieved official free status through sustained test-and-slaughter. In southern Africa, bTB is maintained in African buffalo populations in the Kruger ecosystem and in parts of Botswana's northern wildlife areas, with periodic spillback into cattle.

aetiology.summary: Infection is acquired almost entirely by inhaling aerosols from the respiratory tract of an infected animal in close confinement, or by ingesting the organism — from infected milk in calves, or from contaminated pasture where wildlife have shed the organism. Close contact and time are both required; bTB spreads slowly within a herd.
determinants: Prolonged close contact with a shedding animal, particularly indoors or at feed and water points
A wildlife maintenance reservoir with access to pasture or shared water
Introduction of an infected but undetected animal into a naive herd
Inhalation of droplet nuclei from coughing animals, especially in housed or crowded conditions
Consumption of unpasteurised milk from an infected cow by calves or people
risk_factors: Intensive or housed systems with poor ventilation
Herds in or adjacent to wildlife areas with buffalo or badger populations
Purchase of cattle without pre-movement testing
Large herd size, which increases the probability of within-herd transmission before detection
Absence of a routine tuberculin testing programme
aetiology.epidemiology: Within-herd prevalence rises slowly and can take years to become visible. Transmission is density-dependent, so small extensively managed herds may remain infected at very low prevalence for long periods. The organism is shed intermittently, which is why a single negative test does not establish freedom. The wildlife reservoir is the decisive factor in eradication: where it exists, cattle-only control cannot eliminate the disease.

pathophysiology.summary: Inhaled bacilli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but block phagosome-lysosome fusion and replicate intracellularly. A cell-mediated response walls the infection into granulomas, which contain the organism but do not eliminate it — producing the characteristic caseous, mineralised tubercles and the lifelong latency that makes the disease so difficult to detect and clear.

cascade.title: Inhalation and alveolar uptake
cascade.detail: Droplet nuclei of 1-5 micrometres reach the alveoli, where resident macrophages engulf the bacilli without killing them because the lipid-rich cell wall prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion.

cascade.title: Intracellular replication and lymph drainage
cascade.detail: Bacilli multiply within macrophages and are carried to the regional (usually bronchial or mediastinal) lymph node, where the first lesion typically forms — which is why the lymph node, not the lung, is often the most reliable post-mortem site to examine.

cascade.title: Granuloma formation
cascade.detail: A Th1 cell-mediated response recruits lymphocytes and macrophages, forming a granuloma with a caseous necrotic centre, a zone of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells, and a fibrous capsule. Caseous material mineralises over time, producing the gritty pale nodules seen at post-mortem.

cascade.title: Latency
cascade.detail: The granuloma contains but does not clear infection. Bacilli can remain viable for years, and reactivation follows immunosuppression, parturition or ageing — which is why disease can appear in an animal that was infected long before it entered the herd.

cascade.title: Progressive disease and shedding
cascade.detail: As granulomas enlarge and coalesce, caseous material erodes into bronchi and is coughed out, producing the infectious aerosol. This stage determines transmission and is the reason advanced lesions correlate with infectivity.

lesions: Caseous, yellow-white, mineralised granulomas in the lungs, most often in the caudal and dorsal regions
Enlarged, caseous bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes — frequently the earliest lesion
Lesions in the retropharyngeal and mesenteric lymph nodes after alimentary infection
Pearls — small tubercles on the pleura and peritoneum
Extensive caseation with cavitation in advanced pulmonary disease
Tuberculous mastitis, an important route of milk-borne human exposure
clinical_signs: Often no signs at all — subclinical infection is the norm in low-prevalence herds
Chronic, intermittent soft cough that worsens with exercise or cold air
Progressive weight loss and reduction in milk yield
Enlarged superficial lymph nodes, particularly the prescapular and retropharyngeal nodes
Dyspnoea in advanced pulmonary disease
Unthriftiness that fails to respond to feeding or anthelmintic treatment

antemortem: Single intradermal comparative cervical tuberculin (SICCT) test, measuring skin thickness change 72 hours after injection of avian and bovine tuberculin
Interferon-gamma release assay on whole blood, used alongside or instead of tuberculin testing
Clinical examination noting chronic cough, weight loss and lymphadenopathy
postmortem: Examine lungs and both bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes by systematic incision and palpation
Inspect the retropharyngeal, mesenteric and hepatic lymph nodes and the pleura for pearls
Record lesion distribution and severity, as this informs the herd-level risk assessment
laboratory: Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine-O staining of lesion material for acid-fast bacilli
Mycobacterial culture, which is slow (6-12 weeks) but remains the reference method
PCR or spoligotyping directly on lesions, which is faster and allows strain typing to trace sources
Histopathology showing caseating granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells
differentials: Actinomycosis or actinobacillosis — chronic but usually localised to soft tissue or bone, not caseating granulomas
Chronic pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma, Pasteurella or Dictyocaulus
Caseous lymphadenitis in small ruminants (Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis)
Mycobacterium avium complex, which causes cross-reaction in tuberculin testing and is a major cause of false positives
Neoplasia, particularly lymphoma in the lungs and lymph nodes

prevention: Test-and-slaughter with regular whole-herd screening, repeated until two consecutive clear tests
Pre-movement testing of all purchased cattle
Restrict cattle access to pasture and water shared with wildlife reservoirs
Pasteurise all milk intended for human consumption or calf feeding
Maintain closed herds where practical and record all introductions
control.vaccination: No licensed vaccine is in routine use for cattle. BCG has been investigated and provides partial, inconsistent protection that interferes with tuberculin testing. Vaccination is not part of any national control programme for cattle at present.
treatment: Treatment of cattle is not permitted in most jurisdictions and is not practised — it would create a persistent, undetectable reservoir and risk antimicrobial resistance
The control response is removal of reactors, not therapy
In exceptional circumstances and only under veterinary authority, individual treatment has been attempted, but it is not a herd strategy
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority; bTB is notifiable in most countries
Impose movement restrictions on the affected premises
Slaughter confirmed reactors and carry out post-mortem examination with culture or PCR confirmation
Test all in-contact animals and repeat at defined intervals to catch animals tested in the incubation window
Investigate wildlife contact as a potential maintenance source
Review and trace cattle movements for at least two years retrospectively
public_health: Human M. bovis infection is typically extrapulmonary and acquired from unpasteurised milk
Boiling or pasteurising milk destroys the organism
Occupational exposure occurs in abattoir workers and veterinarians handling lesions
Human-to-cattle transmission is possible and is a relevant consideration in tuberculosis-endemic human populations
control.notes: The diagnostic sensitivity of the tuberculin test is imperfect (roughly 80% at best), which is why programmes insist on repeated whole-herd testing rather than single rounds. A single negative herd test is not evidence of freedom.

diseases.prognosis: Individual animals with confirmed infection have a poor prognosis and are removed. At herd level, the prognosis depends entirely on whether a wildlife reservoir is involved: without one, eradication is achievable; with one, sustained control rather than elimination is the realistic objective.

diseases.name: Bovine viral diarrhoea

agents.name: Bovine viral diarrhoea virus
agents.notes: Genus Pestivirus, family Flaviviridae. A small, enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus. Two species are recognised — BVDV-1 and BVDV-2 — and two biotypes exist, cytopathic and non-cytopathic. The biotype distinction is central: only non-cytopathic virus establishes persistent infection in fetuses.
agents.reservoir: Persistently infected (PI) cattle, which shed virus continuously for life; sheep and other ruminants can carry related pestiviruses

hosts.notes: Cattle are the principal host. The most important host population is not the sick animal but the persistently infected calf — immunotolerant, virus-shedding and apparently healthy.

notifiable.note: Not a WOAH-listed disease, but subject to national control programmes in many countries and to voluntary or industry-led eradication schemes. Not a human pathogen.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide wherever cattle are intensively managed. Many European countries have eradication programmes in progress or completed. In southern Africa, BVD is present in cattle populations and is a recognised cause of reproductive wastage and ill-thrift, though systematic surveillance is limited.

aetiology.summary: The disease is perpetuated by a single mechanism: a non-cytopathic virus infects a fetus before its immune system can recognise the virus, and the calf is born immunotolerant and persistently infected. PI cattle shed virus for life and are the reservoir that sustains herd transmission, while the acute infections they cause are usually mild and transient.
determinants: Infection of a susceptible pregnant cow with a non-cytopathic biotype between roughly day 40 and day 125 of gestation
Immune competence of the fetus at the time of infection — before about day 150 the fetus cannot mount an effective response
Presence of a persistently infected animal shedding virus continuously
Direct contact between naive cattle and a PI animal, or contaminated equipment and vehicles
risk_factors: Introduction of untested pregnant females or untested calves into a herd
Common calving areas and shared equipment
Herds with no biosecurity or vaccination programme
Show, market and auction mixing of cattle from multiple sources
Failure to identify and remove PI animals, the single most important risk factor
aetiology.epidemiology: The epidemiology is dominated by the PI animal rather than by acute infection. A PI animal sheds enormous quantities of virus in all secretions and can infect every susceptible animal that comes into contact with it. Acute infections last a few days to weeks and are usually self-limiting. If a PI female survives to breeding age and calves, she will almost always produce another PI calf, creating a self-sustaining lineage within the herd. Control programmes work by identifying and removing PI animals, not by treating disease.

pathophysiology.summary: BVDV has two distinct lesions that depend on the age of the animal and the biotype involved. In a fetus infected before immune competence develops, the virus establishes lifelong persistent infection. In a PI animal later superinfected with a cytopathic biotype, immune-mediated destruction of virus-infected tissue produces mucosal disease, a uniformly fatal enteritis.

cascade.title: Fetal infection before immune competence
cascade.detail: A susceptible dam is infected with non-cytopathic virus between approximately day 40 and day 125 of gestation. The fetal immune system recognises the virus as self and does not mount a response.

cascade.title: Persistent infection and immunotolerance
cascade.detail: The calf is born with lifelong viraemia and sheds virus from all secretions. Because it is immunotolerant, it does not seroconvert — which is why antibody testing cannot detect PI animals and antigen testing is required.

cascade.title: Mucosal disease after superinfection
cascade.detail: If a PI animal is later infected with a cytopathic biotype — usually by mutation of the resident virus or by a heterologous strain — the immune system recognises the shared antigens and destroys virus-infected cells throughout the gut, skin and lymphoid tissue. This produces the classic mucosal disease syndrome.

cascade.title: Immunosuppression
cascade.detail: Even transient acute infection suppresses neutrophil and lymphocyte function, predisposing to secondary bacterial pneumonia and enteritis, which is often the clinically apparent disease rather than BVD itself.

cascade.title: Reproductive failure
cascade.detail: Depending on the gestational stage, infection causes early embryonic death, abortion, stillbirth, congenital defects (particularly cerebellar hypoplasia in calves infected in the second trimester) or the birth of a PI calf.

lesions: Oral erosions and ulcers, particularly on the hard palate, dental pad, tongue and gingiva
Erosions throughout the oesophagus, rumen and abomasum with haemorrhagic margins
Severe necrotising enteritis with Peyer's patch destruction
Interdigital erosion and coronitis causing lameness
Cerebellar hypoplasia and hydranencephaly in calves infected mid-gestation
Atrophy of the thymus and lymphoid depletion
Secondary bacterial bronchopneumonia
clinical_signs: Most acute infections are subclinical — a large proportion of infections are never noticed
Transient fever, leucopenia and mild diarrhoea in acutely infected animals
Ill-thrift, poor growth and immunosuppression in young stock
Abortion, stillbirth and early embryonic loss at the herd level
Calves born with cerebellar hypoplasia and ataxia
In mucosal disease: profuse watery diarrhoea, weight loss, oral erosion, lameness and death within weeks
Poor reproductive performance that is otherwise unexplained

antemortem: Antigen ELISA or PCR on whole blood or ear-notch tissue for the detection of PI animals
Serology (ELISA or neutralisation) for herd exposure — but serology cannot identify PI animals because they are seronegative
Bulk tank milk PCR or ELISA as a herd-level screening tool
postmortem: Examine the oral cavity, oesophagus, rumen and small intestine for erosions and Peyer's patch necrosis
Inspect the cerebellum in calves with neurological signs
Submit spleen, lymph node and intestinal tissue for virus detection
laboratory: Antigen ELISA on blood or ear notch — the primary PI detection test
RT-PCR on blood, tissue or milk
Virus isolation in cell culture for confirmation and biotype determination
Immunohistochemistry on ear-notch or skin biopsy, widely used in eradication programmes
Histopathology of mucosal and lymphoid lesions
differentials: Malignant catarrhal fever — similar mucosal lesions but with a different epidemiological context and no PI animals
Bovine papular stomatitis — mild and transient lesions
Foot-and-mouth disease and vesicular stomatitis — vesicles, not erosions
Salmonellosis and other enteritis-causing bacteria
Parasitic gastritis and coccidiosis
Mucosal disease is often mistaken for 'poisoning' when the oral lesions are prominent

prevention: Identify and remove all PI animals — this is the foundation of every successful control programme
Test all purchased cattle for PI status and quarantine before introduction
Test calves at birth with ear-notch antigen testing in herds with a known problem
Vaccinate where vaccines are available, primarily to reduce fetal infection and reproductive loss
Maintain biosecurity on equipment, vehicles and personnel, and avoid sharing bulls or semen from untested sources
control.vaccination: Inactivated and modified-live vaccines are available. Inactivated vaccines are safe in pregnancy but require a primary course followed by annual boosters. Modified-live vaccines give stronger and longer immunity but must not be given to pregnant animals or calves with unknown PI status. Vaccination reduces fetal infection and clinical disease but does not compensate for the presence of PI animals.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists
Supportive care for acute cases: fluids, electrolytes and nutritional support
Antibiotics only for secondary bacterial infection
Mucosal disease is uniformly fatal; euthanasia on welfare grounds is the appropriate response
PI animals should be culled rather than treated
outbreak: Identify and remove PI animals promptly — this is the intervention that stops transmission
Test all calves born in the following year, as PI calves may still be in utero at the time of the outbreak
Vaccinate susceptible breeding stock
Review biosecurity and the source of the introduced infection
Notify the veterinary authority where a national control programme exists
public_health: BVDV is not a human pathogen and has no public health significance
control.notes: The clinically important insight is that a healthy-looking calf can be the source of an entire herd's reproductive failure. Control is an administrative and testing problem, not a treatment problem.

diseases.prognosis: Acute infections usually resolve with full recovery and lifelong immunity. PI animals have a poor prognosis — many die before 2 years of age, and those that survive are a persistent source of infection. Mucosal disease is uniformly fatal.

WOAH — Manual of Diagnostic Tests and Vaccines for Terrestrial Animals

diseases.name: Brucellosis

agents.name: Brucella abortus
agents.notes: Gram-negative, facultatively intracellular coccobacillus with a preference for the gravid uterus and the mammary gland. B. abortus is the classical cattle pathogen; B. melitensis predominates in sheep and goats and is the most virulent in humans. B. suis affects pigs and B. ovis affects sheep. All are zoonotic.
agents.reservoir: Infected cattle, sheep and goats; wildlife including African buffalo and various ungulates; humans with occupational exposure

hosts.notes: Cattle are the main host for B. abortus; sheep and goats for B. melitensis and B. ovis; pigs for B. suis. Sexually mature animals are the most affected, and the gravid uterus is the principal target organ.

notifiable.note: Brucellosis is one of the most important occupational zoonoses of livestock handlers, veterinarians, abattoir workers and laboratory staff. Control in animals is a public health intervention as much as an agricultural one.

diseases.distribution: Widespread in Africa, the Middle East, central Asia and Latin America, particularly where small ruminants are managed extensively. Many high-income countries have eradicated B. abortus from cattle through test-and-slaughter. In southern Africa, B. abortus remains present in cattle populations across Botswana, Zimbabwe and South Africa.

aetiology.summary: Infection is acquired by ingesting the organism, most importantly when a susceptible animal licks a placenta, fetal fluids or aborted material left on pasture. The organism penetrates the oral and pharyngeal mucosa, then travels to regional lymph nodes and eventually to the gravid uterus or mammary gland, where its affinity for erythritol-rich tissue drives late-term abortion.
determinants: Exposure of susceptible animals to placentae, fetal fluids, aborted fetuses or vaginal discharge
Ingestion of the organism from contaminated pasture, water or feed
Entry through mucous membranes, conjunctiva or abraded skin
In utero the bacterium binds erythritol, a sugar abundant in the fetal cotyledons of cattle, sheep and pigs, which explains the uterine tropism
Non-pregnant animals are infected but do not show uterine disease until they are bred and become pregnant
risk_factors: Unassisted calvings and lambings where people and other animals contact placentae
Herds with no testing or vaccination programme
Introduction of untested animals, particularly females over 6 months of age
Shared grazing and water with infected neighbouring herds or wildlife
Consumption of raw milk and unpasteurised dairy products
aetiology.epidemiology: Within-herd spread is driven by the explosive contamination of the environment at abortion or parturition — a single aborting cow can shed enormous numbers of organisms. The incubation period to abortion is typically 2-5 months. Infected animals remain infected for life in most cases, and shedding recurs at each subsequent calving or lambing, which is why control requires repeated testing rather than a single round.

pathophysiology.summary: Brucella enters through mucosa, survives inside macrophages by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion, and disseminates to the reticuloendothelial system and the gravid uterus. In the placenta, the erythritol-rich fetal cotyledons support massive bacterial multiplication, and the resulting necrotising placentitis destroys the fetal-maternal interface and causes late-term abortion.

cascade.title: Mucosal invasion
cascade.detail: The organism enters through the oral, pharyngeal or conjunctival mucosa, or through abraded skin, and is taken up by local macrophages and dendritic cells.

cascade.title: Intracellular survival and dissemination
cascade.detail: Brucella inhibits phagosome-lysosome fusion and survives and replicates inside macrophages, draining to regional lymph nodes and then spreading haematogenously to the spleen, liver, mammary gland and reproductive tract.

cascade.title: Uterine colonisation
cascade.detail: In pregnancy, the fetal trophoblast of ruminants is rich in erythritol, which the bacterium uses to support very rapid growth. The organism colonises the cotyledons and the chorion, producing a severe necrotising placentitis with purulent, brownish exudate.

cascade.title: Fetal death and abortion
cascade.detail: Destruction of the placentomes deprives the fetus of oxygen and nutrients, and bacterial invasion of the fetal tissues causes fetal death, usually in the last third of gestation. Abortion, stillbirth or birth of weak calves follows.

cascade.title: Chronic persistence and intermittent shedding
cascade.detail: The organism persists in the mammary gland, supramammary lymph nodes and reproductive tract. Shedding in milk and vaginal discharge continues intermittently, especially around subsequent parturitions, which sustains herd transmission even after the clinical abortion has been forgotten.

lesions: Necrotising placentitis with thickened, leathery cotyledons and yellowish-brown exudate
Aborted fetus with subcutaneous oedema, serosanguinous fluid in the cavities and enlarged liver and spleen
Enlarged, caseous or granulomatous supramammary and regional lymph nodes
Granulomatous mastitis
Orchitis and epididymitis in bulls, sometimes progressing to abscessation and testicular atrophy
Hygromas and bursitis in some chronically infected animals
Metritis and retained placenta in animals that abort late
clinical_signs: Late-term abortion (usually the last trimester), often without any preceding sign of illness
Retained placenta and metritis after an abortion or calving
Weak, unthrifty calves born alive, with a high neonatal mortality
Reduced milk yield and mastitis, sometimes in an animal that has not aborted at all
Orchitis and tail-swelling in bulls, with reduced fertility
Infertility and prolonged calving interval at herd level
Arthritis, bursitis and hygromas in chronic cases

antemortem: Blood sampling for serology is the mainstay: Rose Bengal plate test as a screen, with ELISA or complement fixation as confirmation
Culture of the placenta, vaginal discharge or milk isolates the organism but is not a routine field test
Bulk tank milk PCR is a useful herd-level surveillance tool
postmortem: Examine the aborted fetus and placenta, noting cotyledon appearance and exudate
Inspect the supramammary and iliac lymph nodes for enlargement and caseation
Check the testes and epididymides in bulls for orchitis
laboratory: Rose Bengal plate agglutination test for rapid screening
Indirect or competitive ELISA for confirmation and for distinguishing vaccine antibody from infection antibody
Complement fixation test — historically the reference method
Bacterial culture from placenta, fetal stomach contents, milk or lymph nodes, requiring prolonged incubation and strict biosafety
PCR for species-level identification, useful for differentiating vaccine and field strains
differentials: Campylobacteriosis and trichomonosis — also cause abortion but usually early in gestation, with a fetal liver lesion in campylobacter
Leptospirosis — abortion with haemoglobinuria, jaundice and often at any stage of gestation
Neosporosis — specifically causes abortion in the same late-gestation window in cattle
Salmonellosis — abortion with systemic illness and diarrhoea
Vitamin A deficiency and other nutritional causes of weak calves
Q fever and chlamydiosis — abortifacients but with different serology

prevention: Test all incoming animals, particularly breeding females over 6 months old, and isolate them for a period with retesting
Vaccinate replacement heifers with a reduced-dose or killed vaccine under a defined scheme
Remove placentae and aborted tissue immediately and dispose of them properly; do not allow dogs or scavengers access
Pasteurise milk or boil it before consumption
Maintain herd biosecurity and avoid shared pasture and water with untested herds
control.vaccination: Whole-cell vaccines — S19 in cattle and Rev-1 in sheep and goats — give substantial protection but are rough on their own design: they are infectious to humans, cause abortion if given to pregnant animals, and produce antibody that confounds diagnostic serology. S19 is usually given to heifers at 4-8 months of age. Rough-strain and glycoprotein-based subunit vaccines reduce the diagnostic interference problem. Vaccination protects the herd; it does not eliminate the organism from an already infected one.
treatment: Antibiotic treatment of cattle is not recommended — it does not clear the organism, masks infection and creates a carrier that is serologically negative
In sheep and goats some clinicians use long courses of tetracycline or combination therapy, with indifferent results
In humans, prolonged doxycycline combined with rifampicin or streptomycin is the standard regimen, and relapse is common without completing it
The control response in herds is removal of reactors, not therapy
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority — brucellosis is notifiable in most jurisdictions
Isolate the aborting animal and quarantine the premises
Submit the aborted fetus and placenta for laboratory confirmation
Test the whole herd and remove reactors, or adopt a vaccination-and-retest strategy under official direction
Wear gloves and protective clothing when handling aborting animals, and disinfect the area thoroughly
Trace the source of infection — purchase history, neighbouring herds or wildlife contact
public_health: Human brucellosis presents as undulant fever, night sweats, arthralgia and fatigue, and is easily mistaken for influenza or malaria
The most common exposure routes are unpasteurised milk, fresh cheese and direct contact with aborting animals or placentae
Veterinarians, abattoir workers, shepherds and laboratory staff are the main occupational groups
B. melitensis from sheep and goats is the most virulent human pathogen of this genus and is a serious concern in the small-ruminant sector
Suspected human cases require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy under medical direction
control.notes: The erythritol/uterine-tropism point is the key to understanding both the disease and the control strategy. Non-pregnant animals are infected but silent, and the abortion is the moment the herd is contaminated.

diseases.prognosis: Infected animals remain infected for life in most cases and are culled. At herd level, control is achievable with sustained vaccination and testing, but eradication from a heavily infected herd is a multi-year project.

diseases.name: Dermatophilosis

agents.name: Dermatophilus congolensis
agents.notes: A Gram-positive, filamentous, branching actinomycete that forms motile zoospores. The zoospores are the infective stage and require a moist environment and skin compromise to establish infection. The organism is not invasive — it colonises the epidermis.
agents.reservoir: Carrier animals with subclinical infection; zoospores survive in scabs and on fomites

hosts.notes: Cattle are the most economically affected species, particularly in humid tropical environments. Sheep are commonly affected on the back and withers after shearing. The disease is a major cause of hide damage in Africa.

notifiable.note: Not WOAH-listed. Human infection occurs occasionally in people handling infected animals, presenting as localised pustular dermatitis.

diseases.distribution: Widespread in the humid tropics and subtropics, including much of sub-Saharan Africa. In southern Africa, it is a significant cattle disease in higher-rainfall areas and after prolonged wet weather — the local name 'Senkobo' refers to a district in Zambia.

aetiology.summary: Dermatophilosis requires a wet environment and broken skin. Zoospores cannot penetrate intact, dry epidermis; a period of prolonged moisture macerates the stratum corneum and allows the flagellated zoospores to invade. The disease is therefore an environmental and management disease as much as an infectious one.
determinants: Prolonged skin wetness from rain, high humidity or flooding
Breakdown of the epidermal barrier by biting flies, ticks, thorns or trauma
Contact with carrier animals or contaminated fomites
Temperature and humidity high enough to support zoospore activity
risk_factors: Rainy season and humid climates
Heavy tick or biting-fly burdens causing skin damage
Overstocking and congregation, increasing contact and contamination
Thick coats and long hair retaining moisture
Shearing injuries and castration or tagging wounds
Immunosuppression, poor nutrition and concurrent disease, which increase severity
aetiology.epidemiology: The disease is endemic in humid, high-rainfall zones and epidemic in dry areas during exceptional rainfall. Within a herd, prevalence can reach high levels during the wet season and fall dramatically in the dry season. Carriers maintain the organism between seasons in scabs and in subclinical skin lesions. The morbidity is high but mortality is low.

pathophysiology.summary: Zoospores invade the macerated epidermis and germinate into branching filaments that spread along the stratum spinosum and into the follicular infundibula. The resulting neutrophilic inflammation produces an exudate that hardens into a scab, beneath which the epidermis is eroded and the hair follicle is damaged, leading to hair loss and hide damage.

cascade.title: Skin maceration
cascade.detail: Prolonged wetness softens and swells the stratum corneum, and mechanical damage from flies or ticks breaches the surface, creating the conditions zoospores need.

cascade.title: Zoospore invasion
cascade.detail: Flagellated zoospores migrate into the damaged epidermis and germinate into branching, filamentous mycelial forms that extend along the epidermal layer.

cascade.title: Neutrophilic exudation
cascade.detail: Filament growth triggers an intense neutrophilic response, producing a serous to purulent exudate that lifts the outer epidermis and dries into a characteristic scab.

cascade.title: Follicular damage and hair loss
cascade.detail: Extension of filaments into the follicular infundibulum damages the follicle shaft. The hair becomes matted and lifts with the scab, producing patchy alopecia and the 'paintbrush' consistency of the lesions.

cascade.title: Scarring and hide degradation
cascade.detail: After healing, the damaged follicles produce fibrotic scar tissue and the hide is permanently degraded, which is the principal economic loss in cattle and sheep.

lesions: Matted, paintbrush-like tufts of hair that lift on gentle traction
Thick, yellowish to brown crusts and scabs, often coalescing into irregular plaques
Eroded, moist epidermis beneath removed scabs
Distribution typically on the back, rump, flanks, ears and udder
In severe cases, generalized exfoliative dermatitis with weight loss
Hide damage with permanent scar and grain defects after healing
clinical_signs: Patchy hair loss with scab formation on the dorsum and flanks
Paintbrush tufts of hair that come away with the underlying scab
Itching and rubbing in some animals
Affected animals may be otherwise healthy; severe cases show poor growth and weight loss
Lambs and calves can be more severely affected, with extensive lesions

antemortem: Clinical examination: characteristic paintbrush scabs on the back in a humid, wet-season context
Remove a scab and examine the moist underside — the diagnosis is usually apparent grossly
Skin scraping or impression smear of the underside of a scab for cytology
postmortem: Skin lesions are usually inspected on the live animal; no systemic lesion is present
In hides, the diagnosis can be confirmed from the interfollicular epidermis in the abattoir
laboratory: Gram stain of smears from the underside of a scab, showing branching, filamentous Gram-positive structures
Culture on blood agar under aerobic conditions, producing small, adherent, greyish colonies
Histopathology of a skin biopsy showing filamentous bacteria in the epidermis with neutrophilic exudation
PCR for species confirmation, though not routinely required
differentials: Ringworm (Trichophyton, Microsporum) — circular lesions with raised margins and hair loss, different cytology
Mange (Sarcoptes, Psoroptes, Chorioptes) — intense pruritus with typical distribution, mites visible on scraping
Photosensitisation — dermatitis on unpigmented skin, no scabs of this type
Zinc deficiency — parakeratosis and crusting on the face, legs and teats
Bovine papular stomatitis — oral and muzzle lesions rather than body scabs
Fly and tick irritation without infection — superficial dermatitis that resolves

prevention: Provide shelter or dry areas during prolonged rain where feasible
Control ticks and biting flies to prevent skin damage
Avoid overcrowding, which increases contact and moisture retention
Maintain good nutrition and manage immunosuppressive disease
Treat clinically affected animals promptly to reduce the environmental load
control.vaccination: Vaccines have been developed from whole-cell preparations and used in some countries with variable success. Vaccination is not widely available or routinely used in southern Africa, and control relies on husbandry and treatment.
treatment: Long-acting oxytetracycline is the most practical systemic treatment in extensive cattle herds
Penicillin and streptomycin combination is effective but requires repeated handling
Topical treatment with iodine or chlorhexidine is useful for individual animals but not practical at herd scale
Zinc supplementation may improve recovery in deficient herds
Treated animals should be separated to reduce environmental contamination and re-exposure
outbreak: Treat affected animals and isolate them where practical
Reduce stocking density and improve drainage in holding areas
Step up tick and fly control
Review the timing of shearing and handling to avoid skin damage during wet periods
Notify the veterinary authority only where the disease has trade or hide-quality implications
public_health: Human infection is uncommon and presents as a localised, pustular skin lesion at the site of contact
Wear gloves when handling infected animals or hides
The infection responds to appropriate antibiotic treatment and is not a significant public health threat
control.notes: This is the clearest example in this reference of a disease where environment and skin integrity matter more than the pathogen. Removing the wetness removes the disease.

diseases.prognosis: Good for individual animals with treatment and improved conditions. The economic loss lies in hide damage and reduced growth rather than mortality. Relapse is common if the wet environment persists.
