diseases.name: Digital dermatitis

agents.name: Treponema species
agents.notes: A group of spirochaetes — Treponema medium, T. phagedenis and related phylotypes — consistently found in the lesions. A specific causative single species has not been identified, and the disease is regarded as a polymicrobial infection in which treponemes are the dominant and probably essential component. The organisms are obligate anaerobes and are found deep within the lesion, not on the surface.
agents.reservoir: Infected cattle hooves and the environment — the organism survives in slurry and on hoof trimmers' equipment

hosts.notes: Dairy cattle are the principal species affected, particularly confined housed animals. The disease is uncommon in cattle that are on dry pasture year-round.

notifiable.note: A production and welfare disease with no public health significance. It is one of the most common causes of lameness in dairy herds worldwide, and its spread has been described as explosive since the 1970s.

diseases.distribution: Now present in most dairy-producing countries. It spread rapidly through Europe and North America in the late 20th century. In southern Africa, digital dermatitis is recognised in intensive dairy herds and is becoming an increasing problem as herds intensify and move to confined housing.

aetiology.summary: Digital dermatitis is an infectious disease of the heel skin driven by treponemes, but its expression is inseparable from the environment. The organisms require damaged, moist skin and anaerobic conditions in the interdigital space, which are created by slurry, concrete flooring and prolonged standing.
determinants: Exposure to treponeme-infected animals or contaminated equipment
Maceration of the skin from slurry, urine and wet bedding
Damage to the skin barrier from abrasive flooring and hoof trauma
Anaerobic conditions in the interdigital space, which the treponemes require
The introduction of an infected animal into a naive herd
risk_factors: Wet, slurry-covered flooring and poor drainage
Concrete and abrasive flooring
High stocking density and prolonged standing
Introduced cattle, particularly purchased animals infected subclinically
Hoof trimmers moving between farms without disinfecting equipment
Poor foot hygiene and no foot bathing programme
Calving pens shared by many animals
aetiology.epidemiology: Digital dermatitis is highly contagious and spreads through a herd by direct contact and contaminated equipment. In affected herds, prevalence can be high and it is a major cause of lameness, reduced milk yield, reduced fertility and culling. The disease often affects the hind feet first. Trimmers' knives and hoof stands are a well-documented transmission route between farms.

pathophysiology.summary: Treponemes gain access through macerated, damaged skin of the heel or interdigital cleft and proliferate in the anaerobic environment. They invade the deeper layers of the epidermis and dermis and trigger an intense proliferative inflammatory response that produces the characteristic strawberry-like papillomatous lesion, with pain on weight-bearing.

cascade.title: Skin maceration and barrier breach
cascade.detail: Prolonged exposure to slurry and urine macerates the stratum corneum of the heel, while abrasive flooring removes the protective superficial layers. This creates the entry point and the anaerobic environment the treponemes require.

cascade.title: Treponeme colonisation
cascade.detail: Treponemes colonise the damaged epidermis and penetrate into the deeper layers, where they are protected from the surface environment and from superficial antiseptics.

cascade.title: Proliferative inflammatory response
cascade.detail: The immune response to the infection produces a marked epidermal hyperplasia with elongated rete pegs, superficial necrosis and an inflammatory infiltrate. The resulting lesion is raised, red and granular — the 'strawberry' appearance.

cascade.title: Pain and altered locomotion
cascade.detail: The lesion is painful and the animal shifts weight to the opposite limb, which increases the load on the contralateral hoof and predisposes to sole ulceration and further lameness. The altered gait reduces feed intake and milk yield.

cascade.title: Chronicity and spread
cascade.detail: Untreated lesions become chronic, with deeper invasion and the potential for extensive tissue destruction. The animal remains a source of infection for the herd, and the cycle continues through the environment.

lesions: Circumscribed, raised, red and granular lesion on the heel or in the interdigital cleft
Strawberry-like papillomatous surface, often with a grey or white hairy fringe
Thickened, hyperkeratotic skin at the margins
Seven distinct M-stages described: early, acute, chronic and regressive forms
Possible extension to the interdigital space and the coronary band in chronic cases
clinical_signs: Lameness, often subtle at first and most evident at the walk
Lifting or shaking of the affected limb
Reluctance to bear weight on the affected hoof
Visible lesion on the heel when the hoof is lifted
Reduced feed intake and milk yield
Reduced fertility due to the association of lameness with poor reproductive performance
Heel bulb swelling and foul odour in chronic cases

antemortem: Careful inspection of the heel and interdigital cleft after cleaning the foot — the lesion is usually obvious once visible
Use a hoof stand and adequate lighting; the lesion is often missed without proper examination
Lameness scoring to identify affected animals that do not show obvious signs at a distance
postmortem: Examine the hooves for the characteristic lesions
Note any concurrent hoof lesions such as sole ulcer or white line disease
laboratory: Diagnosis is clinical in the field
Histopathology of biopsy showing the characteristic treponeme-associated proliferative dermatitis
PCR for Treponema phylotypes, used in research and in cases of diagnostic uncertainty
Bacteriology is of limited clinical value because of the polymicrobial nature of the lesion
differentials: Foot rot (interdigital phlegmon) — acute, painful swelling of the whole foot with fever, not a chronic proliferative lesion
Heel horn erosion (slurry heel) — a consequence of the same environment but without the treponeme lesion
Sole ulcer and white line disease — lesions of the sole rather than the heel
Laminitis — generalised lameness with different hoof lesions
Foreign body in the interdigital space

prevention: Keep flooring and lying areas dry and clean, with good drainage
Use foot baths with an appropriate disinfectant (copper sulphate, formalin or a proprietary product) at herd level
Maintain good foot hygiene and regularly clean the hooves
Quarantine and examine incoming cattle before introduction
Require hoof trimmers to disinfect equipment between farms
Reduce stocking density and minimise time standing on concrete
Lameness score the herd regularly to detect the problem early
control.vaccination: No commercial vaccine is available. Research into treponeme vaccines is ongoing, but control currently relies on hygiene, foot bathing and individual treatment.
treatment: Individual treatment: clean the lesion, apply a topical antibiotic (typically a tetracycline or lincomycin spray) and bandage
Systemic antibiotics (penicillin or a tetracycline) for severe or non-responsive cases, under veterinary direction
Hoof trimming to remove under-run horn and relieve pressure
Foot bathing with a suitable disinfectant for herd-level control
Repeat treatment may be required, as the lesion is often chronic
Note that antibiotic use should be minimised where possible and always under veterinary supervision
outbreak: Identify and treat affected animals promptly
Implement herd-level foot bathing
Review housing and flooring to reduce slurry exposure
Examine all newly introduced cattle and quarantine them
Review hoof trimming practice and equipment hygiene
Consider the whole-herd lameness picture rather than treating individual cases in isolation
public_health: Digital dermatitis has no human health significance
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any antibiotics used, particularly topical products
Responsible antibiotic use matters for antimicrobial stewardship even though the public health risk here is indirect
control.notes: Digital dermatitis is a disease where the environment is the real pathogen. Treating individual feet without changing the slurry, flooring and foot-bathing regime produces temporary relief followed by a high recurrence rate.

diseases.prognosis: Good for individual lesions with treatment, but recurrence is common unless the environmental conditions are corrected. At herd level, control is achievable with consistent hygiene and foot bathing, but eradication from a housed herd is difficult.

diseases.name: Foot rot

agents.name: Fusobacterium necrophorum
agents.notes: A Gram-negative, anaerobic rod and a normal inhabitant of the rumen and faeces. It is an opportunistic pathogen that requires a damaged interdigital skin to establish infection, and it is the primary cause of the acute necrotising lesion.

agents.name: Porphyromonas levii
agents.notes: An anaerobic bacterium that frequently co-infects with F. necrophorum and is associated with the severity of the lesion. The combination of the two organisms is more pathogenic than either alone.

hosts.notes: Foot rot in cattle (interdigital phlegmon) is a disease of all ages but most common in adults. Sheep foot rot is caused by a different combination of bacteria, principally Dichelobacter nodosus and Fusobacterium necrophorum, and is a distinct disease with a different epidemiology.

notifiable.note: A production and welfare disease with no public health significance, but one of the most economically important causes of lameness in cattle.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide. It is particularly associated with wet, muddy conditions and with intensive cattle production. In southern Africa, foot rot is common in feedlots and dairy herds during wet periods and on muddy ground.

aetiology.summary: Foot rot is an opportunistic infection that requires a skin breach. Fusobacterium necrophorum is present in faeces and slurry everywhere, but it cannot penetrate intact skin. Maceration of the interdigital skin from wet, muddy conditions, or physical damage from footing, allows the bacteria to invade and produce the acute necrotising infection.
determinants: Maceration and damage of the interdigital skin from wet, muddy conditions or abrasive flooring
Exposure to faecal contamination, the source of F. necrophorum
Anaerobic conditions in the interdigital space, required by the bacteria
Physical trauma from stones, footing or a foreign body in the interdigital space
risk_factors: Wet, muddy pens and holding yards
Slurry and high faecal contamination in the hoof environment
Abrasive or uneven flooring
Warm, humid conditions that maintain moisture in the interdigital space
Overcrowding and standing in wet conditions for long periods
Introduction of infected animals into a clean herd
aetiology.epidemiology: Foot rot is sporadic in most herds but can reach epidemic proportions in wet conditions, particularly in feedlots during rainy periods. It is more common in cattle on wet ground than in those on dry pasture. Sheep foot rot, by contrast, is a true contagious disease maintained in the flock by carrier animals, which is why eradication is possible in sheep but not in cattle.

pathophysiology.summary: Once the bacteria enter the damaged interdigital skin, they multiply in the anaerobic environment and produce a rapidly spreading necrotising infection of the subcutaneous tissue. The resulting swelling and necrosis produce acute pain and lameness, and the endotoxaemia from the necrotic tissue contributes to the systemic signs.

cascade.title: Skin breach
cascade.detail: The intact interdigital skin is an effective barrier. Maceration from prolonged moisture, or a physical abrasion, breaches the stratum corneum and allows faecal bacteria to access the deeper tissue.

cascade.title: Bacterial invasion and multiplication
cascade.detail: Fusobacterium necrophorum and Porphyromonas levii colonise the damaged tissue and multiply rapidly in the anaerobic environment of the interdigital space, protected from the circulation and from surface antiseptics.

cascade.title: Necrotising inflammation and swelling
cascade.detail: The bacteria produce toxins, including leukotoxin, that destroy neutrophils and local tissue. The resulting necrotising cellulitis produces marked swelling of the interdigital space, with the two digits forced apart and the skin of the heel and pastern distended.

cascade.title: Pain and lameness
cascade.detail: The swelling and tissue tension are intensely painful, producing acute lameness in which the animal bears little or no weight on the affected limb. The pain may be severe enough to produce a marked systemic response.

cascade.title: Systemic effects and complications
cascade.detail: Endotoxins from the necrotic tissue produce fever and reduced feed intake. In severe cases, the infection can extend to the deeper structures of the foot, causing septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and tendon necrosis, which are far more difficult to treat and often require amputation or culling.

lesions: Swelling of the interdigital space with separation of the two digits
Necrotic, greyish-white ulceration of the interdigital skin
Foul-smelling necrotic tissue in the interdigital cleft
Swelling extending to the heel and pastern
Possible extension to deeper structures, with tendon necrosis and septic arthritis in advanced cases
Sloughing of the interdigital skin in severe cases
clinical_signs: Sudden onset of severe lameness, often in one limb
Swelling of the affected foot, particularly the interdigital space
Fever (40-41 degrees Celsius)
Reluctance to bear weight and a rapid, painful gait
Reduced feed intake and milk yield
Foul odour from the affected foot
Recumbency in severe cases
Welfare and production losses even in animals that recover

antemortem: Clinical examination of the foot: acute interdigital swelling with necrosis and a foul smell is diagnostic
Clean the foot to visualise the lesion and exclude a foreign body
Differentiate from digital dermatitis, which is a chronic proliferative heel lesion rather than an acute necrotising infection
postmortem: Examine the affected foot for interdigital necrosis and deeper extension
Note the presence of a foreign body if one is present
laboratory: Diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory test is required in the field
Culture of F. necrophorum from the lesion requires anaerobic conditions and is not routinely performed
Histopathology of the affected interdigital tissue may be used in research or in atypical cases
differentials: Digital dermatitis — chronic proliferative heel lesion, no acute systemic signs
Interdigital hyperplasia — a chronic fibrotic swelling between the digits, not painful or acute
Foot abscess or sole penetration — a different lesion site, usually without interdigital swelling
Fracture of the pedal bone
Snakebite or insect sting on the foot
Septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint
Laminitis — generalised rather than a single acute foot

prevention: Keep grazing and housing areas dry and well drained
Minimise slurry and standing water in pens and holding yards
Use foot baths with an appropriate disinfectant in high-risk periods
Maintain good hoof health and regular trimming
Reduce crowding and long periods of standing
Isolate and treat affected animals promptly to limit spread
control.vaccination: A vaccine against F. necrophorum has been developed and is used in some countries, and may reduce the incidence and severity of foot rot. It is not widely used in southern Africa, and control largely relies on management and hygiene.
treatment: Systemic antibiotics are the mainstay: penicillin, oxytetracycline or a cephalosporin
Trim and clean the foot, and remove any foreign body or devitalised tissue
Apply a topical antiseptic or antibiotic dressing after cleaning
NSAIDs for pain relief and to reduce the inflammatory response
Foot bandaging may be useful in severe cases
Animals that do not respond within a few days, or that develop deeper infection, may require surgical intervention or culling
outbreak: Identify and treat affected animals promptly
Review the environment — wetness and faecal contamination are the usual source
Introduce foot bathing in the affected group
Provide dry lying areas and improve drainage
Check for a foreign body problem, such as sharp stones on a trackway
public_health: Foot rot has no human health significance
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any antibiotics used
Antibiotic stewardship is important even where the direct public health risk is low
control.notes: The distinction from digital dermatitis is practical and important: foot rot is an acute, systemic, treatable infection, whereas digital dermatitis is a chronic, environment-driven, recurrent lesion.

diseases.prognosis: Good if treated early — most cases respond within days. Guarded if the infection has extended to deeper structures, which frequently requires culling. Recurrence is likely if the wet, contaminated environment persists.

diseases.name: Foot-and-mouth disease

agents.name: Foot-and-mouth disease virus
agents.notes: Genus Aphthovirus, family Picornaviridae. Seven serotypes — O, A, C, SAT 1, SAT 2, SAT 3 and Asia 1 — with no cross-protection between them. Southern Africa's SAT serotypes are maintained in African buffalo.
agents.vector: Not arthropod-borne, but mechanically spread on vehicles, clothing, feed and by wind-borne aerosol over land
agents.reservoir: African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) in endemic regions; persistently infected carrier cattle and sheep

hosts.notes: Cattle and pigs show the most dramatic signs; sheep and goats are often mildly affected and are the classic source of missed diagnosis. Camelids are susceptible.

notifiable.note: One of the most economically damaging notifiable diseases. In Botswana and neighbouring states, a single case closes export markets for beef, which is the dominant agricultural export.

diseases.distribution: Endemic across much of Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Southern Africa is divided into zones: infected buffalo areas, protection zones and FMD-free zones that underpin beef export. Botswana has repeatedly lost export status following outbreaks in the northern buffalo-contact areas.

aetiology.summary: Infection requires direct or close indirect contact with virus shed in respiratory and salivary secretions from an infected animal. The virus is among the most infectious known: tiny doses establish disease, and wind-borne plumes can carry infection several kilometres over land.
determinants: Contact between susceptible livestock and infected animals or contaminated fomites
Viral serotype — immunity to one serotype does not protect against another
Introduction of infected animals, semen or animal products from an endemic zone
Shared water points and kraals where animals from different groups mix
Movement of people, vehicles and equipment between premises without disinfection
risk_factors: Livestock production adjacent to a buffalo area or a game fence
Uncontrolled livestock movement and informal trade across borders
Market and auction gatherings where animals from many sources mix
Sheep and goats, which shed virus while showing minimal signs and mask spread
Wind and low humidity favouring aerosol transmission
aetiology.epidemiology: Morbidity can approach 100% in a naive herd; mortality in adult cattle is usually low (1-5%) but rises sharply in calves and lambs, where it can exceed 50% because of myocardial involvement. Transmission is respiratory and direct-contact driven, with an incubation period of 2-14 days. The maintenance strategy in Africa is the buffalo-carrier system: buffalo remain subclinically infected and periodically infect cattle that contact them.

pathophysiology.summary: The virus replicates first in the pharyngeal epithelium and regional lymph nodes, then produces a brief viraemia that seeds epithelial tissues with high mitotic activity, especially the tongue, dental pad, coronary band and teat. Vesicle formation and subsequent erosion cause the pain that stops eating and walking, while viral replication in the myocardium of young animals is the mechanism of sudden death.

cascade.title: Primary replication
cascade.detail: After inhalation or ingestion, virus replicates in the pharyngeal epithelium and drains to regional lymph nodes, producing a 24-72 hour viraemia before any clinical sign appears.

cascade.title: Epithelial localisation
cascade.detail: Viraemic virus targets stratified squamous epithelium at sites of mechanical stress and high turnover — the tongue, dental pad, ruminal pillars, coronary band and teat skin.

cascade.title: Ballooning degeneration and vesicle formation
cascade.detail: Cytopathic viral replication causes intracellular oedema and cell rounding, which coalesce into a fluid-filled vesicle between the epithelial layers. The vesicle ruptures within 24-48 hours, leaving a raw, painful erosion.

cascade.title: Pain-driven failure of intake
cascade.detail: Oral erosions make eating painful, producing drooling, anorexia and rapid condition loss. Coronary band lesions cause lameness and reluctance to walk, which compounds the reduction in feed intake.

cascade.title: Myocardial involvement in the young
cascade.detail: Virus replicates in cardiac muscle in calves, piglets and lambs, causing acute myocarditis and arrhythmia. This is the mechanism of the sudden deaths that characterise FMD in young stock, and it can occur with no oral lesions.

lesions: Vesicles and subsequent erosions on the tongue, dental pad, gums and palate
Vesicles at the coronary band and interdigital skin, often progressing to complete sloughing of the hoof horn
Vesicles on teats, leading to mastitis and loss of milk yield
Pale, streaked 'tiger heart' myocarditis in young animals from focal necrosis
Rumenal pillar erosions
Secondary bacterial infection of eroded areas with purulent exudate
clinical_signs: Profuse, ropy salivation and lip-smacking
Fever of 40-41 degrees Celsius at the onset, often resolving before lesions are seen
Lameness, reluctance to move and shifting weight between feet
Oral vesicles and ragged erosions after they rupture
Sudden death in calves, lambs and piglets
Sharp drop in milk yield and abortion in some cases

antemortem: Inspect the mouth, feet and teats of every animal in a suspect group — sheep require close examination of the dental pad and coronary band
Collect epithelium from a ruptured vesicle or vesicular fluid in buffered glycerol saline for transport
Oropharyngeal swab and serum from a probang sample in recovering animals
postmortem: Look for oral and coronary band erosions and examine the myocardium of young animals for streaking
Rumenal pillar erosions are a useful confirmatory finding
laboratory: Virus isolation in cell culture, with neutralisation for serotype identification
RT-PCR targeting conserved regions, followed by VP1 sequencing for serotype and strain
Antigen ELISA for rapid field confirmation
Serology: virus neutralisation or ELISA for antibody, noting that vaccinal and infection-derived antibody are indistinguishable
differentials: Vesicular stomatitis — indistinguishable clinically, and zoonotic
Swine vesicular disease — pigs only
Bluetongue — oral erosions possible, but with oedema and nasal discharge
Bovine papular stomatitis and pseudocowpox — milder, no lameness typically
Chemical or caustic burns of the mouth
Peste des petits ruminants in small ruminants — oral necrosis with pneumonia and diarrhoea

prevention: Maintain and enforce movement controls between infected, protection and free zones
Vaccinate strategically with serotype-matched vaccine appropriate to the zone
Quarantine and test incoming animals, particularly from endemic areas
Disinfect vehicles, equipment and footwear at farm and boundary entry points
Maintain game fencing and buffer zones between buffalo areas and livestock
control.vaccination: Inactivated, serotype-specific vaccines are used in endemic and buffer zones. Protection is short-lived — revaccination every 4-6 months is common in high-risk areas — and vaccination does not prevent infection or carriage, only clinical disease. Inactivated vaccines also complicate serological surveillance, because vaccine and infection antibody cannot be distinguished.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists
Supportive care: soft palatable feed, water, and analgesia
Treat secondary bacterial infection of oral and foot lesions with appropriate antibiotics
Wound care for sloughed hooves; affected animals may need weeks of protection from hard ground
Milk affected cows separately and manage mastitis
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority immediately — this is a mandatory report in every FMD-free jurisdiction
Impose immediate standstill on the premises and restrict all animal and vehicle movement
Ring vaccination around the index premises where policy permits
Stamping out (culling of affected and in-contact animals) where the policy objective is regaining free status quickly
Trace all movements from the premises for 21 days before detection
Establish a surveillance zone with intensive clinical inspection and sampling
public_health: FMD is not a human health threat and is not transmitted through properly cooked meat or pasteurised milk
Human infections reported historically were mild and are not a management consideration
The public health consequence is economic and nutritional, through loss of livestock income and protein supply
control.notes: FMD is the archetype of a disease where the control decision is economic rather than clinical. Vaccination controls disease; only movement control and stamping out restore trade status.

diseases.prognosis: Most adult animals recover within two to three weeks but may be permanently unthrifty, with chronic lameness and reduced milk yield. Mortality in young stock can exceed 50% from myocarditis. At population level, the economic prognosis of an outbreak in an export-dependent country is severe regardless of animal survival.

diseases.name: Heartwater

agents.name: Ehrlichia ruminantium
agents.notes: An obligately intracellular rickettsia that invades endothelial cells. Formerly Cowdria ruminantium. The organism's tropism for the vascular endothelium of the brain and heart is the basis of both the name and the pathogenesis.
agents.vector: Amblyomma hebraeum (bont tick) and other Amblyomma species
agents.reservoir: Infected ticks and persistently infected ruminants; the organism is maintained in the tick population transstadially

hosts.notes: Ruminants are the natural hosts. Wild ruminants including buffalo and various antelope serve as reservoir hosts without showing disease. Sheep and goats are more susceptible than cattle in some regions.

notifiable.note: WOAH-listed. Human ehrlichiosis is caused by different Ehrlichia species and is not acquired from livestock.

diseases.distribution: Restricted to sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean, following the distribution of Amblyomma ticks. In southern Africa it is endemic in the eastern and northern parts of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Mozambique and northern Botswana, with a distribution closely tied to the bont tick.

aetiology.summary: Heartwater is a tick-borne rickettsial disease transmitted by Amblyomma ticks, whose long mouthparts and three-host life cycle mean they are harder to control than one-host cattle ticks. The disease is a classic example of enzootic instability: in areas where ticks are abundant and calves are infected early, disease is rare, whereas introduced naive animals die quickly.
determinants: Presence of infected Amblyomma ticks on the pasture
Susceptibility of the host, which is highest in naive animals introduced to an endemic area
Age-related resistance in calves and lambs, which suffer mild disease that confers lifelong immunity
The three-host life cycle of Amblyomma, which makes tick control far more difficult than for one-host ticks
risk_factors: Moving naive animals into an endemic area
Poor acaricide coverage, particularly of the predilection feeding sites on the legs, perineum and udder
Abundant game or unmanaged grazing with high tick loads
Interrupting tick control abruptly in a herd that has lost natural immunity
Late introduction of susceptible breeds into endemic areas
aetiology.epidemiology: In endemic areas, the disease occurs mainly in young animals with mild signs, producing lifelong immunity. The enzootically unstable situation — where the tick is present but challenge is insufficient to immunise calves — is the most dangerous, because the herd remains fully susceptible while the risk of exposure persists. Case fatality can exceed 60-80% in naive adults.

pathophysiology.summary: Ehrlichia ruminantium multiplies in the endothelial cells lining small blood vessels throughout the body, particularly in the brain, heart and kidneys. The resulting vasculitis and increased vascular permeability produce the effusions that give the disease its name and the neurological signs that dominate the clinical picture.

cascade.title: Tick inoculation and endothelial invasion
cascade.detail: Infective organisms are inoculated during tick feeding and rapidly invade the endothelial cells of small blood vessels, where they replicate in cytoplasmic vacuoles.

cascade.title: Endothelial cell destruction
cascade.detail: Replication causes necrosis and sloughing of endothelial cells, exposing the subendothelial matrix and triggering platelet activation, coagulation and widespread vasculitis.

cascade.title: Increased vascular permeability
cascade.detail: Damaged endothelium leaks plasma into the pericardial sac, pleural cavity and peritoneal cavity. The characteristic hydropericardium — a large volume of straw-coloured fluid around the heart — is the lesion that gave the disease its name.

cascade.title: Pulmonary and cerebral oedema
cascade.detail: Increased vascular permeability in the lungs produces interstitial and alveolar oedema with severe respiratory compromise, while oedema in the brain produces the hyperaesthesia, head pressing and convulsions characteristic of the nervous form.

cascade.title: Circulatory failure and death
cascade.detail: Pericardial effusion restricts cardiac filling, and myocardial damage from vasculitis further impairs output. Combined with hypovolaemia from fluid loss, this produces circulatory collapse and death, usually within a week of onset.

lesions: Hydropericardium — a large volume of straw-coloured or blood-tinged fluid in the pericardial sac
Petechial haemorrhages on the epicardium and endocardium
Pulmonary oedema with heavy, wet lungs
Oedema of the mediastinum and perirenal tissues
Enlarged lymph nodes
Ascites and pleural effusion
Frothy fluid in the trachea and bronchi
Microscopic vasculitis and endothelial necrosis in the brain and heart
clinical_signs: Sudden high fever (40-42 degrees Celsius) that may be the only early sign
Loss of appetite and listlessness
Nervous signs: hyperaesthesia, muscle twitching, head pressing, circling and convulsions
Laboured breathing with a moist cough
Pale to slightly jaundiced mucous membranes
Salivation and profuse nasal discharge in some cases
Recumbency and death within a few days in untreated animals
In calves, mild and transient fever that may go unnoticed

antemortem: Clinical suspicion in a febrile animal from an endemic area with nervous signs
Examine a brain biopsy or blood smear for morulae within endothelial cells — very low sensitivity
PCR on whole blood is the practical confirmatory test
postmortem: Hydropericardium is the hallmark lesion — always examine the pericardial sac
Pulmonary oedema and petechiae on the epicardium
Nervous signs with a relatively normal-looking brain macroscopically
laboratory: PCR on whole blood, brain or other tissues
Demonstration of morulae in endothelial cells of brain capillaries on histology
Culture is difficult and not routinely performed
Serology for herd prevalence, with cross-reactivity between Ehrlichia species as a limitation
differentials: Babesiosis and anaplasmosis — anaemia and jaundice without the nervous signs and hydropericardium
Theileriosis — lymph node enlargement and pulmonary oedema, but different vascular lesions
Rabies — nervous signs, but with behavioural change and no fever
Tetanus — rigidity and trismus rather than oedema
Poisoning with plants causing nervous signs
Meningitis or encephalitis of other causes

prevention: Maintain regular acaricide treatment with attention to predilection sites on the legs, perineum, udder and ears
Use the infection-and-treatment method to immunise naive animals before introduction into endemic areas
Avoid abrupt cessation of tick control in endemic herds
Quarantine and monitor animals moved between zones
Consider the tick's three-host life cycle when designing control: the larval and nymphal stages on small mammals and ground-feeding birds must also be interrupted
control.vaccination: The infection-and-treatment method remains the main prophylactic approach — intravenous inoculation of live-infected blood followed by tetracycline treatment to abort the infection while allowing immunity to develop. An inactivated vaccine has been researched but is not commercially available. The method requires veterinary supervision and carries a risk of vaccine-derived disease if not handled correctly.
treatment: Oxytetracycline is the treatment of choice and is effective if given early in the febrile stage
Doxycycline is an acceptable alternative
Supportive care: fluids, NSAIDs and management of the cerebral oedema
Treatment late in the course, once nervous signs are established, is usually unsuccessful
In naive animals, treatment must begin at the first fever, before the vascular phase is established
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority where required
Treat in-contact febrile animals immediately rather than waiting for confirmation
Intensify acaricide application to reduce tick challenge
Restrict movement of animals out of the affected area
Review the acaricide programme and consider immunisation of the herd
public_health: Heartwater does not affect humans
Human ehrlichiosis is caused by different species and is tick-transmitted from wildlife reservoirs, not from livestock
control.notes: The Ammblyomma tick's attachment sites are the practical key to control. Acaricide applied to the body may miss the legs, udder and perineum where the bont tick actually feeds.

diseases.prognosis: Poor in naive animals once clinical signs are established, with case fatality commonly 60-80%. Animals treated early in the febrile phase recover. Survivors are immune for life.

diseases.name: Lumpy skin disease

agents.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
agents.notes: Genus Capripoxvirus, family Poxviridae. A large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus that is exceptionally stable in dried scabs and lesion material, remaining infectious for months in the environment.
agents.vector: Biting arthropods — stable flies (Stomoxys), mosquitoes (Aedes, Culex) and biting midges (Culicoides) — with mechanical transmission between animals; iatrogenic spread via contaminated needles and vaccination equipment is also documented
agents.reservoir: Infected cattle; the virus persists in scabs and in the environment; a wildlife reservoir has not been clearly established

hosts.notes: Cattle are the main host. All ages are susceptible; young calves and lactating cows are most severely affected. The disease is not a risk to humans.

notifiable.note: A transboundary disease of major economic significance because of hide damage, milk loss, abortion and trade restrictions. Notifiable in most cattle-producing countries.

diseases.distribution: Historically confined to sub-Saharan Africa, but since the 2010s it has spread rapidly through the Middle East, the Balkans, Turkey, Russia, the Caucasus and across Asia, reaching India and South-East Asia. In southern Africa it is endemic in parts of Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa, with periodic epidemic waves following good rains.

aetiology.summary: LSD spreads mechanically between cattle by biting arthropods, which transmit virus from skin lesions, scabs and the viraemic blood of infected animals. Because the virus survives in lesion material and on fomites, mechanical spread by flies, needles, and contaminated equipment is central. Direct contact is a less important route than biting flies.
determinants: High biting-arthropod populations, particularly Stomoxys and Culicoides
The presence of viraemic animals with active skin lesions
Virus stability in dried scabs, enabling persistence in the environment and on fomites
Susceptibility of a completely naive cattle population
Iatrogenic transmission through shared needles or poorly sterilised vaccination equipment
risk_factors: Warm, humid conditions after rains that support explosive fly and midge populations
Introduction of untested or unquarantined cattle from endemic areas
Dense cattle concentrations at water points, kraals or markets
Lack of vaccination or waning herd immunity
aetiology.epidemiology: Morbidity in a naive herd can reach 45-100%, while mortality is usually 1-10% but can be higher in calves. Transmission is seasonal, peaking when vector numbers are high after rains. The virus spreads slowly — roughly 1-2 kilometres per week in a naive population — but spreads rapidly within a herd once introduced. Overwintering in the environment is key to the seasonal cycle.

pathophysiology.summary: Following mechanical inoculation by an arthropod, the virus replicates locally in the skin and drains to regional lymph nodes, producing a viraemia that seeds the skin, mucous membranes and internal organs. The characteristic nodules are full-thickness areas of dermal necrosis and vasculitis, which slough and leave deep ulcers that heal slowly and scar permanently.

cascade.title: Mechanical inoculation
cascade.detail: An infected fly or midge feeds on an animal, picks up virus from a skin lesion or blood, and deposits it in the skin of the next animal within minutes — the virus requires no replication in the insect.

cascade.title: Local replication and lymph node spread
cascade.detail: Virus replicates in the dermis and drains to regional lymph nodes, which enlarge and become the source of subsequent haematogenous dissemination.

cascade.title: Viraemia and skin localisation
cascade.detail: During the viraemic phase — typically 4-12 days after infection — virus seeds the skin at many sites, the mucous membranes of the respiratory and alimentary tracts, and internal organs.

cascade.title: Dermal vasculitis and necrosis
cascade.detail: Viral replication in dermal endothelial cells causes necrotising vasculitis, with thrombosis, oedema and necrosis of the surrounding tissue. This produces the full-thickness, sharply demarcated nodules that give the disease its name.

cascade.title: Sloughing, ulceration and secondary infection
cascade.detail: The necrotic centre of a nodule detaches to leave a deep, granulating ulcer that is prone to myiasis and secondary bacterial infection. Healing is by fibrosis, leaving a permanent hide scar, and the process can take months.

lesions: Firm, raised, oval skin nodules 1-5 centimetres across, distributed over the head, neck, udder, perineum and limbs
Nodules that become necrotic and slough to leave deep ulcers, sometimes full-thickness through the skin
Enlarged regional and prescapular lymph nodes
Nodules and erosions on the mucous membranes of the muzzle, oesophagus, rumen and trachea
Oedema of the limbs, brisket and udder
Pox lesions in the lungs and, occasionally, the alimentary tract
Hide damage and permanent scarring in recovered animals
clinical_signs: Fever of 40-41 degrees Celsius two to three days before skin lesions appear
Firm, painful skin nodules appearing first on the head, neck and udder
Watery discharge from eyes and nose, with corneal involvement in some cases
Marked oedema of the limbs and brisket
Lameness from nodules on the limbs and coronary band
Enlarged superficial lymph nodes
Sharp drop in milk yield and abortion or infertility in some animals
Secondary myiasis in necrotic skin lesions

antemortem: Clinical examination: the pattern of firm skin nodules, fever and lymphadenopathy is highly suggestive in a naive herd
Collect skin biopsies from the margin of a fresh nodule, or a scab, in buffered formalin for histology and fresh for PCR
postmortem: Examine the skin, mucous membranes, trachea and lungs for nodules and ulcers
Look for oedema and enlarged lymph nodes; internal lesions may be subtle
laboratory: PCR on skin biopsy, scab or blood — the standard confirmatory test
Virus isolation in cell culture, confirming with neutralisation
Histopathology showing eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies and ballooning degeneration in the dermis
Electron microscopy of lesion material showing poxvirus particles, useful when PCR is unavailable
differentials: Pseudolumpy skin disease (bovine herpesvirus 2) — milder nodules that are not full-thickness and resolve without ulceration
Bovine papular stomatitis — small papules on the muzzle and oral cavity, no systemic illness
Dermatophilosis — scaly, crusty lesions, often along the back, with no nodules
Mange (Sarcoptes, Psoroptes) — intense pruritus and alopecia, no fever
Photosensitisation — dermatitis on unpigmented skin
Insect and tick bites or urticaria — transient swelling without necrosis
Bovine viral diarrhoea mucosal disease — erosions rather than nodules

prevention: Vaccinate the whole herd annually with a homologous capripox vaccine
Quarantine and examine all introduced cattle for at least 28 days
Control biting arthropods with pour-on insecticides and fly control around kraals and water points
Use a fresh needle for every animal and sterilise equipment between animals
Avoid moving cattle during an outbreak and restrict access to markets
control.vaccination: Live attenuated homologous vaccines — Neethling strain in southern Africa, and LSDV-based vaccines elsewhere — provide solid, long-lasting immunity from a single dose. Vaccinate before the rainy season. A small proportion of vaccinated animals develop a mild local reaction, which is expected. Heterologous sheeppox or goatpox vaccines are used where homologous vaccine is unavailable and give cross-protection.
treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists; management is supportive
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection of skin ulcers and for mastitis
Wound care and fly control on ulcerated lesions to prevent myiasis
NSAIDs for fever and pain, and fluids for dehydrated animals
Soft feed and water for animals with oral lesions
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority immediately
Impose movement restrictions on the affected premises and a surrounding area
Vaccinate all cattle in the ring around the outbreak, including apparently healthy animals
Isolate affected animals and restrict contact with the rest of the herd
Vector control around affected and at-risk premises
Avoid ring culling where vaccination can contain spread — the economic case for culling is much weaker than for FMD
public_health: LSD is not a zoonosis and poses no direct human health risk
The public health significance is indirect — loss of milk and meat supply and of household income
control.notes: The economic impact of LSD is dominated by hide damage and milk loss rather than mortality, which is why control programmes are justified even when case fatality is low.

diseases.prognosis: Most affected cattle survive, but recovery is slow, milk yield may never return to previous levels, and hides are permanently scarred. Calves and heavily affected animals can die. Herd immunity after an outbreak or vaccination is long-lasting.

diseases.name: Malignant catarrhal fever

agents.name: Ovine herpesvirus 2
agents.notes: Genus Macavirus, family Herpesviridae. The sheep-associated form of MCF in southern Africa is caused by OvHV-2, which is carried asymptomatically by sheep and shed in nasal secretions. In wildebeest, the related AlHV-1 causes the same syndrome in cattle — the source of the Afrikaans name 'snotsiekte'.

agents.name: Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1
agents.notes: The wildebeest-associated form, shed in ocular and nasal secretions of wildebeest calves and lambs, particularly in the first months of life. Both viruses cause an identical disease in cattle.

hosts.notes: Sheep and wildebeest are the reservoir hosts and are themselves unaffected. Cattle, deer and other susceptible species are dead-end hosts — there is no cattle-to-cattle transmission.

notifiable.note: Not WOAH-listed. The economic importance lies in individual animal losses rather than trade restrictions, but the fear it generates among cattle owners is disproportionate because the case fatality is so high.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide, wherever cattle are grazed in proximity to sheep or wildebeest. In southern Africa, the wildebeest-associated form is a well-recognised risk in the Okavango and other areas where cattle and wildebeest overlap — particularly on the fringes of the delta and around game reserves.

aetiology.summary: MCF in cattle is an aberrant, dead-end infection acquired by close contact with the reservoir host — sheep or wildebeest — shedding virus in nasal and ocular secretions. The disease arises from an immune response that attacks the animal's own tissues as well as the virus, which is why it is invariably fatal despite the virus being present in only small amounts.
determinants: Close physical proximity of cattle to sheep or wildebeest, especially during lambing or calving when virus shedding peaks
Shedding of OvHV-2 in nasal secretions by sheep, particularly lambs aged 2-6 months
Shedding of AlHV-1 by wildebeest calves in their first months of life
An immunological response in cattle that is disordered and self-destructive rather than protective
risk_factors: Grazing cattle on pasture shared with or downwind of sheep flocks
Cattle in contact with wildebeest, especially wildebeest calving areas
Confinement of sheep and cattle in adjacent pens with shared airspace
Seasonal — wildebeest calving season creates the peak risk
Young cattle appear more susceptible than adults
aetiology.epidemiology: Cases are usually sporadic and few in number, because the disease is not transmitted cattle-to-cattle and the organism is inefficiently transmitted from the reservoir. The key epidemiological observation is the association with the presence of sheep or wildebeest. Outbreaks can involve a small cluster of cattle grazing a particular paddock.

pathophysiology.summary: Virus enters the cattle host and infects T lymphocytes and endothelial cells, but the small viral load means tissue damage comes from the host's own immune response. A massive, misdirected T-cell response produces generalised lymphoid proliferation and vasculitis, which is the lesion that accounts for every clinical sign in the disease.

cascade.title: Transmission from the reservoir host
cascade.detail: Cattle inhale OvHV-2 or AlHV-1 from the nasal or ocular secretions of sheep or wildebeest. The virus does not spread between cattle.

cascade.title: Lymphocyte infection and dissemination
cascade.detail: The virus infects CD8+ T lymphocytes and spreads throughout the body within these cells, seeding the lymphoid tissues and the vascular endothelium.

cascade.title: Dysregulated T-cell proliferation
cascade.detail: Rather than mounting an effective antiviral response, the host develops generalised lymphoid proliferation with large numbers of activated CD8+ T cells, both in lymph nodes and infiltrating tissues.

cascade.title: Vasculitis and mucosal necrosis
cascade.detail: The proliferating lymphocytes accumulate around small blood vessels throughout the body, causing a widespread vasculitis. Ischaemia and necrosis follow in the most vascular tissues — the nasal mucosa, oral cavity, conjunctiva, gut and skin.

cascade.title: Organ failure and death
cascade.detail: The combined effects of mucosal necrosis, gut involvement, renal injury and neurological damage progress over days to weeks. Death is usual, and there is no treatment that alters the course.

lesions: Extensive necrosis and erosion of the nasal mucosa, hard palate and oral cavity
Granular or gelatinous exudate in the nasal passages and sinuses
Conjunctivitis with corneal opacity and photophobia
Enlarged, oedematous lymph nodes with lymphoid proliferation on histology
Vasculitis and perivascular lymphoid cuffing in the kidney, liver and brain
Erosive lesions in the abomasum and intestine
Dermatitis, particularly on the muzzle and teats
Keratitis with a characteristic 'painted' appearance of the limbus
clinical_signs: Sudden high fever (40.5-42 degrees Celsius) that does not respond to antibiotics
Profuse nasal discharge progressing from serous to mucopurulent, with crusting around the nose
Corneal opacity and conjunctivitis with excessive lacrimation and photophobia
Erosions and ulcers in the mouth and on the nasal planum
Enlarged superficial lymph nodes
Profuse watery diarrhoea in the intestinal form
Muscle tremors, head pressing and other neurological signs
Rapid weight loss and death over 3-10 days, sometimes within 24 hours in the peracute form

antemortem: Clinical picture of fever unresponsive to antibiotics, with nasal discharge, corneal opacity and oral erosions
History of contact with sheep or wildebeest is the key epidemiological clue
PCR on blood, nasal swab or conjunctival swab — the practical confirmatory test
postmortem: Examine nasal cavity, oral cavity and conjunctiva for necrosis and exudate
Note generalised lymphadenopathy and renal lesions
Histology is particularly valuable: vasculitis with perivascular lymphoid accumulation is characteristic
laboratory: PCR for OvHV-2 or AlHV-1 on blood, nasal secretions or tissue — the test of choice
Histopathology demonstrating vasculitis and lymphoid proliferation
Virus isolation is difficult and not routinely performed
Serology is of little diagnostic value because most cattle are seronegative and the antibody response is inconsistent
differentials: Bovine viral diarrhoea and mucosal disease — similar oral erosions but with PI animals and no sheep or wildebeest association
Foot-and-mouth disease and vesicular stomatitis — vesicular rather than erosive lesions
Infectious bovine rhinotracheitis (IBR) — respiratory disease with nasal lesions but a different course and PCR result
Blue tongue in cattle — usually inapparent, occasionally with oral lesions
Photosensitisation — dermatitis in unpigmented skin without fever
Plant poisoning, particularly with plants causing mucosal necrosis

prevention: Separate cattle from sheep and wildebeest, especially during lambing and calving seasons
Avoid grazing cattle on pasture recently occupied by sheep or wildebeest
Maintain physical barriers and avoid shared airspace in housed systems
Time cattle grazing to avoid wildebeest calving concentrations
If sheep and cattle must coexist, graze sheep ahead of cattle with a delay, or use separate paddocks
control.vaccination: No commercial vaccine is available. Experimental vaccines against AlHV-1 have shown partial protection in wildebeest but are not licensed or practical for cattle.
treatment: There is no effective treatment — the disease is almost invariably fatal
Supportive care, including fluids and NSAIDs, is palliative only
Antibiotics are often given initially for suspected bacterial respiratory disease but have no effect on MCF
Euthanasia on welfare grounds is appropriate once the diagnosis is confirmed
Corticosteroids may transiently reduce the immune reaction but do not alter the outcome
outbreak: Confirm the diagnosis and identify the reservoir species involved
Remove cattle from pasture shared with sheep or wildebeest immediately
Do not treat surviving animals as a source of infection — they are not infectious to other cattle
Notify the veterinary authority, particularly where wildebeest are involved and neighbouring herds may be at risk
Review grazing plans for the following season
public_health: MCF is not a human pathogen and poses no public health risk
control.notes: This disease is best understood as an immunological accident. The virus is present in very small amounts, and the damage is done by the host's own T cells. That explains why antibiotics never work and why the case fatality is essentially 100%.

diseases.prognosis: Almost uniformly fatal. A small number of animals survive with chronic disease, but they remain unthrifty. There is no treatment that changes the outcome once clinical signs appear.

diseases.name: Peste des petits ruminants

agents.name: Peste des petits ruminants virus
agents.notes: A morbillivirus of the family Paramyxoviridae, closely related to rinderpest and measles. It is enveloped and therefore fragile in the environment, requiring close contact for transmission. A single serotype exists, which is what makes global eradication feasible.
agents.reservoir: Infected sheep and goats; the virus does not persist in wildlife on the continent, and recovered animals are immune for life

hosts.notes: Goats are generally more severely affected than sheep. Cattle and pigs are not infected. The disease is a major constraint on small-ruminant production across Africa and Asia.

notifiable.note: A WOAH-listed transboundary disease and the target of a global eradication programme led by WOAH and FAO, with the goal of eradication by 2030. It is notifiable in every country.

diseases.distribution: Endemic across much of Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Its expansion has been a major concern of the global eradication effort. In southern Africa, PPR is not endemic in the southernmost countries, which makes its introduction a serious event, and it is present in Angola, Zambia and other countries to the north and west.

aetiology.summary: PPR spreads by close contact between infected and susceptible small ruminants, principally through respiratory aerosols and contact with eye and nose secretions. As with rinderpest and measles, it is an immunising infection: recoverers are immune for life and animals that have never been exposed are fully susceptible.
determinants: Close contact between infected and naive sheep or goats
Inhalation of infectious droplets from coughing or sneezing animals
Contact with eye, nose and mouth secretions, and with faeces
Movement of animals at markets, for seasonal grazing or across borders
Absence of vaccination in the population
risk_factors: Markets, auctions and shared grazing that mix animals from many sources
Transhumance and seasonal movement across borders
Introduction of untested animals into a naive flock
Flocks with no vaccination history
Dense husbandry and mixing of sheep and goats
aetiology.epidemiology: Morbidity in a naive flock can reach very high levels, and mortality may exceed 50%. Transmission is efficient in close-contact settings, and the main driver of spread is animal movement. The virus is single-serotype and there is only one natural reservoir — sheep and goats — which is the biological basis for the eradication programme.

pathophysiology.summary: PPR virus infects the epithelial cells of the respiratory tract, initially in the pharynx and lungs, and then spreads to the lymphoid tissues and the epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract. The result is a combined respiratory enteritis with mucosal necrosis, leukopenia and immunosuppression, which is responsible for the high mortality.

cascade.title: Inhalation and pharyngeal replication
cascade.detail: The virus is inhaled into the respiratory tract and replicates in the epithelial cells of the pharynx and the regional lymph nodes, producing a short incubation period of about 3-6 days.

cascade.title: Viraemia and lymphoid dissemination
cascade.detail: The virus spreads through the bloodstream within lymphocytes to the lymphoid tissues throughout the body, producing a marked leukopenia and the immunosuppression that permits secondary infection.

cascade.title: Respiratory and intestinal epithelial necrosis
cascade.detail: Infection of the epithelial cells of the respiratory tract and the alimentary tract produces necrosis and erosions. The mucosal lesions in the mouth, oesophagus and gut explain the profuse diarrhoea and the salivation.

cascade.title: Diarrhoea, dehydration and electrolyte loss
cascade.detail: Necrotising enteritis produces profuse watery diarrhoea with dehydration, electrolyte loss and metabolic acidosis. Secondary bacterial infection of the damaged gut is common.

cascade.title: Pneumonia and death
cascade.detail: Bronchointerstitial pneumonia and secondary bacterial pneumonia are the terminal events, particularly in young animals. Death usually occurs 5-10 days after infection, with younger animals dying faster.

lesions: Necrotising and erosive stomatitis with lesions on the tongue, gums and dental pad
Necrotising pharyngitis and laryngitis
Interstitial and bronchointerstitial pneumonia with consolidated, dark-red lungs
Necrotising and haemorrhagic enteritis, particularly in the ileum and large intestine
Erosion and necrosis of Peyer's patches
Generalised lymphadenopathy with lymphoid depletion
Enlarged spleen with necrosis in some cases
clinical_signs: Sudden high fever (40-41 degrees Celsius)
Nasal discharge progressing from serous to mucopurulent, with crusts around the nostrils
Excessive salivation and oral erosions
Watery diarrhoea with a characteristic, foul smell
Coughing, sneezing and laboured respiration
Conjunctivitis with mucopurulent ocular discharge
Pale mucous membranes and dehydration
Death within 5-10 days in severe cases

antemortem: Clinical picture of fever, nasal discharge, oral erosions and diarrhoea in a naive flock
Collect nasal and ocular swabs and whole blood for virus detection
Rapid field tests such as lateral flow assays for antigen detection
postmortem: Examine the oral cavity, pharynx and intestine for necrotising lesions
Note the characteristic necrotising enteritis in the ileum, caecum and colon
Look for interstitial pneumonia with consolidated lungs
laboratory: RT-PCR on swabs, blood or tissue — the standard confirmatory test
Antigen ELISA for rapid confirmation
Virus isolation, though it is technically demanding and not routinely needed
Serology by ELISA or neutralisation for surveillance and to demonstrate absence of infection
differentials: Rinderpest — the historical differential, now eradicated but must be considered for reassurance
Foot-and-mouth disease — oral vesicles and salivation but no diarrhoea or pneumonia
Bluetongue — oral lesions and respiratory signs but with a different epidemiology
Contagious ecthyma (orf) — proliferative oral lesions rather than erosions
Coccidiosis and parasitic gastroenteritis causing diarrhoea
Bovine viral diarrhoea in cattle (small ruminants can be infected with pestiviruses)

prevention: Vaccinate the whole flock with the live attenuated PPR vaccine, which provides lifelong immunity after a single dose
Quarantine and test all introduced animals
Control animal movements, particularly at markets and across borders
Establish surveillance and early-warning systems through participatory disease surveillance
Maintain a cold chain for vaccine delivery in remote areas
control.vaccination: The live attenuated PPR vaccine (Nigeria 75/1 strain) is highly effective, safe and gives immunity for life after a single dose. It is the foundation of the global eradication strategy. Post-vaccination serosurveillance requires a test that can distinguish vaccinated from infected animals, which is the main technical constraint on the programme.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment
Supportive care: oral rehydration, fluids and electrolytes
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial pneumonia and enteritis
NSAIDs for fever and oral pain
Soft feed and water for animals with oral lesions
Euthanasia on welfare grounds for severely affected animals
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority immediately — PPR is notifiable in every jurisdiction and a suspected case is a national emergency
Impose immediate movement restrictions on the affected premises and the surrounding area
Ring vaccination around the outbreak, with a target coverage of high levels across the whole population
Cull affected and in-contact animals where the eradication policy requires it
Trace animal movements and identify the source of introduction
Conduct surveillance in the surrounding area to detect further cases
public_health: PPR is not a zoonosis and poses no human health risk
The public health significance is indirect — loss of a major dietary protein source and household income for smallholder producers
control.notes: PPR is biologically one of the most eradicable diseases known: single serotype, single reservoir, no wildlife maintenance, and a highly effective vaccine. The obstacles are logistical and political, not biological.

diseases.prognosis: Poor — case fatality in a naive flock commonly exceeds 50%, and is higher in young animals. Recovered animals are immune for life. At flock level, the only satisfactory intervention is vaccination before exposure.

diseases.name: Q fever

agents.name: Coxiella burnetii
agents.notes: Gram-negative, obligately intracellular bacterium with a small-cell form that is highly resistant to drying, heat and disinfectants. It does not require an arthropod vector for transmission to livestock but ticks are involved in wildlife maintenance. Aerosol infection is the dominant route, and the organism is excreted in enormous quantities in placental tissue and birth fluids.
agents.reservoir: Cattle, sheep and goats, particularly at parturition; goats are the major source of human outbreaks; wildlife including ticks

hosts.notes: Ruminants are the maintenance hosts. Humans are infected by aerosols from parturient animals or contaminated dust. The organism is shed in birth fluids, placenta, urine, faeces and milk.

notifiable.note: One of the most infectious zoonoses — a single organism can establish human infection by inhalation. Q fever is a serious occupational risk for farmers, veterinarians and abattoir workers.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide. In southern Africa, Q fever is reported in cattle, sheep and goats, and human seroprevalence is significant, but surveillance is limited and the disease is probably underdiagnosed.

aetiology.summary: Q fever is overwhelmingly an aerosol-transmitted disease. Coxiella concentrates in the placenta of infected ruminants and is released in massive quantities at parturition, where it contaminates bedding, wool, soil and dust. Inhalation of a contaminated aerosol — not a bite, not direct contact — is the route of infection for both animals and people.
determinants: The concentration of the organism in placental tissue and birth fluids
Generation of an infectious aerosol by dust, bedding, wool or parturition
Survival of the small-cell form in dry, dusty conditions for months to years
Inhalation of the aerosol by a susceptible host
Windborne dispersal of dust from contaminated premises
risk_factors: Assisting at lambing, kidding or calving without respiratory protection
Handling placentae, aborted material or contaminated bedding
Working in dusty barns, sheds or pens previously used by infected animals
Shearing and handling wool from infected sheep
Abattoir and hide processing work
Proximity of dwellings to livestock birthing areas
aetiology.epidemiology: The domestic ruminant cycle is largely silent — infected animals rarely show clinical disease, and the tip-off is often a human case. Shedding is concentrated at parturition, and the organism is highly infectious: experimental evidence suggests a very small number of organisms, possibly a single one, can cause human infection. Human outbreaks are commonly traced to a lambing or kidding season, or to windborne dust from a farm.

pathophysiology.summary: Inhaled Coxiella is taken up by alveolar macrophages, where its acid-adapted metabolism allows it to survive and replicate in the phagolysosome rather than being killed. In animals this produces a largely subclinical infection with placental colonisation; in humans it produces a systemic febrile illness that may progress to endocarditis or chronic fatigue syndromes.

cascade.title: Inhalation and macrophage uptake
cascade.detail: The small-cell form is inhaled into the alveoli and phagocytosed by macrophages, which are unable to kill it.

cascade.title: Phagolysosomal survival
cascade.detail: Coxiella is adapted to the acidic environment of the phagolysosome and replicates there rather than being digested, a strategy shared with other intracellular pathogens and the basis for its persistence.

cascade.title: Haematogenous dissemination
cascade.detail: The organism spreads through the blood to the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow and, importantly in pregnancy, the placenta.

cascade.title: Placental colonisation and shedding
cascade.detail: In pregnant ruminants, the organism replicates massively in trophoblast cells of the placenta, producing a placentitis that is usually subclinical but leads to enormous shedding at parturition.

cascade.title: Human granulomatous disease and complications
cascade.detail: In people, the infection causes granulomatous hepatitis and pneumonitis. Chronic Q fever follows in a small proportion, particularly in those with pre-existing valvular disease or immunosuppression, and manifests as culture-negative endocarditis.

lesions: Placentitis with grossly normal or slightly thickened cotyledons in ruminants — lesions are often minimal
Granulomatous inflammation of the placenta and uterus on histology
In humans: granulomatous hepatitis and interstitial pneumonitis
In humans with chronic disease: endocarditis vegetations and vascular graft infection
clinical_signs: In livestock: usually no clinical signs at all
Late-term abortion or stillbirth in sheep, goats and cattle, but this is uncommon relative to silent infection
Infertility and reproductive wastage in some flocks
In humans: sudden onset of high fever, severe headache, myalgia and profuse sweating
In humans: pneumonia and hepatitis in the acute form
In humans: chronic fatigue, night sweats and weight loss in the chronic form

antemortem: Serology is the mainstay: indirect immunofluorescence assay for phase I and phase II antibodies
Phase II antibodies predominate in acute infection; high phase I titres indicate chronic infection
PCR on blood, milk or placental tissue
postmortem: Examine the placenta for mild thickening and cotyledon pathology
Note that gross placental lesions are often unremarkable, and the diagnosis depends on laboratory testing
laboratory: Indirect immunofluorescence assay for phase I and phase II IgG and IgM
ELISA for serological screening
PCR on placenta, birth fluids, milk or blood
Culture is hazardous and requires biosafety level 3 containment; it is not a routine diagnostic approach
differentials: Brucellosis — causes the same late-term abortion syndrome with similar occupational risk, but with distinct serology
Chlamydiosis — abortion and reproductive disease with different serology
Campylobacteriosis and trichomonosis — earlier abortion and different lesion distribution
Leptospirosis — haemoglobinuria and jaundice accompanying abortion
Toxoplasmosis and neosporosis — protozoal abortifacients
Influenza and other acute febrile illnesses in humans — Q fever is frequently missed

prevention: Wear respiratory protection (P2/N95 or better) when assisting at parturition or handling placentae
Dispose of placentae and birth fluids promptly and hygienically; do not spread them on pasture
Avoid dust-generating activities in lambing and kidding sheds without respiratory protection
Vaccinate high-risk livestock where an approved vaccine is available
Pasteurise milk before human consumption
Keep birthing areas away from houses and prevailing wind toward dwellings
control.vaccination: An inactivated phase I vaccine (Coxevac) is licensed for cattle and goats in some countries and reduces shedding at parturition. Human vaccination with the Q-Vax vaccine is used in high-risk occupational groups in Australia and is highly effective but requires pre-screening for prior exposure.
treatment: Antibiotic treatment in livestock is not indicated — it does not eliminate the organism and is not economically justified
In humans, doxycycline for 2-3 weeks is the standard acute treatment
Chronic Q fever requires prolonged combination therapy, typically doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine for 18 months or more
Treatment of infected animals is not a control measure; management is aimed at reducing exposure to parturient material
outbreak: Notify the public health and veterinary authorities — Q fever is reportable in many jurisdictions
Identify the source premises and restrict access to the birthing area
Warn and screen exposed persons, particularly those who assisted at parturition
Avoid moving bedding, manure or animals from the affected premises during the outbreak
Consider vaccinating at-risk livestock and at-risk people under medical direction
public_health: Q fever is among the most infectious zoonoses known — a very low inhaled dose can cause human infection
Pregnant women, people with valvular heart disease and immunocompromised people should avoid contact with lambing and kidding
Human infection presents as a non-specific febrile illness and is underdiagnosed as a result
Chronic Q fever endocarditis is life-threatening and requires long-term specialist treatment
Notification of human cases to public health authorities is essential to identify the animal source
control.notes: The striking feature of Q fever is the asymmetry between animal and human disease: livestock are almost always asymptomatic while people can become seriously ill from the same exposure event.

diseases.prognosis: Livestock recover without treatment and remain infected carriers, with shedding at subsequent parturitions. In humans, acute Q fever usually resolves with appropriate antibiotic treatment; chronic Q fever has a guarded prognosis even with prolonged therapy.

diseases.name: Rabies

agents.name: Rabies virus
agents.notes: Genus Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae. A bullet-shaped, enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus. Envelope fragility means it is inactivated rapidly by drying, sunlight and detergent — which is why transmission requires deposition into tissue.
agents.reservoir: Domestic dogs are the reservoir for over 99% of human deaths globally; insectivorous and vampire bats maintain independent cycles

hosts.notes: All mammals are susceptible. Carnivores and bats are the maintenance hosts; herbivores are almost always dead-end hosts infected by a rabid carnivore.

notifiable.note: Rabies is the only disease in this reference where the animal diagnosis is inseparable from a human life-or-death decision. Every suspected case requires immediate notification to both veterinary and human health authorities.

diseases.distribution: Present on every continent except Antarctica. In southern Africa, domestic dog rabies remains endemic in parts of Botswana, Zimbabwe, South Africa and Mozambique, with wildlife cycles in jackal and bat-eared fox populations. Botswana's human cases are overwhelmingly dog-mediated.

aetiology.summary: Transmission requires the virus to be introduced into tissue, almost always through a bite that deposits saliva containing virus into muscle or subcutaneous tissue. The virus does not cross intact skin and does not survive long outside the host.
determinants: A rabid animal shedding virus in saliva, typically from 1-5 days before clinical signs appear
Penetrating exposure — a bite, scratch or mucosal contamination — not mere contact
Viral dose and the innervation density of the bite site
Failure to provide timely post-exposure prophylaxis to an exposed person
Absence of an effective dog vaccination programme maintaining herd immunity
risk_factors: Unvaccinated free-roaming dog populations
Bite wounds to the head, face, hands and neck, where the distance to the central nervous system is short
Children, who are bitten more often and report exposures less reliably
Occupational handling of wildlife or unvaccinated dogs
Bat exposures in caves or roosts, where bites may go unnoticed
aetiology.epidemiology: Case fatality approaches 100% once clinical signs develop — rabies is the most lethal known infectious disease of humans. Dog-mediated transmission accounts for the overwhelming majority of human cases. The incubation period is typically 1-3 months in humans and 2-8 weeks in animals, but can range from days to years depending on wound site and viral load. Control is entirely a question of maintaining dog vaccination coverage above roughly 70%.

pathophysiology.summary: Rabies virus replicates in striated muscle at the wound site, enters peripheral nerve endings, and travels by retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord and brain without triggering an immune response. Once in the central nervous system it causes a non-suppurative encephalitis that produces the behavioural change and loss of swallowing coordination responsible for salivary shedding, before spreading centrifugally to the salivary glands.

cascade.title: Local replication
cascade.detail: Virus replicates in striated muscle cells at the inoculation site for days to weeks. This eclipse phase is the therapeutic window — post-exposure prophylaxis works here and stops working once virus reaches nerve.

cascade.title: Centripetal axonal transport
cascade.detail: Virus binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction and travels retrograde along axons at roughly 50-100 millimetres per day toward the dorsal root ganglia and spinal cord.

cascade.title: CNS dissemination and encephalitis
cascade.detail: Once in the brain, virus spreads cell to cell across synapses and causes non-suppurative encephalitis with Negri bodies in hippocampal and Purkinje neurons. Crucially, it does not trigger a detectable immune response at this stage — the virus suppresses interferon signalling and evades antibody.

cascade.title: Centrifugal spread to salivary glands
cascade.detail: Virus travels outward along parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves to the salivary glands and is shed in saliva before clinical signs appear, which is why an apparently healthy dog can transmit the disease.

cascade.title: Brainstem dysfunction and death
cascade.detail: Involvement of the brainstem and cranial nerve nuclei abolishes swallowing and produces the classic inability to drink while still attempting to, with hypersalivation and hydrophobia. Death follows from respiratory and cardiac failure caused by brainstem destruction, not by the virus directly damaging those organs.

lesions: Gross lesions are typically absent — a normal brain at post-mortem does not exclude rabies
Non-suppurative encephalomyelitis with perivascular cuffing and gliosis on histology
Negri bodies — eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in hippocampal pyramidal cells and Purkinje cells
Ganglionitis of the dorsal root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia
Salivary gland inflammation with virus demonstrable in acinar cells
clinical_signs: Behavioural change — aggression, restlessness or unusual depression and hiding
Hypersalivation and difficulty swallowing, with attempts to drink but inability to do so (the origin of 'hydrophobia')
Altered phonation — a change or loss of bark
Progressive paralysis, often ascending, with lower motor neuron signs
Ataxia, seizures and terminal coma
In cattle, bellowing, tenesmus and posterior paresis that can mimic bloat or a foreign body

antemortem: No reliable antemortem test exists for animals. Clinical suspicion is managed by isolation, not by testing.
In humans, skin biopsy from the nape of the neck, saliva and cerebrospinal fluid can be tested, but a negative result does not exclude disease
postmortem: Submit the intact head or the brain fresh, chilled and unfixed — do not freeze if histology is required
Gross examination is unremarkable and has no diagnostic value
laboratory: Direct fluorescent antibody test on brain tissue — the standard confirmatory test, results within hours
RT-PCR on brain tissue, saliva or cerebrospinal fluid
Histological demonstration of Negri bodies is supportive but insensitive
Virus isolation in cell culture or mouse inoculation as a confirmatory adjunct
differentials: Canine distemper — respiratory and gastrointestinal signs with myoclonus, but no hypersalivation of this pattern
Tetanus — rigidity and 'sardonic grin' with intact consciousness
Botulism — flaccid paralysis with no behavioural change
Poliomyelitis or other viral encephalitis
Poisoning with organophosphates, strychnine or lead
Laryngeal foreign body or oesophageal obstruction, which mimic the swallowing failure

prevention: Sustain mass dog vaccination at or above 70% coverage — this is the single intervention that eliminates human rabies
Sterilise and manage free-roaming dog populations
Quarantine and observe any animal that bites a person for 10 days
Vaccinate cats, cattle and horses in endemic areas as a secondary barrier
Educate communities to seek care immediately after any bite and to wash wounds with soap and water for 15 minutes
control.vaccination: Inactivated cell-culture vaccines are safe and highly effective in animals and humans. Dogs require a primary course from 12 weeks of age and boosters; humans require pre-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk occupations and post-exposure regimens of vaccine with rabies immunoglobulin for category III exposures.
treatment: There is no effective treatment for clinical rabies in animals. Management is palliative and aimed at preventing human exposure.
In humans, the Milwaukee protocol has produced a handful of survivors but is not a reliable treatment; prevention is the only dependable strategy
Immediate wound washing with soap and water for at least 15 minutes substantially reduces the risk of infection
outbreak: Notify veterinary and public health authorities immediately — a rabid animal is a public health emergency
Isolate and confine the suspect animal; do not attempt home treatment or observation without veterinary direction
Identify and trace every person and animal exposed to the suspect animal's saliva
Refer all exposed persons for post-exposure prophylaxis without delay — do not wait for the animal's test result when the exposure was significant
Submit the brain for fluorescent antibody testing if the animal dies or is euthanased
Implement ring vaccination of dogs in the affected area
public_health: Wash any bite or scratch immediately with soap and water for 15 minutes and seek medical care the same day
Post-exposure prophylaxis must not wait for laboratory confirmation when the exposure warrants it
Rabies immunoglobulin is indicated for category III exposures — transdermal bites, scratches, and mucosal or saliva contamination of broken skin
Human deaths from rabies are almost entirely preventable and almost always reflect a failure of access to prophylaxis, not of vaccine efficacy
control.notes: This record deliberately states the post-exposure position bluntly. The commonest fatal error in rabies management is a delay waiting for an animal to be observed or tested.
