diseases.prognosis: Uniformly fatal once clinical signs appear in any species. The prognosis is excellent if post-exposure prophylaxis is completed before symptom onset, and good for animals with a verified current vaccination and a provoked, minimal exposure.

diseases.name: Rotavirus scour

agents.name: Bovine rotavirus
agents.notes: A non-enveloped, segmented double-stranded RNA virus of the Reoviridae, with a wheel-like appearance on electron microscopy. Group A rotaviruses are the most important cause of neonatal calf diarrhoea. The segmented genome allows reassortment between strains, which complicates vaccine strain selection.
agents.reservoir: Infected calves and adult carriers; the virus is shed in very high numbers in the faeces and persists in the environment

hosts.notes: Neonates are affected almost exclusively. The most severe disease occurs in calves between 1 and 3 weeks of age, particularly when colostrum intake has been inadequate.

notifiable.note: Not notifiable. Human rotavirus is a major cause of infant diarrhoea worldwide but is a different epidemiological problem, transmitted person-to-person rather than from livestock.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide wherever cattle, sheep and pigs are reared. Rotavirus is endemic in most herds, and the disease reflects the interaction between viral challenge and the calf's immune status rather than the introduction of the virus.

aetiology.summary: Rotavirus is ubiquitous in cattle herds. The disease occurs when a susceptible neonate meets a high viral challenge from a contaminated environment at a time when maternal antibody protection has waned. It is therefore a disease of calving management, colostrum feeding and calf-rearing hygiene, not simply of viral presence.
determinants: A high viral challenge in the calf's environment, from contaminated bedding and pens
Inadequate colostrum intake, which leaves the calf without protective maternal antibody
Age of the calf — the most susceptible window is roughly 1-3 weeks, after maternal antibody declines but before active immunity develops
Crowding and mixing of calves of different ages
Failure of hygiene and disinfection in calving and rearing pens
risk_factors: Poor calving hygiene and contaminated calving pens
Inadequate or delayed colostrum feeding
Mixing calves of different ages in rearing pens
Overcrowding and wet bedding
Cold, wet and stressful weather
Continuous calving without an all-in-all-out system
Unvaccinated dams in herds with endemic rotavirus
aetiology.epidemiology: Rotavirus is enzootic on most farms, and the disease appears as calf-rearing outbreaks rather than as a point-source epidemic. The virus is extremely stable in the environment and survives on contaminated surfaces for months. Morbidity in a naive group of calves can be very high, with mortality determined largely by the adequacy of colostrum and the speed of supportive treatment.

pathophysiology.summary: Rotavirus infects the mature enterocytes at the tips of the small intestinal villi, destroying them and leaving the crypt cells to replace them with immature, non-absorbing cells. The result is a malabsorptive, osmotic diarrhoea that is compounded by a loss of brush-border enzymes, particularly lactase, producing a secondary lactose intolerance.

cascade.title: Ingestion and small intestinal infection
cascade.detail: The virus is ingested from the contaminated environment and infects the mature villous enterocytes of the small intestine, particularly in the jejunum.

cascade.title: Enterocyte destruction and villous atrophy
cascade.detail: Viral replication destroys the mature enterocytes, and the crypt cells that replace them are immature and cannot absorb. The villi become shortened and blunted, reducing the absorptive surface area.

cascade.title: Loss of brush-border enzymes
cascade.detail: The mature enterocytes carry the lactase and other disaccharidases needed to digest milk sugars. Their loss produces a transient lactose intolerance, so milk feeding worsens the diarrhoea by drawing water into the gut osmotically.

cascade.title: Osmotic diarrhoea and dehydration
cascade.detail: Undigested nutrients remain in the lumen and hold water osmotically, producing profuse watery diarrhoea. The loss of fluid and electrolytes produces dehydration and metabolic acidosis.

cascade.title: Weakness, acidosis and death
cascade.detail: Without fluid therapy, the calf becomes progressively dehydrated and acidotic, becomes recumbent and dies. Secondary bacterial and cryptosporidial infection is common and worsens the prognosis.

lesions: Fluid small intestinal contents and a thin-walled, translucent intestine
Villous atrophy and blunting on histology
No gross mucosal ulceration, in contrast with coccidiosis
Dehydration and loss of body fat in fatal cases
Possible secondary infection of the gut with bacteria or Cryptosporidium
clinical_signs: Watery, yellow or greenish diarrhoea with a characteristic sour smell
Dehydration with sunken eyes and loss of skin turgor
Reduced suckle reflex and reluctance to feed
Weakness and recumbency
Cold extremities and a subnormal temperature in advanced cases
Metabolic acidosis with a slow, deep respiratory pattern
Death within days if untreated
Subclinical cases show transient softening of the faeces and reduced growth

antemortem: Rapid field test on faecal sample — rotavirus antigen ELISA or lateral flow test
Faecal examination to rule out Cryptosporidium, which frequently co-infects and requires different treatment
Assess dehydration and acid-base status to guide fluid therapy
Age of the calf and the colostrum history are important diagnostic clues
postmortem: Examination of the small intestine shows thin, fluid contents without gross mucosal necrosis
Histopathology shows villous atrophy with enterocyte loss
Submit intestinal tissue and faecal content for testing
laboratory: Rotavirus antigen ELISA or lateral flow test on faeces
Electron microscopy showing characteristic wheel-shaped particles
RT-PCR for confirmation and genotyping
Histopathology of the small intestine showing villous atrophy
differentials: Coronavirus infection — similar neonatal diarrhoea, often more severe and with more respiratory involvement
Cryptosporidiosis — also causes neonatal diarrhoea and commonly co-infects
Coccidiosis — usually in calves older than 3 weeks, with blood and mucus
Escherichia coli enteritis — often presents as septicaemia or peracute diarrhoea in the first days of life
Salmonellosis — diarrhoea with systemic signs and a different epidemiology
Nutritional or dietary scour — no fever, no virus detected, resolves with dietary correction

prevention: Ensure adequate colostrum intake within the first 6 hours of life, with a measured volume of good-quality colostrum
Maintain clean, dry calving pens and single-use bedding
Use all-in-all-out calf rearing with disinfection between groups
Avoid mixing calves of different ages
Vaccinate dams in late pregnancy to increase colostral antibody
Feed calves individually and clean feeding utensils thoroughly
control.vaccination: Inactivated and modified-live rotavirus vaccines are available for administration to cows in late pregnancy, increasing the concentration of specific antibody in colostrum. This is the standard approach in dairy herds. Calf-level vaccination is not generally used for rotavirus.
treatment: Oral rehydration solution is the mainstay of treatment, with the volume and frequency determined by the degree of dehydration
Intravenous fluid therapy for calves that are recumbent or unable to suckle
Correct the metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate-containing solutions in severe cases
Continue milk feeding — starvation prolongs recovery; reduce the volume and increase the frequency rather than stopping milk entirely
Do not use antibiotics routinely — they do not affect the virus and contribute to resistance; use them only where secondary bacterial infection is suspected
Supportive care: warmth, a dry environment and ease of access to feed
outbreak: Isolate affected calves and clean and disinfect the rearing area
Review colostrum management — the commonest root cause
Ensure all affected calves are rehydrated promptly
Submit faecal samples for diagnosis rather than assuming rotavirus
Review calving pen hygiene and calf moving practice
public_health: Bovine rotavirus is not considered a human pathogen; human rotavirus is a different epidemiological problem
Good hygiene when handling scouring calves is advisable for general biosecurity
Observe withdrawal periods for any veterinary medicines used
control.notes: The single most important intervention for rotavirus scour is colostrum. No treatment compensates for a calf that received too little colostrum too late.

diseases.prognosis: Good with prompt oral rehydration — most calves recover within a week. Poor in calves with severe dehydration, recumbency or concurrent infection. The underlying prevention problem recurs each calving season unless colostrum and hygiene are addressed.

diseases.name: Tetanus

agents.name: Clostridium tetani
agents.notes: Gram-positive, spore-forming, strictly anaerobic rod. Spores are ubiquitous in soil and in the intestinal tract of animals and humans. The vegetative form is a normal gut inhabitant; disease requires the spores to germinate in an anaerobic wound.
agents.reservoir: Soil and dust spore bank; intestinal tract of herbivores and humans

hosts.notes: Horses and small ruminants are the most susceptible domestic species. Cattle are relatively resistant. Neonatal tetanus after umbilical infection is a significant cause of lamb and calf mortality in unhygienic conditions.

notifiable.note: Not WOAH-listed. Human tetanus remains a significant cause of death globally, particularly in neonates where maternal vaccination is incomplete, but animal cases carry no human transmission risk.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide. Spores are present in soil everywhere, so the risk is defined by wound management and by vaccination status rather than by geography.

aetiology.summary: Tetanus is an intoxication, not an invasive infection. Spores introduced into a deep, anaerobic wound germinate and produce tetanospasmin, which travels up the motor nerves and enters the central nervous system to block inhibitory neurotransmission. The bacterium stays at the wound site; the toxin does the damage.
determinants: Introduction of spores into a wound with a low redox potential — deep puncture, crush injury, contaminated surgical site or the umbilical stump
Anaerobic conditions favouring spore germination and toxin production
Absence of protective antitoxin from vaccination or colostrum
Devitalised tissue, foreign bodies or concurrent infection creating the anaerobic niche
risk_factors: Unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated animals
Castration, tail docking and ear tagging without hygiene or antitoxin cover
Umbilical infection in neonates born in contaminated environments
Deep puncture wounds, particularly from nails, wire or thorns
Retained placenta and uterine infection after calving or lambing
Surgical procedures and dystocia without prophylactic antitoxin
aetiology.epidemiology: Sporadic and always wound-associated. There is no animal-to-animal transmission. Morbidity is low but case fatality is high. In small ruminants, the peak incidence is in lambs and kids around castration and tail docking, and in neonates with umbilical infection. Herds with a tetanus history usually reflect a management gap rather than an environmental anomaly.

pathophysiology.summary: Tetanospasmin is a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory interneurons, preventing the release of GABA and glycine. The result is loss of inhibition across the spinal cord and brainstem, producing unopposed motor activity — rigidity, spasm and the characteristic hypertonicity — with consciousness fully preserved.

cascade.title: Anaerobic wound colonisation
cascade.detail: Spores enter a wound and germinate only where oxygen tension is low — deep puncture wounds, crushed tissue or the devitalised umbilical cord. The vegetative bacterium remains localised at the wound site.

cascade.title: Toxin release and axonal transport
cascade.detail: Tetanospasmin is released and binds the presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons, travelling by retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord and brainstem over days.

cascade.title: Inhibitory synapse blockade
cascade.detail: Once in the central nervous system, the toxin moves trans-synaptically into inhibitory interneurons and cleaves synaptobrevin, preventing the release of glycine and GABA.

cascade.title: Loss of inhibition and rigidity
cascade.detail: Without inhibitory input, alpha motor neurons fire continuously and unopposed. This produces generalised muscle rigidity, with the extensor muscles of the limbs and jaw affected most prominently.

cascade.title: Spasm, respiratory failure and death
cascade.detail: Any sensory stimulus triggers uncontrolled spasm of all muscles at once, including the larynx and diaphragm. Death is from respiratory failure, aspiration or exhaustion, and the animal remains fully conscious throughout.

lesions: No specific gross lesions — the lesion is functional, not structural
The wound may be small, healed over or barely visible
Possible evidence of the primary wound or of aspiration pneumonia secondary to respiratory compromise
clinical_signs: Generalised muscle rigidity, with the animal moving reluctantly and stiffly
Trismus — 'lockjaw' — with the jaw held firmly closed
Prolapse of the third eyelid in small ruminants when the head is raised
Ears held erect and back, tail stiff, with a 'sardonic grin' from facial muscle spasm
Hypersensitivity to noise, light and touch, triggering full-body spasm
In horses, sawhorse stance, flared nostrils and sweating
Difficulty swallowing and drooling
Terminal convulsions and respiratory failure

antemortem: Clinical diagnosis: the combination of rigidity, trismus, hyperaesthesia and normal consciousness is highly characteristic
Search for a wound or a recent history of castration, docking, lambing or trauma
Differentiate from hypocalcaemia, which responds to calcium, and from strychnine poisoning, which has a similar presentation
postmortem: No diagnostic lesion is present
Look for the primary wound or an umbilical infection, and note evidence of aspiration pneumonia
laboratory: Isolation of C. tetani from the wound requires anaerobic culture and is insensitive
Demonstration of toxin in wound exudate by mouse bioassay is definitive but rarely necessary or available
PCR for the tetanus toxin gene tetX can be performed on wound material but has limited added value when the clinical picture is characteristic
differentials: Strychnine poisoning — very similar presentation, but with a history of exposure and rapid onset
Hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia — respond to specific therapy
Rabies — behavioural change and fever, with progression to paralysis rather than rigidity
Meningitis or encephalitis — fever and altered consciousness, absent here
Organophosphate poisoning — parasympathetic signs and fasciculations rather than sustained rigidity
Myotonia congenita — rare and lifelong rather than acute

prevention: Vaccinate with tetanus toxoid as part of routine herd or flock vaccination, especially in horses and small ruminants
Give prophylactic antitoxin at the time of castration, docking or any contaminated surgery
Maintain hygienic conditions for lambing, calving and foaling, and treat the umbilical stump with iodine
Clean and debride wounds promptly and thoroughly
Check vaccination status before any surgical procedure or after any deep wound
control.vaccination: Tetanus toxoid provides excellent, long-lasting protection. Horses require annual boosters; cattle and sheep every one to three years. Neonates acquire passive immunity from colostrum if the dam is vaccinated, so dam vaccination in late pregnancy protects the offspring.
treatment: Tetanus antitoxin to neutralise circulating toxin that has not yet entered the central nervous system — valuable early but cannot reverse toxin already bound
High-dose penicillin or metronidazole to eliminate the vegetative bacteria at the wound site
Debridement of the wound and removal of devitalised tissue and foreign material
Nursing care: dark, quiet environment to minimise spasm triggers, and supportive fluids
Muscle relaxants, sedation and even mechanical ventilation in valuable animals
In humans, treatment requires intensive care with tracheostomy and ventilatory support — the animal equivalent is rarely available
outbreak: Review and correct the wound-management practice that caused the case
Give all in-contact animals at-risk tetanus antitoxin and review their vaccination status
Improve hygiene at castration and parturition sites
Notify the veterinary authority only where the cause is an iatrogenic or reportable management failure
public_health: Human tetanus is a medical emergency and requires immediate medical attention
The infection is not transmitted from animals to humans; both are infected from the same environmental spore bank
Human vaccination status should be maintained — a booster every 10 years, and a booster with a contaminated wound if status is unknown
Tetanus in humans is preventable by vaccination and is a marker of poor maternal and neonatal health in resource-limited settings
control.notes: The single most useful clinical observation is that the animal is fully conscious. Rigidity with normal mentation is tetanus until proven otherwise.

diseases.prognosis: Guarded to poor. In horses and small ruminants, case fatality without intensive care is high, often above 50-80%. With early antitoxin, antibiotics and nursing care, recovery is possible but slow, and recovering animals may remain stiff for weeks.

diseases.name: Babesiosis

agents.name: Babesia bovis
agents.notes: An intraerythrocytic apicomplexan parasite. B. bovis is the most virulent species in cattle and is transmitted transovarially by Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus. It causes cerebral babesiosis through sequestration of infected erythrocytes in capillaries.
agents.reservoir: Persistently infected cattle and the tick population itself

agents.name: Babesia bigemina
agents.notes: The other major cattle species in southern Africa, transmitted by the same tick vectors. Generally less virulent than B. bovis and associated with classic haemoglobinuria rather than cerebral disease.
agents.vector: Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus, R. decoloratus, R. annulatus
agents.reservoir: Persistently infected cattle; the tick vector

hosts.notes: Cattle are the principal host. Calves under 9 months show strong age-related resistance to disease even when infected. Adult cattle in an endemic area are usually immune; the disease appears when naive adults enter an endemic zone.

notifiable.note: Bovine babesiosis is a WOAH-listed disease because of its importance to cattle trade and movement. Human babesiosis exists but is caused by different species and is not transmitted from cattle.

diseases.distribution: Widespread wherever the tick vectors occur, which includes much of sub-Saharan Africa, southern Europe, Asia, Australia and the Americas. In southern Africa, babesiosis is endemic in the higher-rainfall eastern areas and in the coastal belt of South Africa; in Botswana it is present in areas with suitable tick populations, and is a serious risk for cattle moved from tick-free to tick-infested zones.

aetiology.summary: Babesiosis is a tick-transmitted haemoparasite disease. The tick acquires the parasite while feeding on an infected animal, and the parasite is transmitted to subsequent tick generations transovarially — so an infected tick population is itself a lasting reservoir. Disease is therefore less about the parasite than about the immunological status of the host relative to the local tick challenge.
determinants: Presence of infected Rhipicephalus ticks on the pasture
A susceptible, non-immune host — either a naive animal introduced to an endemic area or an animal whose immunity has waned
Tick challenge sufficient to deliver a dose of parasites
Absence of enzootic stability — where ticks are abundant and calves are infected early, herd immunity develops naturally
risk_factors: Moving naive cattle from a tick-free to an endemic area without vaccination
Cessation of tick control in a herd where enzootic stability has not been established
Young calves entering tick-infested pasture in a herd with no natural challenge
Live vaccine failures or vaccine unavailability, which create a gap in herd immunity
Splitting one herd into a tick-controlled and a tick-exposed group so that immunity is lost in part of the herd
aetiology.epidemiology: In endemic areas with continuous tick challenge, calves become infected while still protected by maternal antibody and age resistance, develop mild disease and emerge immune — the state known as enzootic stability. Disease emerges when this equilibrium breaks: naive animals are introduced, tick control is relaxed abruptly, or herd immunity wanes. Mortality in a fully naive adult herd can be very high — 30-50% or more with B. bovis.

pathophysiology.summary: Babesia invades erythrocytes, replicates by binary fission and ruptures them, producing a haemolytic anaemia that accounts for the haemoglobinuria and jaundice. B. bovis adds a second and more dangerous mechanism: infected erythrocytes become sticky and sequester in the capillaries of the brain, lungs and kidneys, producing cerebral babesiosis and organ failure.

cascade.title: Sporozoite inoculation
cascade.detail: The tick inoculates sporozoites during feeding. Sporozoites invade erythrocytes directly and begin the intraerythrocytic cycle.

cascade.title: Erythrocyte invasion and replication
cascade.detail: Trophozoites undergo merogony within erythrocytes, producing merozoites that lyse the host cell and invade neighbouring erythrocytes. B. bovis preferentially parasitises older erythrocytes and can reach very high parasitaemias.

cascade.title: Haemolysis
cascade.detail: Rupture of infected erythrocytes releases haemoglobin into the plasma, which exceeds the haptoglobin-binding capacity. Free haemoglobin is excreted in urine, producing the dark red to port-coloured urine that gives the disease its name.

cascade.title: Sequestration and microvascular obstruction
cascade.detail: In B. bovis infection, parasitised erythrocytes adhere to capillary endothelium in the brain, lungs and kidneys, obstructing microcirculation. This produces cerebral babesiosis with ataxia, head pressing, seizures and coma, and can produce respiratory and renal failure.

cascade.title: Anaemia, hypoxia and death
cascade.detail: The combination of massive erythrocyte destruction, impaired microcirculation and a systemic inflammatory response produces severe anaemia, hypoxia, acidosis and death. Tissue hypoxia from anaemia is compounded by capillary obstruction.

lesions: Pale, jaundiced mucous membranes and body fat
Enlarged, dark-red to black spleen
Enlarged liver with a yellowish-brown hue and gall bladder distension
Kidneys swollen and dark, with haemoglobinuric casts in the tubules
Haemoglobinuria — dark red to port-wine urine in the bladder
Pulmonary oedema and congestion, particularly in B. bovis infection
Petechial haemorrhages on serosal surfaces
Brain congestion and oedema with capillary sequestration in cerebral cases
clinical_signs: High fever (41 degrees Celsius or above) that rises rapidly
Dark, red-brown urine — the cardinal sign of redwater
Pale or jaundiced mucous membranes with anaemia
Reluctance to move, weakness and rapid respiration
Dehydration and anorexia
Cerebral signs in B. bovis infection: ataxia, head pressing, seizures and coma
Abortion in pregnant cows
Sudden death in the peracute form

antemortem: Examine a thin blood smear from the ear or tail vein, stained with Giemsa — pear-shaped organisms within erythrocytes are diagnostic
Examine urine: dark, haemoglobin-positive on dipstick
Assess packed cell volume and note anaemia and jaundice
postmortem: Note jaundice, pale mucous membranes, enlarged spleen and liver
Examine a blood smear from the heart or a peripheral vessel
Look for dark urine in the bladder and pulmonary oedema
laboratory: Giemsa-stained thin blood smear showing intraerythrocytic piroplasms — the rapid field test
PCR for species-level identification and differentiation between B. bovis and B. bigemina
Serology for herd immunity assessment, not for individual diagnosis
Haematology showing anaemia and thrombocytopenia
differentials: Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma marginale) — causes anaemia and jaundice but the organisms are at the erythrocyte margin and urine is usually normal
Theileriosis — enlarged lymph nodes and piroplasms of a different form, plus a different tick vector
Leptospirosis — haemoglobinuria with jaundice, but a different epidemiological picture
Chronic copper poisoning — haemolytic crisis with jaundice and haemoglobinuria
Bacillary haemoglobinuria (C. novyi type D) — sudden death with haemoglobinuria and liver lesions
Babesiosis and anaplasmosis frequently occur together and both should be considered

prevention: Vaccinate naive cattle with live attenuated B. bovis and B. bigemina vaccine before moving into endemic areas
Maintain a planned tick control programme with acaricides, rotating compounds to manage resistance
Avoid abrupt cessation of tick control in a herd that has not established enzootic stability
Quarantine and monitor animals moved between zones
Keep herd immunity by allowing controlled exposure in enzootically stable herds
control.vaccination: Live attenuated vaccines containing B. bovis and B. bigemina are the standard control in southern Africa. They produce solid immunity but must be handled and stored as live products, and they should not be used in cattle already immune or in the last trimester of pregnancy. Vaccination does not prevent infection, it prevents disease.
treatment: Imidocarb dipropionate is the treatment of choice and is effective against both species
Diminazene aceturate (berenil) is an alternative
Supportive care: blood transfusion for severe anaemia, intravenous fluids and anti-inflammatory therapy
Corticosteroids are used in cerebral babesiosis to reduce the inflammatory component
Treat early — the prognosis falls sharply once parasitaemia and anaemia are advanced
outbreak: Treat affected animals promptly and identify the extent of the outbreak
Assess herd immunity and consider vaccinating unaffected naive animals
Intensify tick control to reduce challenge, while being careful not to remove the challenge that maintains herd immunity
Notify the veterinary authority in areas where the disease is not endemic
Investigate the source: movement of cattle, tick spread on vehicles or animal carriers
public_health: Bovine babesiosis is not a human disease
Human babesiosis is caused by different species and is rare — it is not acquired from cattle
control.notes: The critical concept here is enzootic stability. In an endemic area, the disease is a problem of broken immunity, not of parasite presence.

diseases.prognosis: With early treatment, recovery is usual but convalescence is slow. Without treatment, mortality in naive adult cattle can reach 30-50% for B. bovis. Calves generally recover well. Animals that recover remain carriers for months to years.

diseases.name: Bovine anaplasmosis

agents.name: Anaplasma marginale
agents.notes: A rickettsial organism now classified among the Anaplasmataceae, occupying the margin of erythrocytes. It is transmitted biologically by ticks and mechanically by biting flies and contaminated instruments — the latter is a defining and often overlooked route.
agents.vector: Rhipicephalus ticks biologically; Tabanid flies and mosquitoes mechanically
agents.reservoir: Persistently infected cattle, which remain carriers for life

hosts.notes: Adults are more severely affected than calves, in contrast to babesiosis. Bulls and older animals tend to develop the most severe disease.

notifiable.note: WOAH-listed. Humans are not infected by A. marginale; human anaplasmosis is caused by A. phagocytophilum, which is a different organism transmitted by different ticks.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in tropical and subtropical regions. In southern Africa it is widespread in cattle areas and is arguably more common than babesiosis in many districts. The organism is present in most of Botswana's cattle-rearing areas.

aetiology.summary: Anaplasmosis is transmitted both biologically by ticks and mechanically by blood-contaminated mouthparts of biting flies and by shared needles, ear tags and surgical instruments. Because the organism can be transmitted mechanically, it spreads in herds even where ticks are well controlled.
determinants: Blood transfer from a persistently infected carrier to a susceptible animal
Tick transmission, principally by Rhipicephalus species
Mechanical transmission by Tabanid flies, stable flies and mosquitoes
Iatrogenic transmission via contaminated needles, ear taggers and castration instruments
Susceptibility of adult cattle in an endemic area without prior exposure
risk_factors: Introducing adult cattle into an endemic herd without vaccination
Reusing needles or surgical instruments between animals
High tabanid and stable fly populations
Dense stocking and shared handling facilities
Splitting a herd so that part loses natural exposure and immunity
aetiology.epidemiology: Carriers remain infected for life and are the reservoir. As with babesiosis, enzootic stability develops in endemic areas where calves are infected early and become immune; disease appears when adults are exposed for the first time. Because transmission can be mechanical, anaplasmosis can spread in a herd even under good tick control, which distinguishes it epidemiologically from babesiosis.

pathophysiology.summary: Anaplasma marginale invades erythrocytes and, unlike Babesia, is removed by the spleen through a macrophage-mediated process rather than by direct lysis. Infected erythrocytes are rapidly cleared, producing extravascular haemolysis, progressive anaemia and jaundice, while the parasite is controlled but not eliminated — leaving the animal a lifelong carrier.

cascade.title: Inoculation and erythrocyte invasion
cascade.detail: Organisms are transferred in blood from a carrier animal and invade erythrocytes, initially appearing at the cell margin as small, dense, round bodies.

cascade.title: Opsonisation and splenic clearance
cascade.detail: Infected erythrocytes are recognised as abnormal, opsonised and removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver. This is extravascular haemolysis, so free haemoglobinuria is less prominent than in babesiosis.

cascade.title: Progressive anaemia
cascade.detail: Continued removal of erythrocytes outstrips the bone marrow's regenerative capacity, producing a severe anaemia with pale mucous membranes and weakness. Erythrophagocytosis also leads to jaundice from bilirubin overload.

cascade.title: Fever and metabolic strain
cascade.detail: The destruction of large numbers of erythrocytes and the inflammatory response produce high fever, anorexia and rapid loss of condition, compounding the anaemia.

cascade.title: Hypoxia and death, or chronic carriage
cascade.detail: Animals that survive mount a regenerative response and control parasitaemia, but the organism persists at low levels in erythrocytes for life. Death in the acute phase results from tissue hypoxia and cardiovascular collapse.

lesions: Marked pallor of mucous membranes and internal organs
Jaundice with yellow discolouration of fat, fascia and liver
Enlarged, soft spleen from erythrophagocytosis
Enlarged liver with a distended gall bladder containing thick, dark bile
Thin, watery blood with a low packed cell volume
Petechial haemorrhages in some cases
Emaciation in chronic cases
clinical_signs: High fever (40-41 degrees Celsius) and lethargy
Pale mucous membranes and a weak, rapid pulse
Jaundice, best appreciated in the sclera and unpigmented skin
Anorexia and rapid loss of condition
Constipation followed by diarrhoea in some animals
Incoordination, head pressing and aggression in the late stages
Abortion and reduced fertility in cows
Sudden death in peracute cases, particularly in older animals

antemortem: Blood smear from an ear vein, stained with Giemsa — organisms appear at the erythrocyte margin as small, round, dark-blue dots
Note the difference from Babesia, which sits within the erythrocyte and is often pear-shaped
Haematology showing anaemia with a regenerative response after the acute phase
postmortem: Pale, jaundiced carcase with an enlarged, softened spleen
Examine blood smears from the heart blood or a peripheral vessel
Note the absence of dark urine in the bladder, which helps differentiate from babesiosis
laboratory: Giemsa-stained thin blood smear — the rapid field test
PCR for confirmation, particularly in chronic carriers with low parasitaemia
Competitive ELISA for herd prevalence and carrier detection
Haematology to assess the severity of anaemia
differentials: Babesiosis — dark urine, organisms within erythrocytes, more acute haemolysis
Theileriosis — enlarged lymph nodes and a different organism morphology
Leptospirosis — jaundice with haemoglobinuria and exposure history
Chronic copper poisoning — haemolytic crisis, but with a history of copper excess and liver copper levels
Bacillary haemoglobinuria — sudden death with haemoglobinuria
Iron deficiency or other causes of anaemia

prevention: Vaccinate naive cattle with a live attenuated A. marginale vaccine before introduction into endemic areas
Use a fresh needle for each animal and disinfect instruments between animals
Control ticks and biting flies
Test and monitor animals moved between zones
Maintain natural herd immunity through controlled exposure where appropriate
control.vaccination: Live attenuated A. marginale vaccines are used in southern Africa, giving reliable protection against disease but not against infection — vaccinated animals can still become carriers. The vaccine requires a cold chain and should not be given to animals already immune or in late pregnancy.
treatment: Imidocarb dipropionate is effective and is also used for babesiosis
Oxytetracycline, particularly long-acting formulations, is effective against Anaplasma and is the treatment of choice in some circumstances
Supportive care: blood transfusion for severe anaemia, fluids and anti-inflammatory therapy
Note that treated animals remain carriers, so treatment does not eliminate the reservoir
outbreak: Treat affected animals and identify carriers within the herd
Assess herd immunity and consider vaccination of naive animals
Review needle and instrument hygiene as a likely mechanical transmission route
Step up tick and fly control around the affected group
Notify the veterinary authority where the disease is not endemic
public_health: A. marginale is not infectious to humans
Human granulocytic anaplasmosis is a separate disease caused by A. phagocytophilum and is not transmitted from cattle
control.notes: The mechanical transmission route is the detail that makes anaplasmosis practically different from babesiosis. Herd hygiene with needles and instruments matters as much as tick control.

diseases.prognosis: With treatment, most animals recover but remain carriers for life. Mortality in untreated adult cattle can be 20-50%, with older animals faring worst. Calves usually suffer mild or inapparent infection.

diseases.name: Coccidiosis

agents.name: Eimeria species
agents.notes: Host-specific apicomplexan parasites of the intestinal epithelium. Cattle have many species, of which Eimeria zuernii and E. bovis are the most pathogenic; sheep and goats have their own species, with E. ovinoidalis the most pathogenic in sheep. Identification to species matters because most species are non-pathogenic.
agents.reservoir: Oocysts in faeces, which survive in the environment and are the source of infection

also: Adult cattle and sheep — usually carriers without disease
hosts.notes: Disease is a disease of young animals, typically from 2 weeks to 6 months of age, around weaning or when they are moved to contaminated pens. Adults are immune but serve as a source of environmental contamination.

notifiable.note: Not notifiable and not a human disease; the Eimeria species that infect livestock are host-specific.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in intensive and semi-intensive livestock production, particularly in warm, humid conditions. In southern Africa, coccidiosis is common in calves and lambs in feedlots and confined rearing systems, and after rains in heavily stocked paddocks.

aetiology.summary: Coccidiosis is an environmental contamination disease of young animals. Oocysts shed by infected animals sporulate in a warm, moist environment and become infective; the young animal ingests a large dose from a contaminated pen, trough or pasture, and the resulting epithelial destruction produces diarrhoea. Crowding and poor hygiene are the determining factors.
determinants: A high dose of sporulated oocysts ingested over a short period
Warm, moist conditions allowing oocysts to sporulate — above about 25 degrees Celsius and with adequate moisture
A young animal without acquired immunity
Crowding and contaminated pens, bedding or water troughs
Stress from weaning, transport or a change in diet
risk_factors: Overcrowding in calf pens, lambing sheds or feedlot pens
Dirty bedding and contaminated water troughs
Weaning and mixing of calves from different sources
Warm and rainy periods, which accelerate sporulation
Sudden dietary change or poor sanitation in feedlot introductions
aetiology.epidemiology: The parasite is endemic on most farms and the disease reflects an overwhelming challenge rather than a new introduction. Oocysts are highly resistant and survive for months. Animals that survive develop strong, species-specific immunity, so adult stock are generally unaffected. Outbreaks typically follow a management stress event — weaning, mixing, moving to a contaminated pen or a wet spell.

pathophysiology.summary: Coccidia invade and multiply within the intestinal epithelial cells, destroying them in successive generations of replication. The destruction of the villus epithelium and the resulting villous atrophy produce malabsorption, protein loss and a haemorrhagic diarrhoea, which is the mechanism of clinical disease.

cascade.title: Ingestion of sporulated oocysts
cascade.detail: The young animal ingests oocysts that have sporulated in the environment. Sporozoites are released in the intestine and invade the mucosal epithelial cells.

cascade.title: Asexual replication and cell destruction
cascade.detail: The parasite undergoes several rounds of asexual multiplication within epithelial cells, each round destroying the infected cells and releasing merozoites to invade adjacent cells. This stage produces the most severe tissue damage.

cascade.title: Villous atrophy and malabsorption
cascade.detail: Successive waves of epithelial destruction cause villous blunting and atrophy, reducing the absorptive surface. Undigested nutrients pass into the large intestine and draw osmotically active water into the lumen, producing watery diarrhoea.

cascade.title: Haemorrhage and protein loss
cascade.detail: Deeper invasion damages the lamina propria and small blood vessels, producing haemorrhagic diarrhoea with blood and mucus. Protein loss across the damaged gut produces hypoproteinaemia and weight loss.

cascade.title: Dehydration, acidosis and death
cascade.detail: The combination of diarrhoea, dehydration and metabolic acidosis can kill a young animal within days. Secondary bacterial infection of the damaged gut is common and compounds the severity.

lesions: Fluid small intestinal contents with a putrid odour
Thickened, inflamed intestinal wall with petechial haemorrhages
White, yellowish or blood-tinged plaques on the mucosa
Villous atrophy and fusion on histology
Enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes
Emaciation and dehydration in fatal cases
clinical_signs: Watery diarrhoea, which may contain blood and mucus
Straining and tenesmus
Rapid weight loss and weakness
Dehydration with sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor
Reduced appetite and poor growth
Death within 3-7 days in severe, untreated cases
Subclinical cases show only poor growth and rough coat

antemortem: Faecal flotation to identify oocysts — but note that presence alone does not diagnose disease, because many animals shed oocysts without disease
Species identification on morphological grounds or by PCR, which is important because most species are non-pathogenic
Evaluate the clinical picture together with the oocyst count and the management history
postmortem: Examine the small and large intestine for haemorrhage, plaque formation and thickened wall
Smears from the intestinal mucosa will show the various developmental stages
laboratory: Faecal flotation with McMaster or concentration technique and oocyst count
PCR or restriction analysis for species identification
Histology showing coccidial stages within epithelial cells and villous atrophy
differentials: Parasitic gastroenteritis with nematodes — different age pattern and faecal egg findings
Rotavirus and coronavirus infection in calves and lambs — similar watery diarrhoea in young stock
Salmonellosis and other bacterial enteritis
Bovine viral diarrhoea
Nutritional scour — dietary indiscretion without fever or blood
Gut parasites such as Cryptosporidium, which require different testing

prevention: Keep pens and bedding clean and dry, and remove contaminated bedding promptly
Avoid overcrowding and reduce stocking density in rearing pens
Separate calves and lambs by age group and avoid mixing animals from different sources
Provide clean water and raise troughs to reduce contamination
Use coccidiostats in feed or water during high-risk periods where appropriate
control.vaccination: A live attenuated Eimeria vaccine is available in some countries and is used in cattle and sheep, particularly where coccidiosis is a recurrent problem. It is not widely used in southern Africa. Most control relies on hygiene and coccidiostats.
treatment: Sulfonamides (sulfadimidine, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim) are the traditional treatment
Toltrazuril is highly effective and is the preferred modern treatment for clinical coccidiosis
Amprolium and decoquinate are coccidiostatic and are used for prevention rather than treatment of clinical disease
Fluid and electrolyte therapy for dehydrated animals
Supportive care and separation of affected animals
outbreak: Treat affected animals promptly with toltrazuril or a sulfonamide
Isolate affected animals to reduce environmental contamination
Clean and disinfect pens — oocysts are resistant to many disinfectants, so removal of organic matter is essential
Administer coccidiostat prophylaxis to in-contact animals
Review stocking density and hygiene practice
public_health: Livestock coccidia are host-specific and do not infect humans
Human coccidiosis is caused by different organisms (Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora) and is acquired from contaminated water or food
control.notes: The most common diagnostic error is treating the presence of oocysts as the diagnosis. Many species are harmless, and oocyst counts must be interpreted against the clinical picture and species identification.

diseases.prognosis: Good with prompt treatment and supportive care. Untreated severe cases in young animals can have significant mortality. Survivors usually recover fully and develop immunity.

references.label: WOAH — Manual of Diagnostic Tests and Vaccines for Terrestrial Animals

diseases.name: Fasciolosis

agents.name: Fasciola hepatica
agents.notes: The common liver fluke — a large, leaf-shaped trematode that migrates through the liver parenchyma before settling in the bile ducts. Its life cycle requires a freshwater snail intermediate host, which tightly constrains its geographic distribution.
agents.reservoir: Adult flukes in the bile ducts of ruminants; infected snail intermediate hosts

agents.name: Fasciola gigantica
agents.notes: The tropical liver fluke, larger than F. hepatica and adapted to warmer environments. It is the dominant species in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where its snail host thrives in permanent water bodies.
agents.reservoir: Adult flukes in bile ducts; Lymnaea snail intermediate hosts

hosts.notes: Cattle develop more resistance than sheep and goats, and are more likely to harbour chronic infections with relatively mild disease. Sheep and goats are more susceptible and can die in acute outbreaks.

notifiable.note: Human fasciolosis is a neglected tropical disease and is acquired by eating contaminated watercress or other aquatic plants. It is not acquired from eating infected meat.

diseases.distribution: Fasciola hepatica is present in temperate and subtropical regions worldwide. F. gigantica is the dominant species in much of Africa and Asia. In southern Africa, fasciolosis is a significant constraint in cattle and small ruminants grazed in areas with permanent water, marshes or irrigation — including the Okavango and Chobe districts of Botswana.

aetiology.summary: Fasciolosis requires three things to occur: infected ruminants shedding eggs, a suitable snail population, and a wet environment in which the parasite's free-swimming stages can survive. The disease is therefore a function of hydrology and drainage, not simply of stocking.
determinants: Presence of Lymnaea snail populations in the grazing area
Waterlogged, marshy or irrigated pasture where snails thrive
Shedding of eggs by infected animals, which must reach water to hatch
Ingestion of metacercariae encysted on grass or floating vegetation
The temperature and moisture conditions required for the free-living stages
risk_factors: Grazing near dams, streams, marshes, irrigation canals or floodplains
Warm, wet seasons favouring snail reproduction
High stocking density around water bodies, which concentrates egg deposition
Absence of drainage in irrigated pastures
Grazing aquatic plants or drinking from contaminated water sources
aetiology.epidemiology: The disease is focal — it occurs where the snail habitat exists, so an affected property may have severe problems in one paddock and none in another. Outbreaks follow wet seasons. Chronic disease is more common in cattle; acute disease with mortality occurs more often in sheep and goats. Humans are infected by eating aquatic plants such as watercress, or by drinking contaminated water.

pathophysiology.summary: Fasciola causes disease in two phases. During migration, the young flukes tunnel through the liver parenchyma, causing acute hepatic necrosis and haemorrhage. Once they reach the bile ducts, they provoke a chronic cholangitis and duct thickening, producing anaemia, hypoproteinaemia and ill-thrift that can persist for months.

cascade.title: Ingestion of metacercariae
cascade.detail: Metacercariae encysted on grass are ingested with herbage. The cyst wall is digested in the intestine, releasing young flukes that penetrate the intestinal wall.

cascade.title: Migration through the liver capsule and parenchyma
cascade.detail: Young flukes migrate through the peritoneal cavity, penetrate the liver capsule and tunnel through the parenchyma over several weeks, causing haemorrhage and necrosis along their tracks. This phase causes the acute disease and is the principal cause of death in sheep.

cascade.title: Settlement in the bile ducts
cascade.detail: Flukes enter the bile ducts and mature. Their feeding and the host's response cause chronic cholangitis with duct thickening, fibrosis and, in heavy infections, calcification.

cascade.title: Blood loss, anaemia and hypoproteinaemia
cascade.detail: Adult flukes ingest blood and plasma and damage the biliary epithelium, producing a chronic loss of protein and red cells. The resulting hypoalbuminaemia causes submandibular oedema, weight loss and reduced production.

cascade.title: Fibrosis, liver failure and secondary disease
cascade.detail: Chronic fibrosis impairs hepatic function. Heavy burdens can lead to secondary bacterial infection of the biliary tree and, in cattle, to jaundice and reduced fertility. Coinfection with Clostridium novyi can precipitate bacillary haemoglobinuria.

lesions: Acute: enlarged, haemorrhagic liver with extensive subcapsular and parenchymal haemorrhage and necrotic tracks
Chronic: thickened, fibrotic bile ducts with a pipe-stem appearance
Flukes visible in the bile ducts at post-mortem
Enlarged gall bladder with dark, thickened bile
Pale, oedematous carcase with submandibular oedema
Haemorrhagic enteritis in acute cases
clinical_signs: Weight loss and poor growth, often the only sign in cattle
Submandibular oedema ('bottle jaw') from hypoproteinaemia
Pale mucous membranes from anaemia
Diarrhoea in some animals
Reduced milk yield and poor fertility
Acute disease in sheep and goats: sudden death with haemorrhagic hepatitis, often with no prior signs
Jaundice in severe chronic cases

antemortem: Faecal sedimentation to detect fluke eggs — sensitive in chronic disease but negative during the acute migratory phase
Coprological examination for eggs with a specific gravity allowing the dense eggs to sediment
Antibody ELISA for cattle herds, useful for surveillance but not for individual diagnosis
postmortem: Examine the liver and bile ducts — flukes are visible in the ducts when the liver is opened
Note necrotic tracks and haemorrhage in acute cases
Inspect the bile duct wall for thickening and calcification
laboratory: Faecal sedimentation for Fasciola eggs
ELISA for antibody detection in milk or serum for herd surveillance
Coproantigen ELISA, which detects active infection and does not rely on egg shedding
Post-mortem examination remains one of the most sensitive detection methods
differentials: Parasitic gastroenteritis — anaemia and ill-thrift but with a different faecal profile
Hepatogenous photosensitisation from plant toxins, which also produces liver damage
Bacillary haemoglobinuria — occurs after fluke migration and must be considered in affected animals
Chronic copper poisoning
John's disease (paratuberculosis)
Nutritional protein deficiency causing oedema

prevention: Fence off marshy areas, dams and stream banks to prevent grazing where metacercariae concentrate
Drain waterlogged pasture and improve irrigation management
Supply water from raised troughs rather than allowing access to snail habitat
Treat at appropriate times to reduce pasture contamination by eggs
Consider the snail intermediate host in any control plan — without snails, there is no fluke
control.vaccination: No commercial vaccine is available. Research vaccines based on cathepsin L proteases have shown partial protection but are not licensed for use.
treatment: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice and is effective against both mature and immature flukes — it is the only widely available fasciolicide with good activity against young stages
Nitroxynil is effective against adult flukes but has poor activity against immature stages
Clorsulon is effective against adult flukes and is used in combination with ivermectin
Timing depends on the epidemiology: treat in late summer or autumn to kill flukes before they mature and shed eggs
Note that triclabendazole resistance is emerging in some regions and must be considered when treatment fails
outbreak: Treat affected animals with a fasciolicide effective against the stage present
Move animals away from marshy grazing immediately
Investigate the source and assess the snail habitat
Fence off the affected area or drain it
Submit livers for post-mortem examination to confirm the diagnosis and assess the stage of infection
public_health: Human fasciolosis is acquired by eating contaminated watercress or aquatic plants, not by eating livestock meat
Boiling or thoroughly cooking aquatic plants and drinking safe water prevents human infection
Human cases respond to triclabendazole under medical supervision
Human fasciolosis is a recognised neglected tropical disease in parts of Africa, the Middle East and South America
control.notes: The epidemiological constraint is the snail. A control programme that treats animals but leaves the marshy grazing intact will fail, because reinfection is continuous.

diseases.prognosis: Good if treated before the chronic fibrotic stage. Acute disease in sheep carries high mortality. Chronic infection in cattle imposes permanent production losses even after successful treatment.

diseases.name: Mange

agents.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
agents.notes: A burrowing mite that excavates tunnels in the epidermis and causes intense pruritus. It is highly contagious and can affect humans — the human form is classical scabies, and animal-derived infections cause a self-limiting but intensely itchy dermatitis.
agents.reservoir: Infested animals; the mite does not survive long off the host

agents.name: Psoroptes ovis
agents.notes: A non-burrowing, surface-living mite that feeds on epidermal debris and causes a severe exudative dermatitis with thick scabs. It is the cause of sheep scab, a serious welfare and economic disease in sheep.
agents.reservoir: Infested sheep; the mite can survive on fences and handling equipment for a short period

agents.name: Chorioptes bovis
agents.notes: A surface mite that typically affects the lower limbs and tail of cattle, causing less severe disease than Sarcoptes or Psoroptes. Often associated with 'leg mange' and tail-head dermatitis.
agents.reservoir: Infested cattle

hosts.notes: Each mite species has a preferred host but can often infest related species. Sheep are the most commonly affected livestock species in terms of welfare impact. Goats are highly susceptible to Sarcoptes.

notifiable.note: Psoroptic mange in sheep (sheep scab) is subject to statutory control in several countries and has been a notifiable disease in some jurisdictions. It is not currently WOAH-listed.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide. Mange is a disease of crowding, poor body condition and limited access to veterinary care. In southern Africa, sarcoptic and psoroptic mange are economically significant in sheep, goats and cattle, particularly in communal and extensively managed flocks.

aetiology.summary: Mange is transmitted by direct contact between animals, with mites surviving only briefly off the host. The disease is therefore a function of stocking density, mixing and the immune and nutritional status of the animals. Outbreaks in well-managed herds are usually traceable to an introduced infested animal.
determinants: Direct contact with an infested animal
Mite survival on fomites such as fences, crushes and bedding for short periods
Crowding and mixing of animals from different sources
Compromised immunity and poor body condition
Absence of a treatment or control programme in an affected group
risk_factors: Overcrowding in pens, kraals or transport
Introducing untested or untreatably infested animals into a clean herd
Poor nutrition and concurrent disease, which increase susceptibility and severity
Shared rubbing posts and fences
Shearing and handling equipment that is not cleaned between flocks
aetiology.epidemiology: The mites have a direct life cycle completed entirely on the host, with a generation time of 2-3 weeks. Transmission requires close contact, so the disease spreads slowly through a herd unless animals are crowded. Sarcoptic mange is more contagious and more pruritic than chorioptic mange, which tends to be chronic and localised to the legs and tail.

pathophysiology.summary: The mite's feeding and burrowing damage the epidermis and provoke an intense hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens and faeces. The resultant pruritus drives self-trauma, and the combination of excoriation, secondary bacterial infection and serum exudation produces the thickened, crusted skin that characterises the disease.

cascade.title: Mite establishment
cascade.detail: Mites transfer from an infested animal and establish on the new host. Sarcoptes burrows into the stratum corneum; Psoroptes and Chorioptes remain on the surface and feed on epidermal debris and tissue fluid.

cascade.title: Sensitisation
cascade.detail: After an initial period of 2-3 weeks, the host becomes sensitised to mite antigens and develops an intense type I and type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which is responsible for most of the pruritus.

cascade.title: Self-trauma and excoriation
cascade.detail: Intense itching causes rubbing, biting and scratching, which excoriates the skin, damages hair follicles and creates secondary lesions that spread beyond the original sites of mite activity.

cascade.title: Epidermal hyperplasia and crusting
cascade.detail: Chronic irritation produces hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and a thickened, folded appearance to the skin with adherent crusts, alopecia and lichenification.

cascade.title: Secondary infection and debility
cascade.detail: Bacterial infection of excoriated skin is common. In severe and prolonged cases, chronic pruritus, loss of condition and reduced feed intake produce significant debility and can contribute to mortality, particularly in young or malnourished animals.

lesions: Papules, vesicles and crusts on the face, ears, neck and flanks in sarcoptic mange
Thick, adherent, yellowish scabs over large areas of the body in psoroptic mange
Alopecia, lichenification and thickened, folded skin in chronic cases
Excoriation and secondary pyoderma from self-trauma
Chorioptic mange: lesions on the lower limbs, tail and perineum
Emaciation and poor body condition in severe cases
clinical_signs: Intense pruritus, with persistent rubbing, biting and scratching
Hair loss, starting on the face, ears and neck in sarcoptic mange
Thick scabs and crusts, often with a musty odour
Thickened, corrugated skin in chronic cases
Restlessness and reduced grazing, leading to weight loss
Rubbing against fences and posts to the point of excoriation
Secondary bacterial infection with pustules and exudate

antemortem: Skin scraping from the margin of a fresh lesion — ideally several sites, because mites can be hard to find
Examine the scrapings microscopically; Sarcoptes is best recovered from deep scrapings of the most recent lesions
Consider a therapeutic trial when mites are not found but the clinical picture is compatible
postmortem: Mange is diagnosed on the live animal; post-mortem findings are limited to skin lesions and secondary infection
Note emaciation and the distribution of skin lesions
laboratory: Microscopic examination of skin scrapings for mites or eggs
ELISA for Sarcoptes antibodies, available in some countries for herd screening
PCR-based identification of species from skin lesions, increasingly used for confirmation
Histopathology of skin biopsy, which shows eosinophilic dermatitis with mites in some cases
differentials: Dermatophilosis — paintbrush scabs and a wet-environment association, different organisms on smear
Ringworm — circular lesions with raised margins and hair loss, fungal elements on microscopy
Photosensitisation — dermatitis restricted to unpigmented skin, no mites
Zinc deficiency — crusting on the face and limbs with a nutritional history
Allergic dermatitis from insects or plant contact
Poxvirus skin lesions, such as lumpy skin disease

prevention: Quarantine and treat all incoming animals before mixing with the herd
Avoid overcrowding and reduce stocking density in pens and kraals
Maintain adequate nutrition, as poor body condition increases susceptibility
Clean and disinfect handling equipment, rails and shared rubbing posts
Monitor herds regularly and treat early when pruritus is noticed
control.vaccination: No vaccine is available. Control relies on acaricide treatment and management.
treatment: Macrocyclic lactones, particularly ivermectin and doramectin, are the most effective and widely used treatment
Moxidectin and eprinomectin are alternatives with variable residual activity
Organophosphate or amitraz dips are used in some countries but resistance and residue concerns limit their use
Treat the entire affected group rather than individual animals, because in-contact animals are often infested subclinically
Repeat treatment at intervals matching the mite life cycle — usually two treatments 10-14 days apart
outbreak: Treat all animals in the affected group simultaneously
Repeat treatment to catch newly hatched mites
Isolate and treat affected animals where practical
Clean and disinfect equipment and shared rubbing surfaces
Trace the source — usually an introduced animal — and review biosecurity
Notify the veterinary authority where statutory control applies, notably for sheep scab
public_health: Animal-derived Sarcoptes can cause transient, self-limiting dermatitis in people — an itchy rash on the forearms and hands is common in handlers
Human scabies from the human-adapted mite is a different condition and spreads person-to-person, not from livestock
Wear gloves and protective clothing when handling infested animals, and wash thoroughly afterwards
Animal mites do not establish sustained infestations on humans, so human cases resolve once exposure stops
control.notes: The most common cause of treatment failure is treating only the visibly affected animals. Mites survive at low levels on in-contact animals, and any untreated animal becomes a source of reinfestation.

diseases.prognosis: Good with appropriate treatment of the whole group and improved management. Chronic cases with extensive skin damage take weeks to recover. Welfare implications are significant in untreated animals, and chronic cases can contribute to mortality in already debilitated stock.

references.label: Merck Veterinary Manual — Mange in livestock
WOAH — Manual of Diagnostic Tests and Vaccines for Terrestrial Animals

diseases.name: Parasitic gastroenteritis

agents.name: Haemonchus contortus
agents.notes: The barber's pole worm — a large abomasal nematode that sucks blood. The single most economically important gastrointestinal parasite of small ruminants in warm, humid climates, and the species most associated with acute mortality.
agents.reservoir: Pasture larvae; adult worms in the abomasum of sheep and goats

agents.name: Teladorsagia circumcincta
agents.notes: The brown stomach worm of sheep and goats, causing reduced appetite and diarrhoea rather than blood loss. Subclinical production loss is its main economic effect.
agents.reservoir: Pasture larvae; adult worms in the abomasum

agents.name: Trichostrongylus species
agents.notes: Small intestinal and abomasal worms that cause diarrhoea, ill-thrift and hypoproteinaemia in mixed infections with Haemonchus and Teladorsagia.
agents.reservoir: Pasture larvae; adult worms in the abomasum and small intestine

agents.name: Ostertagia ostertagi
agents.notes: The cattle stomach worm. Larvae can arrest in the abomasal glands and emerge together in a mass outbreak (type II ostertagiasis), a key mechanism of disease in young cattle at the end of the grazing season.
agents.reservoir: Pasture larvae; arrested larvae in the abomasal mucosa

hosts.notes: Young animals are most severely affected because they have no acquired immunity. In sheep, Haemonchus is the dominant cause of acute death; in cattle, Ostertagia is the dominant cause of production loss.

notifiable.note: Not notifiable. The economic significance is enormous and largely invisible: subclinical infection is estimated to be one of the largest causes of lost livestock productivity worldwide.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in grazing ruminants. In southern Africa, Haemonchus is a major constraint in sheep and goats, particularly in the warmer, wetter eastern areas and during the rainy season, and is the principal reason for anthelmintic use in small ruminants.

aetiology.summary: Infection is acquired by ingesting infective third-stage larvae from pasture. The parasite's epidemiology is dominated by the free-living stages on pasture, whose development and survival depend on temperature and moisture. Disease is therefore a function of stocking density, grazing management and weather rather than of contact between animals.
determinants: Contamination of pasture with nematode eggs from infected animals
Warm, moist conditions allowing eggs to hatch and develop to infective larvae
Grazing close to the ground, where larvae concentrate on grass blades
High stocking density and continuous grazing of the same pasture
Absence of effective immunity, which is typical in young animals and in periparturient ewes
risk_factors: Young animals turned out onto contaminated pasture
Periparturient relaxation of immunity in ewes, with a massive increase in egg output around lambing
Overstocking and continuous grazing without rest periods
Rainy season and warm temperatures favouring larval development
Anthelmintic resistance, which is now widespread and undermines routine drenching
aetiology.epidemiology: The peri-parturient rise in egg output from ewes is the single most important source of pasture contamination, and it occurs precisely when the next generation of lambs is most susceptible. Haemonchus has a short generation time and a high fecundity — a single female can produce thousands of eggs a day — so populations can increase explosively within a season. Anthelmintic resistance in Haemonchus is now widespread in southern Africa, which has made traditional drenching programmes unsustainable.

pathophysiology.summary: Disease results from the feeding behaviour of the adult worms and the host response to them. Haemonchus attaches to the abomasal mucosa and sucks blood, producing a direct and continuing blood loss that rapidly causes anaemia and hypoproteinaemia. The other species cause disease mainly through mucosal damage, reduced appetite and protein loss, producing diarrhoea and ill-thrift.

cascade.title: Ingestion and larval establishment
cascade.detail: Infective third-stage larvae are ingested with pasture, exsheath in the rumen and migrate to the abomasum or small intestine, where they develop to adults over 2-3 weeks.

cascade.title: Abomasal attachment and blood feeding
cascade.detail: Adult Haemonchus attach to the abomasal mucosa with a buccal capsule and feed on blood, each worm removing a small but continuous volume. A heavy burden of several thousand worms produces a substantial daily blood loss.

cascade.title: Anaemia and hypoproteinaemia
cascade.detail: Continuous blood loss depletes iron and protein reserves, producing a normocytic anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia. The plasma protein loss into the gut also reduces oncotic pressure, producing oedema — the 'bottle jaw' swelling under the jaw.

cascade.title: Mucosal damage and malabsorption
cascade.detail: Teladorsagia and Ostertagia larvae develop within the abomasal glands, damaging parietal cells and reducing acid secretion. This produces a rise in abomasal pH, impaired protein digestion and a further loss of plasma protein into the gut.

cascade.title: Production loss and death
cascade.detail: The combined effects of anaemia, protein loss, reduced appetite and malabsorption produce weight loss, reduced milk yield and poor growth. Death occurs from acute haemorrhage in heavy Haemonchus infections, particularly during the rainy season.

lesions: Pale mucous membranes and, in severe Haemonchus infection, pale carcase fat and watery blood
Oedema of the submandibular region ('bottle jaw') and ventral abdomen
Abomasal mucosa showing numerous small bleeding points and attached worms ('barber's pole' appearance)
Abomasal mucosa thickened with characteristic 'cobblestone' nodules in ostertagiasis
Fluid intestinal contents with little formed faeces
Poor body condition and reduced fat reserves
clinical_signs: Pale mucous membranes and conjunctiva, which can be scored to estimate anaemia
Submandibular oedema ('bottle jaw') and ascites
Diarrhoea, which may be dark in Haemonchus infection
Weight loss and poor growth in young stock
Reduced milk yield
Lethargy and weakness
Sudden death in acute haemonchosis, especially in lambs during the rainy season

antemortem: FAMACHA scoring of the conjunctiva to assess anaemia and guide selective treatment — the cornerstone of sustainable control
Faecal egg count to estimate pasture contamination, not to diagnose individual disease
Body condition scoring and growth monitoring as production indicators
postmortem: Count adult worms in the abomasum and small intestine
Examine the abomasal mucosa for bleeding points and nodules
Note pale carcase fat and oedema
laboratory: Faecal egg count by McMaster technique
Faecal culture and larval differentiation to identify the species mix
Haematocrit or packed cell volume to quantify anaemia
Anthelmintic efficacy testing by faecal egg count reduction test
differentials: Coccidiosis — diarrhoea in young animals, but with blood and mucus and specific oocysts in faeces
Liver fluke — anaemia and hypoproteinaemia but with a different epidemiology and liver lesions
John's disease (paratuberculosis) — chronic weight loss with diarrhoea in adults
Chronic copper deficiency — anaemia and poor growth
Bovine viral diarrhoea and mucosal disease
Nutritional deficiency causing ill-thrift

prevention: Use targeted selective treatment based on FAMACHA scoring and body condition rather than whole-flock drenching
Rotate grazing and allow pasture rest periods to reduce larval challenge
Avoid overstocking and continuous grazing of the same paddock
Drench ewes around lambing to suppress the peri-parturient rise in egg output
Maintain refugia — leave a proportion of animals untreated to slow the development of resistance
Monitor anthelmintic efficacy with faecal egg count reduction tests
control.vaccination: A commercial Haemonchus vaccine based on a gut antigen (Barbervax) is available in Australia and some other countries and reduces worm burdens and egg output. It is not yet widely available in southern Africa. No effective vaccine exists for the other gastrointestinal nematodes relevant here.
treatment: Use a narrow-spectrum anthelmintic appropriate to the species — albendazole, levamisole or ivermectin
Dose accurately by weight, not by visual estimation
Combine treatment with management change; drenching alone selects for resistance
Treat only animals that need it — use FAMACHA and body condition as decision tools
Test efficacy after treatment to detect resistance early
outbreak: Treat clinically affected and anaemic animals immediately
Investigate the cause of the outbreak — typically a break in the drench programme or a resistant parasite population
Move animals to cleaner pasture if available
Perform a faecal egg count reduction test to check whether the anthelmintic used is still effective
Supportive care for severely anaemic animals, including consideration of blood transfusion in valuable animals
public_health: These gastrointestinal nematodes are not infectious to humans
Anthelmintic residues in meat and milk are the only public health consideration, and withdrawal periods must be observed
control.notes: Anthelmintic resistance is the central practical problem. Any control programme that relies on routine whole-flock drenching will fail within a few seasons, and FAMACHA-guided selective treatment is the most effective countermeasure in sheep and goats.

diseases.prognosis: Good for individual animals if treated before severe anaemia develops. Acute haemonchosis can kill lambs within days. At herd level, the prognosis depends on whether resistance is present and whether grazing management changes.

diseases.name: Theileriosis

agents.name: Theileria parva
agents.notes: An apicomplexan parasite of lymphocytes and erythrocytes. The infection has two distinct forms in southern Africa: a buffalo-derived form (Corridor disease) which is highly pathogenic in cattle, and a cattle-adapted form (January disease) which maintains itself in cattle populations.
agents.vector: Rhipicephalus appendiculatus (brown ear tick) and related Rhipicephalus species
agents.reservoir: African buffalo for the Corridor disease form; persistently infected cattle for the January disease form

agents.name: Theileria parva lawrencei
agents.notes: The buffalo-derived genotype transmitted by the same tick vectors. It produces a more acute and more uniformly fatal disease in cattle than the cattle-adapted T. parva parva.
agents.reservoir: African buffalo (Syncerus caffer)

hosts.notes: Buffalo are the reservoir for Corridor disease and are themselves unaffected. Cattle of all ages are susceptible, and unlike babesiosis there is no strong age-related resistance.

notifiable.note: Corridor disease is a major constraint on cattle production adjacent to buffalo areas across southern Africa and is notifiable wherever it occurs. It is a significant barrier to the movement of cattle from endemic to export zones.

diseases.distribution: Endemic across East and southern Africa. In southern Africa, the buffalo-derived form is a persistent threat in Zimbabwe, South Africa, Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique. In Botswana, theileriosis is a recognised risk in the northern areas where cattle and buffalo ranges overlap, and it constrains livestock movement in those districts.

aetiology.summary: Theileria is transmitted by Rhipicephalus ticks, but the decisive epidemiological feature is that buffalo are a silent reservoir. A single infected buffalo can maintain the parasite in a tick population and infect cattle grazing nearby, which is why buffalo fences and veterinary cordons — not acaricides alone — define the geography of the disease.
determinants: Presence of infected Rhipicephalus appendiculatus ticks
A reservoir of infection — African buffalo or persistently infected cattle
Susceptible cattle grazing in or near the vector and reservoir zone
The parasite's ability to transform host lymphocytes, which gives it a pathogenesis unlike other tick-borne diseases
risk_factors: Cattle grazing adjacent to buffalo areas, game reserves or the buffer zones around them
Introduction of naive cattle into an endemic area without immunisation
Movement of infected ticks on animals, vehicles or vegetation
Inadequate dip tank and acaricide programme
Shared grazing between cattle from different epidemiological zones
aetiology.epidemiology: Corridor disease is characterised by a low infection rate in ticks but very high case fatality in cattle — a small number of infected ticks is enough. January disease, the cattle-adapted form, spreads more efficiently in cattle but causes less dramatic mortality. Outbreaks of the buffalo-derived form often follow the movement of cattle closer to buffalo areas during dry seasons or through gaps in game fencing.

pathophysiology.summary: Theileria is the only eukaryotic pathogen known to transform host cells. Sporozoites invade lymphocytes and induce uncontrolled proliferation, producing a lymphoid hyperplasia that spreads the parasite through the body and causes the enlarged lymph nodes and lymphoid infiltrates that dominate the clinical picture. The subsequent destruction of these proliferating cells produces the anaemia and immunosuppression that ultimately kill the animal.

cascade.title: Sporozoite inoculation and lymphocyte invasion
cascade.detail: Infected ticks inoculate sporozoites during feeding. The sporozoites rapidly invade lymphocytes, particularly T cells in the draining lymph node, and the entry triggers a schizont stage inside the cell.

cascade.title: Reversible host-cell transformation
cascade.detail: The schizont induces the host lymphocyte to proliferate continuously, and the dividing parasite is distributed to both daughter cells. This produces massive clonal expansion of infected lymphocytes and the characteristic generalised lymphadenopathy.

cascade.title: Dissemination and lymphoid infiltration
cascade.detail: Proliferating infected lymphocytes carry the parasite to the lungs, liver, kidney, abomasum and other organs, where the schizont-containing cells infiltrate the tissues and cause the lesions associated with the disease.

cascade.title: Erythrocyte infection and anaemia
cascade.detail: Some parasites develop into piroplasms that infect erythrocytes. The combination of erythrocyte destruction and immune-mediated damage produces severe anaemia, which is the proximate cause of death in most cases.

cascade.title: Immunosuppression and death
cascade.detail: The massive lymphoid proliferation exhausts and dysregulates the immune system, leaving the animal vulnerable to secondary infection. Death is typically from anaemia, pulmonary oedema and secondary pneumonia, usually 2-4 weeks after infection.

lesions: Generalised enlargement of superficial and visceral lymph nodes, often the first gross finding
Pulmonary oedema with a heavy, wet lung and frothy exudate in the airways
Enlarged spleen and liver with lymphoid infiltrates
Pale mucous membranes from anaemia
Erosions and ulcers in the abomasum
Petechial haemorrhages on the serosa and kidneys
Lymphoid infiltrates in the interstitium of the kidney, liver and lungs on histology
clinical_signs: High fever (40-42 degrees Celsius) that starts 1-2 weeks after infection
Markedly enlarged superficial lymph nodes, particularly the parotid and prescapular nodes
Pale mucous membranes from progressive anaemia
Difficult, laboured breathing with a moist cough
Weight loss and rapid deterioration
Diarrhoea in the later stages
Petechial haemorrhages on the conjunctiva and vulva
Neurological signs and recumbency in the terminal phase

antemortem: Examine the prescapular and parotid lymph nodes: marked enlargement in a febrile animal in an endemic area is highly suggestive
Biopsy an enlarged lymph node and examine a smear for Koch bodies (schizonts) in lymphocytes
Examine a thin blood smear for piroplasms, which appear later in the course
postmortem: Note generalised lymphadenopathy and pulmonary oedema
Look for abomasal erosions and pale, anaemic carcase
Examine lymph node smears for schizonts
laboratory: Lymph node biopsy smear showing multinucleate schizonts in lymphocytes
PCR for species and genotype identification, which differentiates buffalo-derived from cattle-derived infection
Serology for herd prevalence surveys
Haematology showing anaemia
differentials: Babesiosis and anaplasmosis — both cause anaemia, but lymph node enlargement is not as marked
Heartwater — neurological signs and hydropericardium are more prominent
Bovine viral diarrhoea — mucosal lesions and PI animals, no enlarged superficial lymph nodes of this pattern
Malignant catarrhal fever — associated with sheep or wildebeest and mucosal necrosis
Lymphoma — lymph node enlargement but an entirely different history and course
Other tick-borne diseases may be present concurrently and complicate the picture

prevention: Maintain game fencing and veterinary cordons between buffalo and cattle areas
Dip or spray cattle regularly with acaricides to reduce tick challenge
Immunise naive cattle with an infection-and-treatment method before entering endemic areas
Quarantine and monitor animals moved between zones
Avoid grazing cattle in buffer zones adjacent to buffalo areas, particularly in dry seasons
control.vaccination: An inactivated schizont vaccine is available in some countries and provides partial protection against the buffalo-derived form. The classical approach is the infection-and-treatment method (ITM) — deliberate inoculation with stabilate followed by tetracycline treatment — which gives solid immunity to homologous challenge but carries the risk of clinical disease.
