ITM is practised only under veterinary supervision and with careful strain matching. There is no widely available conventional vaccine.
treatment: Parvaquone and buparvaquone are specific antitheilerial drugs and are effective if given early in the disease
Supportive care: blood transfusion for anaemia, fluids and anti-inflammatory treatment
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection
Treatment must be started early — once the pulmonary stage is established, response is poor
Halofuginone lactate has been used but is less commonly available
outbreak: Notify the veterinary authority immediately — this is a notifiable disease with trade implications
Impose movement restrictions on the affected premises and the surrounding area
Treat affected animals promptly with buparvaquone
Intensify tick control in an attempt to interrupt transmission
Trace animal movements and identify the source — typically contact with a buffalo area
Assess whether vaccination or immunisation of neighbouring herds is warranted
public_health: Theileria parva does not infect humans and has no public health significance
control.notes: The defining feature of Corridor disease is the tension between wildlife conservation and livestock production. Buffalo cannot be removed and cannot be vaccinated; the disease is managed by separating them.

diseases.prognosis: Poor without early treatment. Corridor disease in naive cattle carries a case fatality rate that can approach 90% once clinical signs are established. January disease is less severe and most animals survive with treatment.

diseases.name: Aflatoxicosis

agents.name: Aflatoxin B1
agents.notes: The most toxic and most common of the aflatoxins, produced by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus. Aflatoxin B1 is a potent hepatotoxin and the most potent natural carcinogen known. It is activated by hepatic cytochrome P450 to an epoxide that binds DNA and protein, causing hepatocellular necrosis and mutations.

agents.name: Aspergillus flavus
agents.notes: A ubiquitous mould that colonises stored grains, oilseeds and nuts. Growth and toxin production are favoured by warm temperatures (25-33 degrees Celsius), high humidity and insect or mechanical damage to the seed coat. Aflatoxin production is not visible — the mould may be present without toxin, and toxin may be present in feed that looks normal.
agents.reservoir: Contaminated stored grain, groundnuts, cottonseed, maize and their by-products

agents.name: Aspergillus parasiticus
agents.notes: A closely related species that produces both the B and G series of aflatoxins. It is less common than A. flavus but is a significant source of contamination in groundnuts in particular.
agents.reservoir: Contaminated groundnuts and oilseeds; soil

hosts.notes: All animals are susceptible, but ruminants are generally more resistant to acute aflatoxicosis than pigs and poultry. Dairy cattle are a special concern because they convert aflatoxin B1 to aflatoxin M1, which is excreted in milk and is a regulated human food contaminant.

notifiable.note: Aflatoxin is a regulated food and feed contaminant rather than a notifiable animal disease. Human exposure is a major public health issue across sub-Saharan Africa, where aflatoxin contamination of staple maize and groundnuts is widespread and contributes to liver cancer and childhood stunting.

diseases.distribution: Endemic in tropical and subtropical regions with warm, humid climates. Sub-Saharan Africa has among the highest dietary aflatoxin exposure levels in the world. In southern Africa, contamination of maize, groundnuts and sorghum is a recurring problem, particularly in years with a wet growing season and poor storage conditions.

aetiology.summary: Aflatoxicosis is caused by ingestion of feed contaminated with aflatoxins produced by Aspergillus moulds growing on poorly stored grain and oilseeds. The toxin is heat-stable and survives normal feed processing, so the only reliable control is preventing mould growth and rejecting contaminated batches.
determinants: Presence of aflatoxin-producing Aspergillus on the feed
Warm, humid storage conditions that allow mould growth and toxin production
Insect or mechanical damage to grain, which provides entry points for the fungus
Prolonged storage of grain at high moisture content
The dose and duration of exposure — chronic low-level exposure is more common than acute poisoning
risk_factors: Feeding stored maize, groundnuts or cottonseed that has been poorly dried or stored
Warm, humid climates and rainy harvests
Damaged or mouldy grain, particularly that which has been damp or insect-infested
Feeding dairy cows contaminated concentrate — the milk residue risk is the critical issue
Feeding pigs and poultry on contaminated rations, as they are the most susceptible species
Poor storage in sacks on the floor, without ventilation or moisture control
aetiology.epidemiology: Aflatoxicosis is a feed-borne problem that affects groups of animals receiving the same ration. Acute outbreaks occur when a highly contaminated batch enters the feed chain. Chronic low-level exposure is far more common and produces subclinical effects — reduced growth, immunosuppression and reduced fertility — which are easy to overlook. In dairy cattle, the economic issue is often the milk residue rather than the cow's health.

pathophysiology.summary: Aflatoxin B1 is absorbed from the gut and transported to the liver, where cytochrome P450 converts it to a reactive epoxide. The epoxide binds covalently to DNA and proteins, causing hepatocellular necrosis, inhibition of protein synthesis and, with chronic exposure, DNA mutations that initiate liver tumours. The same mechanism explains the immunosuppression and the reduced growth.

cascade.title: Ingestion and hepatic uptake
cascade.detail: Aflatoxin B1 is absorbed from the small intestine and transported to the liver via the portal circulation, where it is concentrated in hepatocytes.

cascade.title: Metabolic activation
cascade.detail: Cytochrome P450 enzymes convert aflatoxin B1 to a highly reactive 8,9-epoxide, which is the toxic and carcinogenic metabolite. The balance between activation and detoxification determines species susceptibility.

cascade.title: DNA and protein adduct formation
cascade.detail: The epoxide binds covalently to guanine residues in DNA and to lysine residues in proteins. DNA adducts cause mutations, particularly in the p53 tumour suppressor gene, and protein adducts impair enzyme function and cause cellular injury.

cascade.title: Hepatocellular necrosis and impaired protein synthesis
cascade.detail: Acute high-dose exposure produces centrilobular hepatic necrosis with jaundice and haemorrhage. Chronic exposure inhibits protein synthesis, reducing growth, milk production and immune function.

cascade.title: Immunosuppression, carcinogenesis and milk residues
cascade.detail: Chronic exposure suppresses cell-mediated immunity, increasing susceptibility to infectious disease. In the long term, DNA damage leads to hepatocellular carcinoma. In dairy cattle, aflatoxin B1 is converted to aflatoxin M1 and excreted in milk, creating a human food safety issue even when the cow shows no clinical signs.

lesions: Enlarged, pale, yellow-brown liver with centrilobular necrosis
Gall bladder distension with thickened bile
Subcutaneous and visceral haemorrhages from impaired clotting factor synthesis
Jaundice and generalised oedema in acute cases
Hepatic fibrosis and, in chronic cases, nodular regeneration and tumours
Atrophy of the thymus and lymphoid tissues in chronic exposure
clinical_signs: Reduced feed intake and growth rate
Weight loss and poor feed conversion
Jaundice and pale mucous membranes in acute cases
Diarrhoea, sometimes with blood
Reduced milk yield in dairy cattle
Increased susceptibility to infectious disease from immunosuppression
In pigs: reduced growth, and in severe cases, abortion
In poultry: reduced growth, poor feathering and increased mortality
In acute outbreaks: sudden death in young animals

antemortem: Feed analysis for total aflatoxin concentration — the most direct approach
Serum liver enzyme activity, particularly AST and GGT, which reflects hepatocellular damage
Serum bile acids or bilirubin in cases with jaundice
Feeding history and a comparison with unaffected groups on a different ration
postmortem: Examine the liver for pallor, enlargement and necrosis
Note jaundice, haemorrhages and oedema
Submit liver tissue for histopathology and feed samples for toxin analysis
laboratory: Feed analysis by HPLC, ELISA or lateral flow tests for aflatoxin
Liver histopathology showing centrilobular necrosis and bile duct proliferation
Detection of aflatoxin M1 in milk, which is a regulatory test in many countries
Aflatoxin-DNA or albumin adduct measurement in research and human biomonitoring
differentials: Other mycotoxins — fumonisin, ochratoxin, deoxynivalenol, which produce different syndromes
Pyrrolizidine alkaloid poisoning from plants such as ragwort and Crotalaria — similar hepatic damage
Infectious hepatitis and leptospirosis
Copper poisoning — jaundice and hepatic necrosis with a different exposure history
Photosensitisation from liver damage, which can be a consequence of aflatoxicosis rather than an alternative
Nutritional protein deficiency

prevention: Dry grain to below the safe moisture level before storage and keep it dry
Store feed in cool, dry, well-ventilated conditions and prevent insect damage
Test incoming feed batches for aflatoxin, particularly maize, groundnuts and cottonseed
Buy feed from suppliers with a documented mycotoxin testing programme
Use a mould inhibitor or organic acid preservative in high-risk feeds
Rotate feed stocks and avoid prolonged storage in humid conditions
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for mycotoxicosis. A vaccine for human aflatoxin exposure is in development but is not available.
treatment: Remove the contaminated feed immediately — this is the only specific treatment
Provide clean feed and good-quality forage
Use a toxin binder in the feed — hydrated sodium calcium aluminosilicate or yeast cell wall products — to reduce absorption
Supportive care: fluids, liver support with antioxidants and methionine, and vitamin E supplementation
Do not feed contaminated milk or produce to humans or calves
outbreak: Withdraw the suspect feed and submit samples for analysis
Identify the contaminated batch and its source
Treat affected animals supportively
Test milk for aflatoxin M1 if dairy cattle are involved, and withhold contaminated milk
Review storage and feed procurement practices
public_health: Aflatoxin is a Group 1 human carcinogen and a major cause of hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa
Chronic dietary exposure causes childhood stunting and immune impairment
Aflatoxin M1 in milk is a regulated contaminant, and milk from exposed cows must not enter the human food chain
Maize and groundnuts for human consumption should be tested and stored properly; sorting and processing reduce contamination but do not eliminate it
control.notes: Aflatoxin is heat-stable — cooking, baking and normal feed processing do not destroy it. Prevention is entirely a matter of storage and sourcing.

diseases.prognosis: Good if exposure is removed early and liver damage is limited. Poor in acute high-dose outbreaks with severe hepatic necrosis, where mortality can be significant. Chronic exposure causes permanent production loss and, in dairy cattle, persistent milk residue risk.

diseases.name: Botulism

agents.name: Clostridium botulinum
agents.notes: Gram-positive, spore-forming, strictly anaerobic rod. Spores are widespread in soil and sediment. The bacterium itself does not invade tissue — disease is caused entirely by preformed toxin ingested in feed or water.
agents.reservoir: Soil and aquatic sediment spore banks; decaying animal and plant matter

agents.name: Botulinum neurotoxin
agents.notes: The most potent biological toxin known. It is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that cleaves SNARE proteins at the presynaptic terminal, permanently blocking acetylcholine release. Heat-labile — destroyed by boiling for 10 minutes — but the spores survive boiling and require 120 degrees Celsius under pressure to inactivate.

hosts.notes: Cattle and sheep are affected mainly by toxin types C and D from decaying carcases or poultry litter. Horses are exquisitely sensitive and are usually affected by type B from hay or silage. Waterfowl die in large numbers from type C in anaerobic pond sediment.

notifiable.note: Human botulism is a public health notifiable event in most countries and is almost always food-borne, from home-preserved or improperly canned food rather than from livestock.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide. Spores are ubiquitous in soil, so the disease appears wherever feed or water is allowed to become anaerobic and toxin-producing.

aetiology.summary: Botulism is an intoxication, not an infection. The animal ingests preformed toxin in spoiled feed, contaminated water or decaying carcase material, and the toxin is absorbed from the gut to produce a descending flaccid paralysis. The bacterium does not need to colonise the animal.
determinants: Anaerobic conditions allowing C. botulinum to multiply and produce toxin — waterlogged feed, sealed silage, decaying carcases
Ingestion of the preformed toxin by a susceptible animal
A toxin type the host is sensitive to — type B for horses, C and D for ruminants
For young animals, ingestion of spores that germinate in the immature gut (infant botulism pattern)
Carcase material or poultry litter contaminating feed or pasture
risk_factors: Feeding poorly fermented or wet-wrapped silage, or hay baled damp
Poultry litter or deep litter used as fertiliser or feed
Dead animals or bones in feed, water troughs or pasture
Stagnant water with decaying organic matter in a drought
Phosphorus deficiency causing pica, which drives bone and carcase chewing
Broiler litter or fish-meal based rations in cattle
aetiology.epidemiology: Outbreaks are feed-associated and often involve a group of animals that shared the same ration, so attack rates can be high within a cohort while unaffected groups remain normal. Mortality is high without treatment. The disease is not transmitted between animals. The critical epidemiological clue is that cases appear together after a feed change or exposure to a common source, with no fever.

pathophysiology.summary: Botulinum toxin is absorbed intact from the small intestine, travels in blood to the neuromuscular junction, and irreversibly cleaves the SNARE proteins that mediate acetylcholine vesicle fusion. The result is a failure of cholinergic transmission producing descending flaccid paralysis, with consciousness and sensation fully preserved.

cascade.title: Ingestion and intestinal absorption
cascade.detail: Preformed toxin survives gastric acid, is absorbed across the small intestinal mucosa and enters the lymphatic and portal circulation. In young animals, ingested spores may germinate and produce toxin in the gut instead.

cascade.title: Haematogenous delivery to the neuromuscular junction
cascade.detail: Toxin reaches the presynaptic terminal of cholinergic synapses throughout the body, with a particular affinity for the highly vascularised, high-turnover junctions of the cranial nerves and proximal limb muscles.

cascade.title: SNARE cleavage
cascade.detail: The heavy chain binds the presynaptic membrane and the light chain, a zinc protease, cleaves SNAP-25, syntaxin or synaptobrevin depending on toxin type. Vesicles can no longer dock or fuse, so acetylcholine is not released.

cascade.title: Descending flaccid paralysis
cascade.detail: Without acetylcholine release, muscles receive no excitatory signal. Weakness begins in the hindlimbs and progresses cranially, involving the trunk, forelimbs and then the pharynx, larynx and respiratory muscles.

cascade.title: Respiratory failure and death
cascade.detail: Paralysis of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles produces hypoventilation and hypoxia. Death is from asphyxia, or from aspiration pneumonia after pharyngeal paralysis.

lesions: No gross lesions — post-mortem examination is typically unremarkable, which is itself a diagnostic finding
Possible aspiration pneumonia from pharyngeal paralysis
Gastric or intestinal content may contain suspect feed material
Histology shows no inflammatory lesion in muscle or nerve, as the toxin is functional rather than structural
clinical_signs: Rapidly progressive flaccid paralysis, starting in the hindlimbs and ascending cranially
Normal consciousness, appetite and sensation throughout — the animal is fully aware and unable to move
Dysphagia, drooling and inability to swallow, with food and water returning through the nose
Reduced pupillary light reflex and ptosis late in the course
Weak, shallow respiration progressing to respiratory distress
In cattle, 'downer cow' presentation that must be distinguished from hypocalcaemia and other recumbency causes
Sudden death in waterfowl, often with neck limpness ('limberneck')

antemortem: Clinical picture of flaccid paralysis with intact mentation, no fever and an identifiable feed risk
Examine the feed and water source — the epidemiological history is often more informative than any test
Differentiate from hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia with a blood sample and a therapeutic trial
postmortem: No characteristic lesion; the value of the examination is in excluding other causes
Look for foreign material, bones or carcase remnants in the rumen
Inspect the feed source and troughs for anaerobic spoilage
laboratory: Demonstration of toxin in serum, rumen or intestinal contents, or in the suspect feed, by mouse bioassay or ELISA
Culture of C. botulinum from feed with toxin detection in the culture supernatant
PCR for the neurotoxin genes bont/A-F
Serum is only useful if collected before toxin is cleared, which is early in the course
differentials: Hypocalcaemia — responds to calcium, whereas botulism does not
Hypomagnesaemia — tetany rather than flaccidity
Rabies — behavioural change, aggression and fever absent here
Tick paralysis — often with a visible engorged tick and a faster recovery after removal
Organophosphate poisoning — hypersalivation, miosis and muscle twitching rather than flaccidity
Snake envenomation — local swelling and a defined bite site
Poliomyelitis and other myelopathies

prevention: Feed properly fermented silage and dry, correctly baled hay; reject wet, mouldy or foul-smelling forage
Do not feed poultry litter or manure-contaminated material to cattle without appropriate control
Remove and bury carcases and bones from pasture and water sources promptly and completely
Correct phosphorus deficiency to reduce pica and bone-chewing
Provide clean, flowing water and prevent stagnation in troughs and dams
control.vaccination: Toxoid vaccines are available for cattle and are used in high-risk areas where feed contamination cannot be avoided. Horses and sheep have limited or no widely used licensed vaccines in most jurisdictions.
treatment: Antitoxin (polyvalent) is the specific therapy and is most effective if given very early, before toxin is fixed at nerve terminals
Remove the suspect feed and flush the gut with fluids; activated charcoal may bind remaining toxin in the gut
Supportive care: intravenous fluids, recumbent animal management, and sling support
Mechanical ventilation and tracheostomy in animals with respiratory failure — rarely available in field conditions
Antibiotics are of limited use because the bacterium is not invasive and toxin is already formed
outbreak: Withdraw the suspect feed from the entire group immediately
Submit feed samples for toxin testing before disposal
Identify and remove the source — a silage bunk, a dead animal in the water trough or a batch of litter
Notify the veterinary authority and, where human food is implicated, the public health authority
public_health: Human botulism is a medical emergency and requires immediate antitoxin administration
Home-canned, preserved or vacuum-packed foods are the common vehicle; commercial products are implicated occasionally
Boiling suspect food for at least 10 minutes destroys the toxin, though not the spores
Infants under 12 months should not be given honey, which can carry spores
control.notes: There is no fever in botulism, and that single observation carries a great deal of diagnostic weight in the field.

diseases.prognosis: Guarded to poor without antitoxin, with mortality commonly in the range of 50-90%. Recovery in survivors is slow because recovery requires regeneration of the nerve terminals, taking weeks to months. Animals that survive are generally unaffected long-term.

diseases.name: Nitrate and nitrite poisoning

agents.name: Nitrite (NO2-)
agents.notes: The proximate toxin. Plants accumulate nitrate, and rumen microbes reduce it to nitrite, which is absorbed into the blood, oxidises the ferrous iron of haemoglobin to the ferric form and produces methaemoglobin. Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so the animal effectively suffocates while its blood appears dark brown.

agents.name: Nitrate-accumulating forage and fertiliser
agents.notes: Nitrate accumulates in plants when uptake exceeds the capacity for reduction to protein — typically in drought-stressed plants, after heavy nitrogen fertilisation, or in the rapid growth phase. Cereal crops, brassicas, ryegrass and weeds are the usual sources. Nitrate fertiliser itself is a direct toxic hazard if animals access spills.

hosts.notes: Ruminants are much more susceptible than monogastrics because the rumen converts nitrate to the far more toxic nitrite. Monogastric animals can tolerate higher nitrate intakes, though nitrite itself is still toxic to them. Cattle are the most commonly affected species.

notifiable.note: A plant and fertiliser poisoning with no direct public health significance, though high dietary nitrate is a human food safety consideration in some vegetables.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide wherever nitrogen fertiliser is used on forage crops or where drought conditions cause nitrate accumulation. In southern Africa, nitrate poisoning is associated with fertilised pasture, cereal crops and weeds following drought-breaking rains.

aetiology.summary: Nitrate poisoning occurs when forage containing accumulated nitrate is consumed and rumen microbes reduce it to nitrite faster than the animal can metabolise it. The accumulation in plants depends on the balance between nitrogen uptake and the plant's capacity to convert it to protein, which is why drought-stressed and heavily fertilised plants are dangerous.
determinants: Nitrate accumulation in forage, driven by drought stress, fertilisation, low light or rapid growth
Rumen microbial reduction of nitrate to nitrite
The rate of nitrite absorption relative to the rate of its metabolism
The dose consumed, particularly when animals are hungry and eat greedily
Direct access to nitrate fertiliser
risk_factors: Feeding heavily nitrogen-fertilised pasture or hay
Drought-stressed crops and weeds, particularly cereals, brassicas and ryegrass
Sudden grazing of a nitrate-rich crop after a period of feed shortage
Access to nitrate fertiliser, spills or contaminated water
High nitrate water sources, which can be a significant contributor in drought
Low dietary energy, which limits the animal's ability to detoxify nitrite
aetiology.epidemiology: Outbreaks occur when a group is fed or grazed on the same high-nitrate forage, and severity correlates with intake. Cases often follow drought-breaking rain, which triggers rapid regrowth and nitrate accumulation in already-stressed plants. The condition is frequently confused with prussic acid poisoning because both are acute forage-associated intoxications.

pathophysiology.summary: Nitrate is reduced to nitrite in the rumen, and absorbed nitrite oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen. The result is a functional anaemia: the blood carries less oxygen, the tissues are hypoxic and the animal effectively suffocates. Methaemoglobin also shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve, further impairing oxygen delivery.

cascade.title: Ingestion of high-nitrate forage
cascade.detail: Plants that have accumulated nitrate are consumed, and the nitrate is released into the rumen. Rumen microbial nitrate reductase then reduces nitrate (NO3-) to nitrite (NO2-).

cascade.title: Absorption of nitrite
cascade.detail: Nitrite is absorbed across the rumen wall and into the bloodstream. The rate of absorption depends on rumen pH and the quantity of nitrite produced.

cascade.title: Haemoglobin oxidation
cascade.detail: Nitrite oxidises the ferrous (Fe2+) iron of haemoglobin to the ferric (Fe3+) form, producing methaemoglobin. Methaemoglobin cannot bind oxygen, and the blood takes on a dark brown or chocolate colour.

cascade.title: Impaired oxygen delivery
cascade.detail: Methaemoglobinaemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, and the surviving oxyhaemoglobin releases its oxygen less readily. Tissues become hypoxic despite a normal arterial oxygen tension.

cascade.title: Hypoxia, respiratory distress and death
cascade.detail: The brain and heart are most sensitive to hypoxia, producing weakness, rapid respiration, cyanosis, coma and death. Methaemoglobin levels above about 60-70% are usually fatal.

lesions: Dark brown or chocolate-coloured blood that does not brighten on exposure to air
Brown-tinged mucous membranes and tissues
Congestion and oedema of the lungs
Petechial haemorrhages in some cases
Plant material in the rumen consistent with the source
clinical_signs: Rapid, laboured breathing with a normal or slightly increased body temperature
Brown or blue-brown discolouration of the mucous membranes
Weakness, staggering and muscle tremors
Profuse salivation and abdominal discomfort
Cyanosis progressing to a brown-tinged colour in the oral mucosa
Convulsions and coma in severe cases
Sudden death, often within hours of exposure

antemortem: Rapid field test for methaemoglobin in a blood sample — a drop of blood that remains brown rather than turning bright red on exposure to air is highly suggestive
Blood gas or co-oximetry for methaemoglobin percentage where available
Response to methylene blue is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Forage and water analysis for nitrate concentration
postmortem: Dark brown blood and brown-tinged tissues are the characteristic finding
Note the presence of high-nitrate plant material in the rumen
Submit rumen contents and forage for nitrate analysis
laboratory: Methaemoglobin concentration in blood by co-oximetry
Nitrate measurement in plasma, aqueous humour or rumen fluid
Forage and water nitrate analysis
A bedside test using a drop of blood on filter paper — brown rather than red indicates methaemoglobinaemia
differentials: Prussic acid (cyanide) poisoning — also acute and forage-associated, but the blood is bright red rather than brown
Carbon monoxide poisoning — similar methaemoglobin-like picture but a different exposure history
Respiratory disease causing hypoxia — fever, cough and abnormal lung sounds
Urea poisoning — ruminants can be poisoned by excess urea; rapid death with severe hyperexcitability
Nitrate fertiliser ingestion — the same mechanism but a direct toxic exposure rather than plant accumulation

prevention: Test nitrate levels in forage before feeding, particularly in drought years
Avoid applying excessive nitrogen fertiliser, especially close to grazing
Do not graze drought-stressed or recently fertilised forage
Dilute high-nitrate forage with low-nitrate roughage
Provide adequate energy in the diet, which improves the rumen's capacity to detoxify nitrite
Secure nitrate fertiliser and prevent animal access
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional or fertiliser poisoning.
treatment: Methylene blue (methylthioninium chloride) is the specific antidote — it accelerates the reduction of methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin
Administer slowly intravenously under veterinary supervision, as methylene blue itself can be toxic at high doses
Remove the animal from the source of nitrate immediately
Supportive care: oxygen and fluids
Note that methylene blue is not effective in horses and is not used in that species
outbreak: Remove the offending forage or fertiliser immediately
Submit forage and water samples for nitrate analysis
Treat affected animals with methylene blue
Review fertiliser application and grazing management
Dilute the forage supply or source alternative roughage
public_health: Nitrate poisoning in livestock has no direct public health significance
High nitrate concentrations in drinking water are a human health concern, particularly for infants
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any veterinary medicines used
control.notes: The blood colour is the practical field differentiator: bright red suggests prussic acid, dark brown suggests nitrate. Both are acute forage intoxications and both require immediate removal from the source.

diseases.prognosis: Good with prompt methylene blue treatment — animals can recover rapidly and completely. Poor in severe cases with methaemoglobin above 60%, and many animals are found dead. Survivors generally have no lasting effects.

diseases.name: Prussic acid poisoning

agents.name: Hydrogen cyanide (prussic acid)
agents.notes: Produced when cyanogenic glycosides in plant tissue are hydrolysed by plant enzymes released after cell damage — chewing, wilting, frost damage or drought stress. Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome c oxidase, blocking the final step of oxidative phosphorylation. Death follows from histotoxic hypoxia: the blood remains fully oxygenated but the tissues cannot use the oxygen.
toxins: Cyanogenic glycosides (dhurrin in sorghum, prunasin in Prunus species)

agents.name: Cyanogenic forage and stress conditions
agents.notes: Sorghum, Sudan grass, Johnson grass, and Prunus species (chokecherry, bitter almond) contain cyanogenic glycosides. Young, rapidly growing plants, drought-stressed plants, regrowth after cutting or grazing, and frosted plants have the highest concentrations. Wilting and chopping release the enzymes that liberate cyanide.

hosts.notes: Ruminants are particularly susceptible because rumen microbial digestion releases cyanide from the glycosides. All species are susceptible, and horses are also commonly affected. Acute poisoning can kill within minutes to hours.

notifiable.note: A plant poisoning with no public health significance for livestock products, though the same toxin is a human food safety issue in cassava and bitter almonds.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide wherever cyanogenic plants are grazed or fed. In southern Africa, sorghum, Sudan grass and related forages are widely grown, and prussic acid poisoning is a recognised risk, particularly in drought years and after the first rains on regrowth.

aetiology.summary: Prussic acid poisoning is a lightning-fast intoxication that requires two things: a cyanogenic plant and the conditions that liberate cyanide from it. The plant itself is often harmless when healthy and mature; the danger appears when cells are damaged and the glycoside is hydrolysed to free cyanide.
determinants: Presence of cyanogenic glycosides in the forage
Rapid plant growth, drought stress, frost or regrowth, all of which increase glycoside concentrations
Plant cell damage from chewing, wilting, chopping or frost, which releases the hydrolysing enzymes
Rumen microbial digestion, which liberates cyanide from the glycosides
Consumption on an empty stomach, which increases the rate of toxin absorption
risk_factors: Grazing or feeding sorghum, Sudan grass, Johnson grass or chokecherry
Regrowth after cutting, drought or grazing — the most dangerous stage
Drought-stressed or frosted forage
Feeding wilted or freshly chopped forage, which allows enzyme action before consumption
Hungry animals turned onto dangerous forage
Baling or ensiling high-glycoside forage
aetiology.epidemiology: Poisoning occurs in outbreaks when a group is fed or grazed on the same dangerous forage. Cases are often found dead, and the history typically involves a recent change of pasture or a drought-breaking rain that produced rapid regrowth. The narrow window between exposure and death makes it a particularly feared problem.

pathophysiology.summary: Cyanide binds cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, blocking the cell's ability to use oxygen. The result is histotoxic hypoxia: arterial blood remains bright red and well oxygenated, but the tissues cannot extract the oxygen. The brain and heart, with the highest oxygen demand, fail first.

cascade.title: Liberation of cyanide from the plant
cascade.detail: Cell damage releases plant beta-glucosidases that hydrolyse cyanogenic glycosides, liberating free hydrogen cyanide. Chewing does this within the mouth, and rumen microbes continue the process.

cascade.title: Rapid absorption
cascade.detail: Free cyanide is absorbed rapidly from the rumen and small intestine into the bloodstream. Peak blood concentrations can be reached within minutes of ingestion.

cascade.title: Cytochrome oxidase inhibition
cascade.detail: Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), preventing the transfer of electrons to oxygen. Oxidative phosphorylation stops, and the cell cannot generate ATP despite an adequate oxygen supply.

cascade.title: Histotoxic hypoxia
cascade.detail: Because the block is at the tissue level, the blood remains oxygenated and the mucous membranes may appear bright red or cherry-red rather than cyanosed. Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactic acidosis.

cascade.title: Central nervous system and cardiac failure
cascade.detail: The brain and heart have the highest oxygen demand and fail first. The animal shows excitement, muscle tremors and convulsions, then respiratory depression and cardiac arrest. Death can occur within minutes of ingestion in acute cases.

lesions: Bright red or cherry-red blood and mucous membranes, a consequence of oxygenated blood that cannot be used
No specific gross lesion — the diagnosis is made on history and clinical signs
Congestion and petechial haemorrhages of the brain and meninges
Pulmonary oedema in some cases
Plant material in the rumen consistent with the suspected source
clinical_signs: Rapid onset of excitement, muscle tremors and staggering
Rapid, laboured breathing with a beating-flank appearance
Bright red or cherry-red mucous membranes
Profuse salivation and bloating
Convulsions and opisthotonos in severe cases
Collapse and death, sometimes within minutes of ingestion
In less acute cases, weakness, ataxia and recumbency with a slow recovery

antemortem: History of access to cyanogenic forage with a compatible clinical picture
Response to sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate is dramatic and diagnostic
Blood gas analysis may show a normal or high oxygen tension with a severe metabolic acidosis — the paradox of histotoxic hypoxia
Rapid field test for cyanide in the rumen or plant material, using a picrate paper test
postmortem: The rumen contents should be examined for cyanogenic plant material
The absence of specific lesions is itself a finding, and the diagnosis depends on the history and on plant and rumen analysis
The bright red colour of the blood and mucous membranes is characteristic but not invariable
laboratory: Cyanide quantification in rumen contents and blood, though the toxin degrades rapidly after death and results must be interpreted cautiously
Plant material analysis for cyanogenic glycosides
Picrate paper test on rumen gas as a rapid field test
Histopathology is generally unrevealing
differentials: Nitrate poisoning — also causes rapid death with methaemoglobinaemia, but the blood is dark brown rather than bright red and the clinical picture differs
Acute bloat — abdominal distension and respiratory compromise, but without the cherry-red blood
Botulism — flaccid paralysis rather than excitement and convulsions
Urea poisoning — rapid death with a very high rumen pH and hyperexcitability
Carbon monoxide poisoning — rare in livestock but produces similar signs
Organophosphate poisoning — salivation and muscle twitching but a different history and response to treatment

prevention: Avoid grazing sorghum, Sudan grass or Johnson grass during regrowth after drought, frost or cutting
Do not graze hungry animals onto risky forage — provide hay first
Cut and wilt cyanogenic forage before grazing, and allow the released cyanide to dissipate
Test susceptible forage before feeding it
Avoid feeding frosted or wilted cyanogenic forage
Allow at least 14 days of regrowth before grazing after a stress event
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for plant poisoning.
treatment: Sodium nitrite followed by sodium thiosulfate is the specific antidote — nitrite converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, which binds cyanide and pulls it away from cytochrome oxidase, and thiosulfate provides the sulfur for detoxification to thiocyanate
Administer intravenously and rapidly — the window is very short
Supportive care: oxygen supplementation and fluids
Remove the animal from the source immediately
In an outbreak, treat all affected animals whether or not they show signs
outbreak: Remove animals from the suspect forage immediately
Identify the source — the pasture or the feed batch
Submit plant and rumen samples for analysis
Treat remaining animals prophylactically
Review grazing management and the timing of regrowth grazing
public_health: Livestock poisoning does not create a food safety risk when affected animals are not slaughtered
The same cyanide chemistry matters in human foods such as cassava and bitter almonds, which must be properly processed
Observe meat withdrawal requirements if any veterinary medicines have been used
control.notes: The differential with nitrate poisoning is worth mastering: both kill fast, both are forage-associated, but prussic acid makes the blood bright red while nitrate makes it dark brown.

diseases.prognosis: Very poor in acute cases — animals are often found dead, and those that survive the first hour have a reasonable chance of recovery with the correct antidote. Surviving animals generally have no lasting effects.

diseases.name: Ketosis

agents.name: Negative energy balance
agents.notes: The proximate cause. In early lactation, energy demand for milk production exceeds energy intake, and the cow mobilises body fat. The liver cannot fully oxidise the resulting free fatty acids, which are converted to ketone bodies — acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone — that accumulate in blood, urine and milk.

agents.name: Rumen environment and feed intake
agents.notes: Poor feed quality, sudden dietary change and reduced rumen health reduce energy intake and precipitate the disorder, as does overconditioning at calving, which increases the mobilisation of fat.

hosts.notes: Dairy cows in early lactation are the classic group. Ewes carrying multiple lambs are at risk in the last 6 weeks of pregnancy when the growing fetuses compete with the ewe for glucose. Overconditioned cows are at higher risk than thin ones.

notifiable.note: A production disease with no public health significance. Human ketosis is a separate physiological state and is unrelated to bovine ketosis.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in dairy production, with the highest incidence in intensive systems where cows are fed high-concentrate diets and are selected for very high milk yield. In southern Africa, ketosis is recognised in intensive dairy herds and in ewes in extensive flocks during late pregnancy.

aetiology.summary: Ketosis is a disease of energy imbalance. The cow's energy requirement rises steeply at calving and peaks in early lactation, while feed intake lags behind — the result is a period of negative energy balance in which body fat is mobilised faster than it can be oxidised, and ketone bodies accumulate.
determinants: An energy requirement that exceeds intake, peaking around 2-6 weeks after calving
Impaired adaptation to negative energy balance, with excessive fat mobilisation
Insufficient or unpalatable feed, particularly inadequate concentrate in early lactation
Overconditioning at calving, which increases the amount of fat that can be mobilised
Concurrent conditions — retained placenta, metritis and displaced abomasum all reduce intake and precipitate ketosis
risk_factors: High-producing dairy cows in early lactation
Older cows and those carrying multiple fetuses in sheep
Overconditioned body condition score at calving
Poor transition management and abrupt dietary change
Concurrent disease such as metritis, mastitis or lameness
Hot weather and heat stress reducing intake
In sheep, late pregnancy in ewes carrying twins or triplets
aetiology.epidemiology: Ketosis is most common in the first 4-6 weeks after calving and affects a significant proportion of cows in some herds. It is often subclinical, with only reduced milk yield and fertility as consequences, which makes the true incidence hard to measure. It clusters in herds with poor transition management and in cows with concurrent periparturient disease.

pathophysiology.summary: In negative energy balance, adipose tissue is broken down faster than the liver can process free fatty acids. The liver esterifies excess fatty acids into triglycerides, partly stored and partly exported as very low-density lipoprotein, and the remainder is converted to ketone bodies. When ketone production outpaces utilisation, they accumulate and produce the clinical syndrome, while liver fat accumulation impairs hepatic function.

cascade.title: Negative energy balance
cascade.detail: At calving, energy demand for colostrum and milk synthesis rises abruptly, while dry matter intake falls. The gap is met by mobilising body fat, initially an appropriate adaptation.

cascade.title: Lipid mobilisation and hepatic uptake
cascade.detail: Free fatty acids are released into the circulation and taken up by the liver. When the supply exceeds the liver's capacity for oxidation and export, they are esterified to triglycerides.

cascade.title: Ketone body production
cascade.detail: Excess acetyl-CoA is converted to ketone bodies, which accumulate in the blood and are excreted in milk and urine. Ketones at high concentrations depress appetite, creating a vicious cycle of worsening negative energy balance.

cascade.title: Hepatic lipidosis
cascade.detail: Accumulated triglycerides produce fatty liver, which impairs gluconeogenesis and further reduces the liver's capacity to process the incoming fatty acid load. This is why ketosis and fatty liver are usually described together.

cascade.title: Production loss and clinical signs
cascade.detail: The combination of reduced feed intake, impaired rumen function, liver dysfunction and dehydration produces the clinical picture of a dull, anorexic cow with a rapid drop in milk yield. In sheep, the fetuses continue to demand glucose, and the ewe may progress to recumbency and death.

lesions: Pale, swollen and greasy liver with a fatty, yellow appearance
Increased liver weight with rounded margins
No other specific lesion — diagnosis is primarily clinical and biochemical
Possible evidence of concurrent periparturient disease
clinical_signs: Reduced appetite and reduced feed intake, often with refusal of concentrate
Sharp drop in milk yield, particularly in a high-producing cow
Rapid weight loss
A sweet, acetone-like odour on the breath and in the milk
Dullness, depression and reduced rumination
Hard, dry faeces and reduced rumen motility
In ewes: recumbency, blindness, tremors and eventual death
Subclinical cases show only reduced fertility and reduced milk yield

antemortem: Clinical signs and history of early lactation with reduced appetite and milk yield
Urine dipstick for ketones — a rapid field test with good sensitivity
Milk ketone testing, which is useful for herd-level monitoring
Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement, with concentrations above 1.2 millimoles per litre considered indicative
postmortem: Examine the liver for fatty infiltration, pallor and greasiness
Look for evidence of concurrent disease that precipitated the episode
laboratory: Serum or plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement
Urine ketone dipstick testing
Milk ketone testing
Liver biopsy or post-mortem histology showing fatty change, if required
differentials: Milk fever — recumbency and a response to calcium, not to glucose and ketone management
Displaced abomasum — reduced appetite and milk yield with a characteristic resonant ping
Retained placenta and metritis — fever and vaginal discharge
Rumen acidosis — a different history of concentrate feeding and rumen pH change
Fatty liver disease — usually occurs alongside ketosis rather than as an alternative
In ewes, pregnancy toxaemia is the same pathophysiology and is treated the same way

prevention: Improve transition-cow management, with a properly formulated close-up diet
Avoid overconditioning at calving — aim for a body condition score of about 3.0-3.5
Provide adequate, palatable feed in early lactation and increase concentrate gradually
Monitor early-lactation cows with regular ketone testing of milk or urine
Prevent and treat concurrent periparturient disease promptly
In ewes, feed a balanced diet in late pregnancy and manage litter size stress
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a metabolic disorder.
treatment: Intravenous glucose (usually as a 40-50% dextrose solution) corrects hypoglycaemia and is immediately effective but short-lived
Oral propylene glycol or glycerol provides a sustained glucose precursor and is the mainstay of treatment
Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone mobilise glucose and stimulate appetite, but they are contraindicated in late pregnancy and in animals with concurrent infection
Supportive care: encourage feed intake, provide palatable forage and good-quality hay
In ewes, consider a caesarean section or induction of parturition in severe pregnancy toxaemia, alongside glucose therapy
outbreak: Review the transition diet and the body condition of the affected group
Institution of ketone monitoring in early lactation
Identify and address concurrent disease such as metritis or lameness
Adjust the ration to improve energy density and intake in the first weeks of lactation
In sheep flocks, review the late-pregnancy feeding programme for ewes carrying multiples
public_health: Ketosis has no human health significance
Observe milk withdrawal periods for any corticosteroids or other veterinary medicines used
control.notes: Subclinical ketosis is the economically larger problem. A cow does not need to be visibly ill to lose milk yield and fertility — regular monitoring of early-lactation cows catches it before clinical disease.

diseases.prognosis: Good with prompt treatment — most cows respond to glucose and propylene glycol within 24-48 hours. Guarded if secondary complications develop or if recumbency has occurred. In ewes, pregnancy toxaemia carries a high mortality without early intervention.

references.label: Merck Veterinary Manual — Ketosis in cattle

diseases.name: Laminitis

agents.name: Rumen acidosis and endotoxaemia
agents.notes: The dominant cause in cattle. The sequence is a rumen fermentation crisis producing lactic acid and endotoxins, which enter the circulation and trigger the vascular and inflammatory events in the hoof laminae.

agents.name: Carbohydrate overload and lush pasture
agents.notes: In horses, the classic trigger is a pasture or grain carbohydrate overload. In cattle, the equivalent is a rumen acidosis episode, which may be subclinical and never noticed at the time.

agents.name: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide)
agents.notes: Released from Gram-negative bacteria in the rumen or gut during acidosis or sepsis, and absorbed into the circulation. Endotoxin is the mediator that links a gut event to a hoof lesion.

hosts.notes: Dairy cattle, feedlot cattle and horses are the main species affected. In cattle, laminitis is a disease of the hind hooves most often, and the typical presentation is chronic rather than acute.

notifiable.note: A production and welfare disease with no public health significance. It is one of the most important causes of lameness in dairy cattle worldwide.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in intensive livestock production. Lameness from laminitis and its sequelae is among the top three health and welfare problems in dairy herds globally.

aetiology.summary: Laminitis is a vascular and inflammatory disease of the hoof laminae triggered by a systemic event, most often a rumen fermentation crisis. In cattle, the initiating event is usually rumen acidosis or another source of endotoxaemia; the hoof lesion appears weeks or months later, which is why the cause is often missed.
determinants: A rumen acidosis episode or other source of systemic endotoxaemia
Absorption of endotoxins and vasoactive substances into the circulation
Inflammatory and vascular changes in the lamellar microvasculature
Concurrent conditions such as metritis, mastitis or retained placenta, which also produce endotoxaemia
Genetic and conformational predisposition, and hoof wear and housing factors that compound the risk
risk_factors: High-concentrate rations and rumen acidosis
Lush pasture and carbohydrate overload
Periparturient disease — retained placenta, metritis, mastitis
Concrete flooring and insufficient lying time
Poor hoof trimming and hoof care
Excessive body condition and rapid weight gain
In horses, lush spring pasture and grain overload
aetiology.epidemiology: In dairy herds, laminitis is endemic and its clinical expression is largely chronic — sole ulcers, white line disease and heel erosion. The acute form is uncommon in cattle compared with horses. The lag between the initiating gut event and the hoof lesion means that cases appearing in a herd are evidence of a management problem that occurred weeks or months earlier.

pathophysiology.summary: Endotoxins and vasoactive mediators produce a disturbance in the microcirculation of the hoof laminae, with vasoconstriction followed by congestion, oedema and ischaemia. The lamellar attachment between the hoof wall and the distal phalanx is weakened, and the mechanical load of the animal's weight causes further damage, leading to sinking and rotation of the pedal bone.

cascade.title: Systemic trigger and endotoxaemia
cascade.detail: A rumen acidosis episode or periparturient disease releases endotoxins into the circulation. These act on the vasculature throughout the body, with the hoof being particularly vulnerable because of its terminal blood supply.

cascade.title: Lamellar microvascular disturbance
cascade.detail: Vasoconstriction of the arterioles supplying the lamellar dermal papillae is followed by congestion and increased permeability. The laminae become oedematous and ischaemic.

cascade.title: Inflammatory injury to the lamellar junction
cascade.detail: Ischaemia and inflammatory mediators damage the epidermal-dermal junction that anchors the hoof wall to the distal phalanx. This is the structural lesion of laminitis, and it is not reversible.

cascade.title: Sinking and rotation of the pedal bone
cascade.detail: With the anchoring weakened, the weight of the animal causes the distal phalanx to sink within the hoof capsule and rotate. This compresses the solar corium and produces the clinical signs of sole pain.

cascade.title: Sole ulceration, white line disease and chronic lameness
cascade.detail: The damaged corium produces defective new horn and the resulting sole ulcer or white line separation provides a route for secondary bacterial infection. This chronic phase is what most cattle present with, and it accounts for the majority of the economic loss.

lesions: Congestion and haemorrhage of the lamellar dermis
Separation of the lamellar epidermis from the dermis
Sinking and rotation of the distal phalanx on radiography or post-mortem
Sole ulceration at the typical site, just caudal to the sole-bulb junction
White line disease and separation
Heel erosion and double soles
Secondary bacterial infection of the exposed corium
clinical_signs: Lameness, often in the hindlimbs and frequently bilateral
A stiff, shuffling gait with the animal shifting weight
Heat and swelling in the coronary band in the acute form
Reluctance to stand or walk on hard surfaces
In dairy cows, reduced milk yield, reduced fertility and increased culling
Sole ulcers and white line lesions visible on hoof examination
In severe cases, the animal may become recumbent

antemortem: Clinical lameness examination with hoof testing — sole ulceration at the typical site is diagnostic of chronic laminitis
Inspect the coronary band for heat and swelling in the acute form
Assess the herd prevalence of lameness and hoof lesions — individual diagnosis is relatively straightforward, but the herd problem is the important one
postmortem: Examine the hooves for sole ulceration, white line separation and pedal bone rotation
Sectioning the hoof demonstrates the sinking and rotation of the distal phalanx
laboratory: No specific laboratory test
Radiography of the hoof in valuable animals will show pedal bone rotation
Bacteriology of sole ulcers is useful to guide treatment of secondary infection
differentials: Digital dermatitis — a specific infectious lesion on the heel, not a laminitic lesion
Foot rot and interdigital necrobacillosis — acute swelling and lameness of the foot
Foul in the foot (interdigital phlegmon)
Fracture of the pedal bone or limb bones
Abscess of the sole from a puncture wound
Septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint

prevention: Prevent rumen acidosis through ration management and gradual adaptation
Ensure adequate physically effective fibre and consistent feeding
Maintain good lying comfort and minimise time standing on concrete
Provide regular professional hoof trimming and foot bathing
Treat periparturient disease promptly to reduce endotoxaemia
Manage body condition and avoid overconditioning
Keep cow tracks and walking surfaces in good condition
control.vaccination: A vaccine against Fusobacterium necrophorum has been used for digital dermatitis and interdigital phlegmon, but it is not a laminitis vaccine. There is no vaccine that prevents laminitis itself.
treatment: Correct the primary cause — management of rumen acidosis and treatment of periparturient disease
Sole ulcers: trim the affected claw, apply a block to the sound claw to relieve weight-bearing and treat the lesion
White line disease: explore and drain the lesion and apply a block
Anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) for pain relief and to reduce lamellar inflammation
Hoof bandaging and hygienic management of the affected foot
Culling (i.e. removal from the herd) of animals with unrecoverable, frequently recurring lesions
In horses, the treatment of acute laminitis is much more involved and involves foot support, icing and corrective trimming
outbreak: Investigate the herd-level cause: ration, housing, hoof trimming and foot hygiene
Audit the ration and rumen health of the group
Inspect cow tracks and flooring, and improve lying comfort
Introduce a foot bathing schedule for infectious hoof disease
Review the hoof trimming programme and the training of hoof trimmers
Monitor lameness prevalence and set a reduction target
public_health: Laminitis has no human health significance beyond welfare considerations
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any veterinary medicines used
control.notes: The single most important diagnostic concept is the lag. Hoof lesions seen today reflect a rumen or periparturient event months earlier, so the management investigation must look backwards.

diseases.prognosis: Guarded for the individual animal — laminitis is not reversible, and recovered animals frequently relapse. At herd level, the prognosis is excellent if the underlying rumen and housing problems are corrected, and poor if they are not.

diseases.name: Milk fever

agents.name: Calcium
agents.notes: Not an infectious agent, but a nutrient whose homeostatic control fails at parturition. The disorder is a failure of calcium mobilisation relative to the sudden calcium drain of colostrum and milk production, not a deficiency of calcium in the diet as such.

agents.name: Parturition and onset of lactation
agents.notes: The physiological trigger. The abrupt onset of milk synthesis in a high-producing dairy cow creates a calcium demand that can exceed the ability of the parathyroid hormone and vitamin D axis to mobilise calcium from bone and gut.

hosts.notes: High-producing dairy cows are the classic risk group — older, high-yielding cows in their third or later lactation. Jerseys and Guernseys are more susceptible than Holsteins. Ewes can develop the equivalent disorder in late pregnancy (pregnancy toxaemia-adjacent hypocalcaemia).

notifiable.note: A production disease with no public health or trade significance. Its importance is purely economic and welfare-related.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in dairy production systems. Particularly common in high-producing herds where cows are fed high-potassium forage and are not transitioned onto a controlled pre-calving diet.

aetiology.summary: Milk fever results from the failure of calcium homeostasis at the onset of lactation. The cow's calcium demand rises abruptly with colostrum production and milk synthesis, and the parathyroid response — bone resorption, renal conservation and increased intestinal absorption — is too slow to compensate, particularly when the diet is rich in potassium and low in magnesium.
determinants: A sudden increase in calcium demand at parturition and the onset of lactation
Delayed or inadequate parathyroid hormone response and bone calcium mobilisation
High dietary potassium, which reduces the responsiveness of the calcium-regulating mechanism
Low dietary magnesium, which impairs parathyroid hormone secretion and action
Age and lactation number, with older cows having a reduced capacity to mobilise bone calcium
risk_factors: High-producing dairy cows in their third or later lactation
High-potassium forage, such as lush pasture or silage from heavily fertilised land
Low-magnesium diets, particularly in spring grazing
Jersey and Guernsey breeds, which are genetically more susceptible
Sudden onset of high milk yield after calving
Absence of a transition diet or anionic salt programme before calving
aetiology.epidemiology: Milk fever is one of the most common metabolic disorders of dairy cattle, affecting a significant proportion of cows in some herds. Incidence is highest in the first 48 hours after calving. It recurs in subsequent lactations in affected cows and is a risk factor for secondary conditions, including retained placenta, metritis and displaced abomasum.

pathophysiology.summary: The onset of lactation drains calcium into colostrum faster than the parathyroid axis can mobilise it from bone, producing a rapid fall in ionised calcium. Because calcium is required for neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction and cardiac function, the deficiency produces the flaccid paralysis, recumbency and blunted gut and uterine motility that define the syndrome.

cascade.title: Calcium drain at parturition
cascade.detail: Colostrum contains a large amount of calcium, and the start of milk synthesis removes calcium from the extracellular pool abruptly — the demand can exceed the entire extracellular calcium pool within hours.

cascade.title: Impaired parathyroid response
cascade.detail: The parathyroid gland should respond to falling ionised calcium by increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. In a cow with a high-potassium diet, the parathyroid receptor is less responsive, so the response is delayed and inadequate.

cascade.title: Falling ionised calcium
cascade.detail: Ionised calcium, the physiologically active fraction, falls below around 0.8 millimoles per litre. Because calcium is needed for neurotransmitter vesicle release at the neuromuscular junction, this produces a failure of excitation-contraction coupling.

cascade.title: Flaccid paralysis and recumbency
cascade.detail: Muscle tone is lost, producing the characteristic recumbency, and smooth muscle motility is reduced, producing ruminal stasis and a blunted uterine response. The head often rests on the flank, and the animal may become unable to stand.

cascade.title: Cardiac and respiratory compromise
cascade.detail: Cardiac output falls, producing tachycardia and hypotension. Prolonged recumbency adds pressure myopathy and nerve injury, which explains why some cows do not rise even after calcium correction.

lesions: No characteristic gross lesions — the disorder is functional
Evidence of recumbency-related pressure myopathy in the hindlimbs in prolonged cases
Possible concurrent retained placenta, metritis or displaced abomasum
Aspiration pneumonia in recumbent cows
clinical_signs: Recumbency, usually within 48 hours of calving, with the head resting on the flank
Cold extremities and a subnormal temperature
Flaccid paralysis with the animal unable to rise
Dilated pupils and reduced pupillary reflex
Dry muzzle and skin, with reduced sweating
Ruminal stasis and absent defecation
Tachycardia with weak, arrhythmic heart sounds
In mild cases, tremors, ataxia and a wobbly gait before recumbency

antemortem: Clinical diagnosis based on recumbency within 48 hours of calving in a multiparous dairy cow, with no fever
Response to intravenous calcium is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Blood analysis showing low total and ionised calcium
Differentiate from hypomagnesaemia, ketosis and traumatic injury
postmortem: No diagnostic lesion — diagnosis is made clinically
Examine for secondary complications such as displaced abomasum or aspiration pneumonia
laboratory: Serum calcium below 2.0 millimoles per litre, with ionised calcium below 0.8 millimoles per litre in the acute form
Serum magnesium and phosphorus to identify concurrent deficiencies
Beta-hydroxybutyrate to exclude concurrent ketosis
differentials: Hypomagnesaemia (grass tetany) — similar recumbency but often with tetany, hyperaesthesia and convulsions
Ketosis — recumbency with a ketone smell, reduced appetite and a different response to therapy
Traumatic injury — pelvic fracture or limb fracture after slipping
Displaced abomasum — usually presents with anorexia and reduced milk yield rather than flaccid recumbency
Botulism — flaccid paralysis without the calving-associated timing
Septic metritis — fever and toxaemia distinguish it

prevention: Use a transition diet with a low dietary cation-anion difference (DCAD) before calving to acidify the blood and prime bone calcium mobilisation
Feed low-potassium forage in the close-up dry period
Ensure adequate magnesium in the pre-calving diet
Avoid overconditioning at calving
Provide a calcium binder or oral calcium supplementation to high-risk cows around calving
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a metabolic disorder.
treatment: Intravenous calcium borogluconate (usually as a 23% solution) is the specific and life-saving treatment
Administer slowly while monitoring the heart, because rapid infusion can cause arrhythmia and cardiac arrest
Oral calcium supplements, particularly as gels or boluses, for follow-up or for mild cases
Provide bedding and assist the cow to rise; lift her body to allow circulation to recover
Treat secondary complications such as mastitis, metritis or displaced abomasum
Note that a cow that does not rise after calcium is likely to have pressure myopathy or another problem
outbreak: Review the pre-calving diet and transition management
Check forage potassium and magnesium levels
Introduce a DCAD programme under veterinary supervision
Consider oral calcium boluses for all cows around calving in problem herds
Monitor the incidence and identify the at-risk group
public_health: Milk fever has no human health significance
Milk from treated cows is subject to withdrawal periods only if antibiotics or other veterinary medicines have been administered
control.notes: The 'downer cow' is the practical challenge. Calcium corrects the hypocalcaemia within minutes, but an animal that has been recumbent for hours may already have pressure myopathy that no amount of calcium will reverse.

diseases.prognosis: Excellent with prompt intravenous calcium — many cows stand within minutes to hours. Guarded if recumbency has been prolonged, because of the risk of pressure myopathy, aspiration pneumonia and secondary conditions.

diseases.name: Bloat

agents.name: Rapid fermentative gas production
agents.notes: Gas accumulates in the rumen faster than it can be eructated. Two forms exist — frothy bloat, in which gas is trapped in a stable foam that cannot be eructated, and free gas bloat, in which a physical obstruction prevents eructation.

agents.name: Legume and concentrate pasture composition
agents.notes: Lush, immature legumes — particularly clovers and lucerne — contain soluble proteins that form a stable foam with rumen gas. High-concentrate diets produce excess gas from rapid fermentation. Frost or heavy dew can also precipitate the condition in susceptible pasture.

hosts.notes: Ruminants of all ages are susceptible. Feedlot cattle on high-concentrate rations and dairy cattle on lush legume pasture are the main risk groups.

notifiable.note: An acute production disease with no public health significance, but a significant cause of sudden death.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide wherever ruminants graze lush legume pasture or are fed high-concentrate rations. In southern Africa, frothy bloat is common on lucerne and clover pasture, particularly in the first grazing of the season or after rain.

aetiology.summary: Bloat arises when rumen gas production outpaces the capacity for eructation. In frothy bloat, the gas is trapped in a stable protein foam and cannot form the free gas bubble needed to trigger eructation. In free gas bloat, a physical obstruction prevents eructation entirely. The two forms have different causes and require different management.
determinants: Rapid fermentation producing large volumes of gas
Formation of a stable foam from soluble plant proteins and saponins, which traps gas
Physical obstruction to eructation in free gas bloat — foreign body, oesophageal obstruction, milk fever-induced rumen stasis or lymphadenopathy
The absence of a normal eructation reflex, which can be disturbed by concurrent disease
risk_factors: Grazing lush, immature lucerne, clover or other legume pasture
First grazing of a legume pasture after a period of other feed
Frost or heavy dew on legume pasture, which increases foam formation
Sudden introduction to high-concentrate feed
Hypocalcaemia and rumen stasis, which impair eructation
Oesophageal obstruction from roots or foreign bodies
aetiology.epidemiology: Cases occur in outbreaks rather than individually, because the pasture or ration affects the whole group. Frothy bloat is most common in the morning when animals graze lush pasture after a period off feed. Free gas bloat is sporadic and usually has an identifiable physical cause.

pathophysiology.summary: Distension of the rumen by trapped gas compresses the diaphragm and the caudal vena cava. The result is reduced venous return, impaired cardiac filling and respiratory compromise, which together produce shock and death — the animal essentially suffocates and fails to circulate blood because its rumen has no room to expand.

cascade.title: Gas production in the rumen
cascade.detail: Rapid fermentation of lush pasture or concentrate produces large volumes of carbon dioxide and methane, which in normal animals are eructated continuously.

cascade.title: Foam formation
cascade.detail: Soluble plant proteins and saponins in immature legumes form a stable foam with the gas. The bubbles are too small and the foam too stiff to rise and form the free gas layer that triggers the eructation reflex.

cascade.title: Ruminal distension
cascade.detail: The rumen distends progressively and pushes the diaphragm forward and the abdominal wall laterally, producing a visibly bloated animal with a drum-like left flank.

cascade.title: Compression of the diaphragm and vena cava
cascade.detail: Diaphragmatic compression reduces tidal volume and produces respiratory distress. Compression of the caudal vena cava reduces venous return to the heart, producing a fall in cardiac output and blood pressure.

cascade.title: Shock and death
cascade.detail: The combination of hypoxia and cardiovascular collapse produces shock and death, often within 30 minutes to a few hours of the first sign. Death is a consequence of compression, not of gas toxicity.

lesions: Markedly distended rumen filling the abdominal cavity
Pale, congested or haemorrhagic lungs from compression and hypoxia
Congestion of the liver and spleen from venous obstruction
Frothy material in the rumen in frothy bloat
Evidence of the inciting cause, such as an oesophageal foreign body or hypocalcaemia
clinical_signs: Distension of the left flank, which is drum-like on percussion
Rapid, laboured respiration with grunting and mouth-breathing
Profuse salivation and frequent attempts to eructate
Restlessness, kicking at the abdomen and continual rising and lying down
Rapid heartbeat and weak pulse
Cyanosis of the mucous membranes in advanced cases
Inability to belch, with the animal extending the neck and groaning
Death within a short period in severe cases

antemortem: Clinical diagnosis: left flank distension with a resonant, drum-like note on percussion and a history of lush pasture or concentrate
Pass a stomach tube to distinguish frothy bloat from free gas bloat — gas will escape through the tube in free gas bloat
Examine the animal for signs of hypocalcaemia or an oesophageal obstruction
postmortem: Markedly distended rumen with either frothy contents or free gas
Pale, congested lungs and evidence of venous congestion
Look for the underlying cause of free gas bloat, such as a foreign body in the oesophagus
laboratory: No laboratory diagnosis is required in the field
Rumen fluid analysis for foam stability and pH may be useful in research or retrospective investigation
Serum calcium should be measured if hypocalcaemia is suspected as a contributing cause
differentials: Oesophageal obstruction — free gas bloat with a history of foreign body or root crop
Hypocalcaemia — rumen stasis with bloat as a secondary feature
Vagal indigestion — chronic recurrent bloat with a different history
Tetanus — rigidity with a distended abdomen but different clinical signs
Rumen acidosis — usually with diarrhoea and a different time course
Esophageal injury or stricture

prevention: Introduce cattle gradually to lush legume pasture over 7-10 days
Avoid grazing legumes when they are wet from dew or after frost
Feed hay or fibre before turning animals onto lush pasture
Use anti-bloat oils and surfactants in the drinking water or via a slow-release device
Consider feeding poloxalene or monensin in high-risk grazing situations
Manage pasture height — avoid grazing very short or very lush stands
control.vaccination: A bloat vaccine based on rumen bacterial antigens has been developed and is used in some countries, with variable results. It is not widely available in southern Africa.
treatment: Pass a stomach tube — in free gas bloat this alone may relieve the pressure
For frothy bloat, administer anti-foaming agents such as simethicone or vegetable oil directly via the stomach tube
Stimulate eructation by walking the animal or placing it on an incline with the head downhill
Rumenotomy or trocarisation of the left flank is a last resort for acute, life-threatening distension
Treat underlying causes such as hypocalcaemia or oesophageal obstruction
outbreak: Remove animals from the offending pasture immediately
Provide hay and water and allow animals to settle
Treat affected animals and monitor the group
Review grazing management and introduce anti-bloat measures before returning to the pasture
Identify the pasture species and maturity stage and adjust the grazing plan
public_health: Bloat has no human health significance
control.notes: The distinction between frothy and free gas bloat determines the treatment. A stomach tube relieves free gas but does not help frothy bloat, where the foam must be broken down chemically.

diseases.prognosis: Good if treated early; most animals recover once gas is released or the foam is broken. Poor if the animal is presented late with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise. Untreated severe bloat is rapidly fatal.

diseases.name: Cobalt deficiency

agents.name: Cobalt
agents.notes: Cobalt is required by rumen bacteria to synthesise vitamin B12 (cobalamin). Animals cannot use cobalt directly — the requirement is entirely mediated through rumen microbial synthesis. Deficiency therefore produces a functional vitamin B12 deficiency.

agents.name: Deficient pasture and grazing land
agents.notes: Cobalt deficiency is a property of the soil and the pasture growing on it, and it recurs in the same localities. It is typically associated with sandy, leached or granite-derived soils with low cobalt content.

hosts.notes: All ruminants depend on rumen microbial synthesis of B12 and are therefore susceptible. Young, growing animals are most severely affected because their requirement is highest.

notifiable.note: A nutritional deficiency with no public health significance. It is a classic cause of unexplained ill-thrift in grazing livestock.

diseases.distribution: Occurs worldwide in specific soil types, particularly sandy, granitic or leached soils. Historically documented as 'bush sickness' in New Zealand and Australia, and as 'pine' in Scottish sheep. In southern Africa, cobalt deficiency is recognised as a cause of ill-thrift in grazing livestock on certain soil types, though it is less frequently diagnosed than copper deficiency.

aetiology.summary: Cobalt deficiency is a rumen-microbial problem before it is an animal problem. The rumen bacteria cannot synthesise adequate vitamin B12 without sufficient dietary cobalt, so the animal develops a functional B12 deficiency even though it never receives any B12 in its diet. The resulting impairment of propionate metabolism and of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is what produces the ill-thrift.
determinants: Low cobalt concentration in the pasture or feed
Low cobalt availability in the soil, typical of sandy, granitic or leached soils
The requirement of the rumen microbial population for cobalt to synthesise B12
High demand in young, growing animals and in pregnant or lactating females
Rumen health — anything that disrupts the rumen microbial population reduces B12 synthesis
risk_factors: Grazing on cobalt-deficient soils, particularly sandy or granitic areas
Young, rapidly growing animals
Late pregnancy and lactation
Periods of pasture shortage when animals are forced to graze closer to the soil
Exclusive reliance on conserved forage from deficient land without supplementation
aetiology.epidemiology: Like other trace-element deficiencies, cobalt deficiency is a property of the land and affects whole herds and flocks in defined areas. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is often missed because animals lose condition gradually without specific signs. The clinical picture is indistinguishable from other causes of ill-thrift without laboratory confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Cobalt is a component of the vitamin B12 molecule, which is required for two key reactions: the conversion of propionate to succinate (via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) and the methylation of homocysteine to methionine (via methionine synthase). Deficiency therefore impairs glucose production from propionate and disrupts protein and folate metabolism, producing weight loss, poor growth and anaemia.

cascade.title: Inadequate cobalt in the rumen
cascade.detail: Rumen bacteria require cobalt to synthesise cobalamin. When dietary cobalt is low, the bacterial production of B12 falls, and the animal's supply of vitamin B12 declines even though the animal itself has no direct cobalt requirement.

cascade.title: Impaired propionate metabolism
cascade.detail: The conversion of propionate to succinate requires methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a B12-dependent enzyme. Propionate is the major glucose precursor in ruminants, so its accumulation impairs glucose production and energy metabolism.

cascade.title: Impaired amino acid and folate metabolism
cascade.detail: Methionine synthase, also B12-dependent, is impaired, disrupting the methyl folate cycle and causing functional folate deficiency. Protein synthesis and cell division are affected, explaining the poor growth and anaemia.

cascade.title: Progressive weight loss and ill-thrift
cascade.detail: The animal loses appetite and condition, becomes lethargic and develops a rough coat. The process is gradual, and by the time clinical signs are apparent the animal may have lost considerable weight.

cascade.title: Anaemia, infertility and death in severe cases
cascade.detail: B12 deficiency impairs erythropoiesis, producing a macrocytic anaemia. Reproductive performance declines, and in severe, prolonged deficiency animals can die from progressive emaciation.

lesions: Pale, emaciated carcase with depleted fat reserves
Macrocytic anaemia on haematology
Fatty degeneration of the liver in severe cases
No specific gross lesion — the diagnosis depends on blood or liver B12 measurement and pasture cobalt analysis
clinical_signs: Progressive weight loss and poor growth in young stock
Reduced appetite and feed intake
Rough, dull coat and lethargy
Pale mucous membranes from anaemia
Reduced fertility and delayed puberty
In severe cases, weakness, recumbency and death
Often a herd-level problem rather than individual cases

antemortem: Serum vitamin B12 measurement — the practical diagnostic test
Liver vitamin B12 concentration for a more definitive assessment of status
Forage and soil cobalt analysis to assess the supply
Haematology showing a macrocytic anaemia
postmortem: Note generalised emaciation and pale carcase
Liver B12 measurement on post-mortem tissue
No specific lesion, so the diagnosis rests on laboratory confirmation
laboratory: Serum or plasma vitamin B12 assay
Liver vitamin B12 concentration
Pasture and soil cobalt analysis
Response to cobalt supplementation is a useful retrospective confirmation
differentials: Copper deficiency — also causes ill-thrift and anaemia, and often coexists
Selenium deficiency — weakness and poor growth
Parasitic gastroenteritis — weight loss with a different faecal finding
John's disease (paratuberculosis) — chronic weight loss with diarrhoea
Chronic malnutrition and inadequate protein intake
Chronic liver disease
Generalised chronic disease including tuberculosis

prevention: Supplement cobalt via mineral licks, drenches or slow-release boluses
Use cobalt-containing fertiliser on deficient pasture where practical
Provide cobalt-supplemented concentrate or mineral mixes during high-demand periods
Monitor animals on deficient land and treat groups rather than individuals
Test pasture and soil cobalt before developing new grazing land
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional deficiency.
treatment: Oral cobalt supplementation — cobalt sulphate or cobalt chloride in the drinking water, mineral mix or drench
Vitamin B12 injection for a rapid response in severely affected animals
