Cobalt boluses or slow-release devices for sustained supplementation in extensive systems
Treat the whole group on affected land, because subclinical deficiency is usual
Address pasture cobalt status through fertiliser application for a long-term solution
outbreak: Confirm the diagnosis before blanket supplementation
Analyse the pasture and soil to characterise the deficiency
Implement a supplementation programme appropriate to the grazing system
Monitor weight gain and body condition response over the following weeks
Consider that copper and cobalt deficiencies frequently coexist, and test for both
public_health: Cobalt deficiency in livestock has no direct public health significance
Cobalt is a regulated feed additive, and supplementation levels must comply with local feed regulations
control.notes: The diagnosis is almost always of ill-thrift without a specific sign. Cobalt deficiency is worth testing for whenever a herd shows unexplained poor growth on a soil type known to be deficient.

diseases.prognosis: Excellent if treated before severe emaciation. Recovery of appetite and weight gain follows supplementation within weeks. At herd level, the prognosis is good with a sustained supplementation programme.

diseases.name: Copper deficiency

agents.name: Copper
agents.notes: An essential trace element required for cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase and caeruloplasmin. Its deficiency impairs the cross-linking of collagen and elastin, the maturation of erythrocytes and the protection of cells from oxidative damage.

agents.name: Dietary antagonists and soil conditions
agents.notes: Copper deficiency is usually secondary to excess molybdenum, sulphur or iron in the diet, which form insoluble complexes with copper in the rumen and prevent absorption. Primary deficiency from low soil copper also occurs. The distinction matters because the treatment is different.

hosts.notes: Cattle and sheep differ importantly in tolerance: sheep are much more susceptible to copper toxicity, which constrains the treatment options. Lambs develop the neurological form (swayback/enzootic ataxia) from deficiency in utero.

notifiable.note: A nutritional deficiency with no public health significance, but significant production and welfare effects in deficient areas.

diseases.distribution: Widespread in grazing livestock, particularly on sandy, leached or high-molybdenum soils. In southern Africa, copper deficiency is recognised in several cattle-rearing areas, and the region's often sandy soils and marginal trace-element status make it a relevant diagnosis in ill-thrift investigations.

aetiology.summary: Copper deficiency arises from an absolute shortage of copper in the diet or, more commonly, from interference with absorption by molybdenum, sulphur and iron. The distinction between primary and secondary deficiency determines whether supplementation must be increased or the antagonist addressed.
determinants: Low copper concentration in pasture or feed
High molybdenum intake, which forms insoluble copper-molybdenum-sulphur complexes in the rumen
High sulphur intake, particularly from water or fertiliser, which worsens the copper-molybdenum interaction
High iron intake, which competes with copper for absorption
The animal's copper requirement, which rises in pregnancy and lactation
risk_factors: Grazing on sandy or leached soils with low copper availability
Pasture with high molybdenum or sulphur content, especially on certain soil types
High-iron water or feed supplements
Late pregnancy and lactation, when maternal copper is transferred to the fetus and milk
Sheep breeds with a high copper requirement, and the risks of over-supplementing sheep
Feeding conserved forage and concentrates with marginal copper content over long periods
aetiology.epidemiology: Deficiency is a property of the land and the feed, so it affects whole herds and flocks, and recurs in the same areas. Clinical cases tend to appear in young animals — swayback in lambs, and in calves the neurological and skeletal forms — while adults show subclinical production loss, anaemia and infertility. Molybdenum-induced deficiency can be severe even when pasture copper looks adequate on analysis, which is why forage analysis alone can mislead.

pathophysiology.summary: Copper is required by lysyl oxidase for the cross-linking of collagen and elastin, by cytochrome c oxidase for mitochondrial energy production, and by superoxide dismutase and caeruloplasmin for iron metabolism and oxidative defence. Deficiency therefore produces structural weakness of connective tissue, anaemia and neurological impairment depending on the tissue most affected at the time of the deficit.

cascade.title: Impaired copper absorption
cascade.detail: Copper is absorbed in the rumen and small intestine, where molybdenum and sulphur form insoluble complexes with it. The bioavailability of dietary copper is therefore reduced to a fraction of its total content.

cascade.title: Depletion of liver stores
cascade.detail: Liver copper is the primary reserve. It is depleted progressively in the face of a negative copper balance, and supplementation takes weeks to replenish it, which is why oral dosing has a delayed effect.

cascade.title: Impaired collagen and elastin cross-linking
cascade.detail: Lysyl oxidase requires copper to cross-link collagen and elastin, so deficiency produces weak connective tissue. This manifests as skeletal fragility, arterial wall weakness and poor hoof and hair quality.

cascade.title: Neurological damage in the developing fetus
cascade.detail: Copper is essential for myelination and neuronal development. Deficiency in late pregnancy produces the degenerative spinal cord lesion responsible for swayback in lambs, which develops before birth and is not reversible after birth.

cascade.title: Anaemia and production loss
cascade.detail: Copper is required for iron mobilisation and haemoglobin synthesis. Deficiency produces a microcytic hypochromic anaemia, together with reduced growth, reduced fertility and impaired immune function.

lesions: Pale, anaemic carcase with a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia on haematology
Degeneration of the white matter in the spinal cord and brainstem (swayback) in lambs
Osteoporosis and skeletal fragility, particularly in calves
Poor hair or wool quality, with 'steely' wool and depigmentation
Weak arterial walls and, rarely, aortic rupture
Low liver copper concentration on tissue analysis
clinical_signs: Ill-thrift and poor growth in young stock
Pale mucous membranes from anaemia
Rough, depigmented coat and poor hair growth
Hindlimb ataxia and swaying gait in lambs (swayback)
In calves, stiffness, reluctance to move and, in severe cases, knuckling of the fetlocks
Reduced fertility and delayed puberty
Poor immune function and increased susceptibility to disease
In horses, developmental orthopaedic disease and weak connective tissue

antemortem: Serum or plasma copper and caeruloplasmin measurement
Liver biopsy for liver copper concentration — the most reliable indicator of body status
Haematology showing a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia
Forage and water analysis for copper, molybdenum, sulphur and iron, interpreted together rather than in isolation
postmortem: Liver copper analysis, which is the definitive test of status
In lambs with swayback, examine the spinal cord for myelin degeneration
Note pale carcase, poor hair quality and skeletal fragility
laboratory: Liver copper concentration by dry-weight analysis
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin
Forage analysis including molybdenum, sulphur and iron to assess copper availability
Histopathology of the spinal cord in neurological cases
differentials: Selenium and vitamin E deficiency — white muscle disease causes similar weakness and gait abnormality
Cobalt deficiency — ill-thrift without the neurological signs
Zinc deficiency — skin and hoof lesions with poor growth
Parasitic gastroenteritis and other causes of ill-thrift
Swayback must be distinguished from other causes of neonatal ataxia, including birth trauma and cerebellar lesions
Enzootic ataxia of sheep and goats requires differentiation from caprine arthritis encephalitis in goats

prevention: Supplement copper according to the level of deficiency and the amount of antagonist in the diet
Use mineral licks, injections or boluses appropriate to the species and the degree of deficiency
Correct excessive molybdenum and sulphur intake rather than simply adding more copper
Monitor liver or serum copper status regularly in high-risk herds
Avoid over-supplementation, particularly in sheep, which are highly susceptible to copper toxicity
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional deficiency.
treatment: Injectable copper glycinate or copper heptanoate gives a rapid response but has limited duration and carries a toxicity risk
Oral copper supplementation via mineral licks, drenches or boluses is the mainstay of herd supplementation
Copper oxide wire particles as rumen boluses provide slow release over several months
Crucially, do not treat sheep with the same dose used for cattle — sheep are 10-fold more susceptible to copper toxicity, which can be fatal
Where molybdenum excess is the cause, reduce molybdenum intake or increase copper supplementation accordingly
outbreak: Confirm the diagnosis with liver or serum copper before supplementing the herd
Analyse the forage, water and soil to identify whether the problem is primary deficiency or antagonism
Implement a supplementation programme appropriate to the species and season
Monitor the response and reassess copper status after several weeks
Review the grazing plan and consider moving animals away from high-molybdenum pasture
public_health: Copper deficiency in livestock has no direct public health significance
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any injectable copper products used
control.notes: The sheep-cattle difference is the most important safety point in this record. Copper supplementation that is appropriate for cattle can kill sheep, and this is a recurring cause of avoidable sheep mortality on mixed farms.

diseases.prognosis: Good if the deficiency is corrected before permanent damage occurs. Neurological damage from swayback in lambs is permanent — those animals should be euthanased on welfare grounds. At herd level, the prognosis depends on correcting the underlying soil, forage or antagonist problem.

diseases.name: Grass tetany

agents.name: Magnesium
agents.notes: The deficient nutrient. Magnesium is essential for parathyroid hormone secretion and action, for neuromuscular transmission and for enzyme function. Ruminants cannot mobilise magnesium from bone reserves, so they depend entirely on continuous dietary intake — the reason hypomagnesaemia can develop within days.

agents.name: Spring grazing and lactation
agents.notes: The management trigger. Lush, rapidly growing grass in spring is low in magnesium and high in potassium, which further reduces magnesium absorption. Lactating cows have an increased magnesium requirement that coincides with the period of lowest dietary supply.

hosts.notes: Lactating cows are the main group affected, particularly older, high-producing animals. Sheep are also affected, usually ewes in late pregnancy or early lactation. Young animals grazing with their dams are less often affected.

notifiable.note: A production disease with no public health significance.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in temperate and subtropical grazing systems. Most common in spring on rapidly growing pasture, and on soils with low magnesium or high potassium. In southern Africa, it occurs in sheep and cattle on lush irrigated or fertilised pasture, and in ewes in late pregnancy.

aetiology.summary: Grass tetany is a failure of magnesium supply rather than of regulation. Because ruminants have no meaningful bone magnesium reserve, plasma magnesium falls within days when intake is low. The problem is compounded by high potassium and nitrogen fertilisation, which reduce magnesium absorption from the rumen.
determinants: Low dietary magnesium intake from pasture that is low in magnesium
High potassium intake from heavily fertilised or rapidly growing grass, which reduces magnesium absorption
High ammonium or protein levels in lush pasture, which compete with magnesium absorption
The increased magnesium demand of lactation and late pregnancy
The absence of any bone magnesium reserve to buffer a shortfall
risk_factors: Spring grazing on lush, rapidly growing pasture
Heavy potassium or nitrogen fertilisation
Lactating cows in early lactation, particularly older high-yielding animals
Ewes in late pregnancy and early lactation
Sudden change from hay or conserved forage to lush pasture
Cold, wet or stressful weather, which reduces grazing intake
Poor magnesium status of the soil, common in sandy or leached soils
aetiology.epidemiology: Grass tetany occurs in outbreaks rather than as isolated cases, because the pasture conditions affect the whole grazing group. The peak is in spring and early lactation, and it is often triggered by a change in weather that reduces feed intake. Untreated cases are rapidly fatal, which makes the disease particularly feared by producers.

pathophysiology.summary: Magnesium is a required cofactor for the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and for the normal function of the calcium-regulating system. When plasma magnesium falls, the neuromuscular junction becomes hyperexcitable — the opposite of the pattern in milk fever — producing tetany, convulsions and death.

cascade.title: Dietary magnesium shortfall
cascade.detail: Ruminants absorb magnesium inefficiently from the rumen and have no significant bone reserve, so plasma magnesium falls within a few days of a low-magnesium intake.

cascade.title: Impaired parathyroid function
cascade.detail: Magnesium is required for parathyroid hormone secretion and for its action on target tissues, so hypomagnesaemia produces a secondary hypocalcaemia in many cases, which worsens the neuromuscular signs.

cascade.title: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability
cascade.detail: Low extracellular magnesium reduces the threshold for nerve and muscle excitation by removing the normal magnesium block on calcium influx at the presynaptic terminal. The result is spontaneous and uncoordinated muscle activity.

cascade.title: Tetany and convulsions
cascade.detail: Hyperexcitability produces muscle tremors, staggering, hyperaesthesia to touch and sound, and eventually tonic-clonic convulsions. Animals may become aggressive or unresponsive.

cascade.title: Cardiac and respiratory arrest
cascade.detail: The terminal event is often cardiac or respiratory arrest during a convulsion. Death can occur within hours of the first signs, and many animals are simply found dead.

lesions: No specific gross lesion — the disorder is functional
Possible bruising or trauma from convulsions and falling
Evidence of low magnesium status in forage and serum analysis
clinical_signs: Muscle tremors and twitching, particularly of the face and flanks
Staggering gait and an unsteady, stiff-legged stance
Hyperaesthesia — exaggerated response to touch, noise and light
Excitement, aggression or unusual behaviour
Tetanic spasms and tonic-clonic convulsions
Profuse sweating and an elevated heart and respiratory rate
Sudden death, often found without any observed prior signs
In sheep, similar signs with a frequent head-back posture during convulsions

antemortem: Clinical picture of tetany and hyperaesthesia in a lactating animal on lush pasture in spring
Response to intravenous magnesium and calcium is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Serum magnesium below 0.8 millimoles per litre, with clinical signs usually appearing below 0.5 millimoles per litre
Serum calcium may also be low, reflecting the secondary hypocalcaemia
postmortem: No specific lesion; the diagnosis is typically made from history and clinical findings
Note any bruising or trauma from convulsions
laboratory: Serum magnesium measurement, ideally before treatment
Serum calcium to detect concurrent hypocalcaemia
Forage analysis for magnesium and potassium content
differentials: Hypocalcaemia (milk fever) — flaccid paralysis rather than tetany, and a different response to therapy
Ketosis — recumbency and inappetence without tetany
Tetanus — also causes rigidity but with trismus and a wound history
Organophosphate poisoning — hypersalivation and miosis with muscle twitching
Acute lead poisoning — convulsions with a different exposure history
Plant poisoning causing convulsions, such as strychnine-containing plants

prevention: Provide magnesium supplementation during the risk period — magnesium oxide or magnesium chloride added to feed, or in a mineral mixture
Use magnesium-containing blocks or licks, though intake can be unreliable
Apply magnesium fertiliser to pasture where deficiency is a recurring problem
Avoid over-fertilisation with potassium and nitrogen, which impair magnesium absorption
Provide hay or fibre alongside lush pasture to improve rumen function and intake
Consider slow-release magnesium boluses for high-risk groups
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional deficiency.
treatment: Intravenous magnesium sulphate, often combined with calcium borogluconate, is the specific treatment
Administer slowly, monitoring for cardiac arrhythmia and respiratory depression
Follow with oral magnesium supplementation to prevent relapse, which is common within days
Provide shelter and quiet handling — affected animals may convulse if handled roughly
Treat in-contact animals with oral magnesium because the whole group is likely to be deficient
outbreak: Administer magnesium to all animals in the affected group
Analyse forage and consider amending the fertiliser programme and the supplementary feeding regime
Identify the pasture conditions that triggered the outbreak
Provide hay or conserved forage to reduce dependence on lush pasture
Review the mineral supplementation programme for the season
public_health: Grass tetany has no human health significance
Observe withdrawal periods if antibiotic or other veterinary treatments have been used alongside magnesium therapy
control.notes: The distinction between milk fever and grass tetany is clinically critical: both cause recumbency in a recently calved cow, but the treatment and the appearance of the animal differ. Flaccid suggests calcium; rigid and twitchy suggests magnesium.

diseases.prognosis: Excellent with prompt intravenous treatment; most animals recover quickly. Guarded for cases found in convulsions or already recumbent. Untreated cases are usually fatal within hours, and relapse after treatment is common without oral follow-up.

diseases.name: Rumen acidosis

agents.name: Excess readily fermentable carbohydrate
agents.notes: The cause is a ration or grazing episode in which rapidly fermentable starch or sugar overwhelms the rumen's buffering and absorptive capacity. The primary insult is dietary, not infectious.

agents.name: Streptococcus bovis
agents.notes: A rumen bacterium that proliferates explosively when starch is abundant, producing lactic acid as the end product of fermentation. Its overgrowth converts a normally near-neutral rumen into an acid-producing vat, and the resulting lactic acid accumulation is the proximate cause of the acidosis.
toxins: Endotoxins released from Gram-negative rumen bacteria on death

agents.name: D-lactic acid
agents.notes: The isomer produced preferentially by S. bovis. It is poorly metabolised by the animal and is absorbed into the bloodstream, contributing to systemic acidosis and neurological signs. Its accumulation distinguishes acute ruminal acidosis from simple low rumen pH.

hosts.notes: Feedlot cattle adapted to high-concentrate rations are the classic group for subacute disease. Any ruminant that gains sudden access to grain — a broken feed bin, a spilled load, a first introduction to concentrate — can develop the acute form.

notifiable.note: A production disease with no public health significance. It is one of the most economically important nutritional disorders in feedlot and intensive dairy systems.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide in intensive ruminant production, particularly feedlots, dairy herds on high-concentrate rations and sheep finishing systems. In southern Africa it is a recognised risk in feedlots and in dairy herds during ration transitions.

aetiology.summary: Rumen acidosis results from a mismatch between the fermentability of the diet and the rumen's adaptive capacity. When a large load of starch or sugar arrives faster than the rumen microbes can adapt, S. bovis outgrows the normal population, lactic acid accumulates faster than it is absorbed or metabolised, and rumen pH falls abruptly.
determinants: A sudden increase in the proportion of readily fermentable carbohydrate
Inadequate adaptation of the rumen microbial population to the new ration
Insufficient physically effective fibre to stimulate rumination and saliva production
The buffering capacity of the rumen, which is exceeded by rapid acid production
Feeding management — slug feeding, irregular feeding times or competition at the trough
risk_factors: Abrupt introduction of grain or high-concentrate feed
Insufficient fibre in the ration
Overmixing of concentrate in a total mixed ration, allowing sorting
Feedlot entry and ration step-up programmes that are too aggressive
Accidental access to a grain store or spilled concentrate
Hot weather reducing feed intake and altering feeding patterns
Low rumen pH in the pre-calving period in dairy cows
aetiology.epidemiology: Acute acidosis is an event, often affecting a group that gained access to a large amount of grain at once. Subacute ruminal acidosis (SARA) is a chronic herd-level problem, prevalent in 20-30% of cows in many dairy herds, and is difficult to detect because it produces no dramatic signs — only reduced fibre digestion, reduced milk fat and laminitis over time.

pathophysiology.summary: Rapid starch fermentation produces lactic acid faster than the rumen can absorb or buffer it, driving rumen pH below the tolerance of the normal fibre-digesting population. The resulting lactic acidosis kills the buffering microbes, releases endotoxin from dying Gram-negative bacteria, and draws water into the rumen osmotically, producing systemic acidosis and dehydration.

cascade.title: Starch overload
cascade.detail: A large load of readily fermentable carbohydrate enters the rumen and is rapidly fermented by the amylolytic bacterial population, particularly Streptococcus bovis and Lactobacillus species.

cascade.title: Lactic acid accumulation
cascade.detail: S. bovis produces lactic acid rather than the volatile fatty acids produced by the normal fibre-digesting population. Lactic acid is a stronger acid and is absorbed and metabolised more slowly, so it accumulates and drives rumen pH below 5.0.

cascade.title: Microbial die-off and endotoxin release
cascade.detail: The low pH kills the acid-sensitive population, including protozoa and the fibre-digesting bacteria, releasing endotoxins from Gram-negative bacteria as they die. These endotoxins are absorbed across a damaged rumen epithelium.

cascade.title: Osmotic fluid shift and dehydration
cascade.detail: The accumulation of lactate and the associated solutes raises rumen osmolarity, drawing water from the circulation into the rumen. The result is systemic dehydration, haemoconcentration and reduced blood volume.

cascade.title: Systemic acidosis and its consequences
cascade.detail: Absorbed D-lactic acid and endotoxin produce a metabolic acidosis, cardiovascular compromise and, in the acute form, death. Survivors frequently develop rumenitis, liver abscesses and laminitis in the weeks that follow.

lesions: Rumen contents that are watery, sour-smelling and low in fibre
Rumen pH below 5.0 in the acute form
Ruminal epithelium that is congested, eroded or sloughing
Rumenitis with secondary bacterial or fungal invasion
Liver abscesses as a sequela of rumenitis in feedlot cattle
Laminitis and hoof lesions in chronic cases
Dehydration and haemoconcentration
clinical_signs: Reduced feed intake and rumination
Diarrhoea, often with undigested grain visible in the faeces
Distended abdomen and a sloshing, fluid-filled rumen
Depression, weakness and reluctance to move
Dehydration with sunken eyes
In acute cases: staggering, recumbency, tachycardia and death
In subacute cases: reduced milk fat, reduced feed efficiency and laminitis
Secondary liver abscesses and caudal vena cava syndrome in chronic feedlot cases

antemortem: Rumen fluid pH measurement via rumenocentesis or stomach tube — the definitive field test
Examine rumen fluid for consistency, colour and protozoal activity
Urine pH, which falls in systemic acidosis
History of a ration change or accidental grain access
postmortem: Measure rumen pH and examine the rumen contents for grain and absence of fibre mat
Inspect the rumen epithelium for congestion, erosion and sloughing
Look for liver abscesses and hoof lesions
laboratory: Rumen fluid pH measurement — below 5.0 indicates acute acidosis, 5.0-5.5 indicates subacute
Blood gas analysis showing metabolic acidosis and low bicarbonate
Serum or plasma lactate, including D-lactate
Urine pH as a proxy for systemic acid-base status
differentials: Bloat — distension without the acidotic signs and different rumen fluid
Simple indigestion from a dietary change — rumen pH near normal
Ketosis — reduced intake and ketones, but with a different metabolic profile
Bovine viral diarrhoea and other enteritis-causing infections
Salmonellosis
Rumen impaction — a different rumen fluid consistency and history

prevention: Step up concentrate rations gradually over at least 3 weeks
Include adequate physically effective fibre to stimulate rumination and saliva flow
Feed total mixed rations and prevent sorting
Maintain consistent feeding times and avoid slug feeding
Use rumen buffers such as sodium bicarbonate in high-risk rations
Monitor rumen pH or milk fat as an early indicator of subacute acidosis
control.vaccination: A vaccine against S. bovis and Lactobacillus has been developed and used in some feedlot systems with modest results. It is not a substitute for ration management and is not widely used in southern Africa.
treatment: Remove the offending feed and provide good-quality hay to stimulate rumination
Correct dehydration and acidosis with intravenous fluids, including bicarbonate where indicated
Rumen buffers — sodium bicarbonate or magnesium hydroxide — by stomach tube in acute cases
Rumenotomy or rumen lavage may be required in severe grain overload
Broad-spectrum antibiotics in severe cases to address the bacterial overgrowth and endotoxaemia
Treat laminitis and liver abscesses as they become apparent in the following weeks
outbreak: Remove access to the offending feed immediately
Provide hay and water and allow animals to stabilise
Treat severely affected animals with fluids and buffers
Review the ration formulation and step-up programme
Monitor for sequelae — laminitis, liver abscesses and reduced performance — over the following weeks
public_health: Rumen acidosis has no human health significance
Observe withdrawal periods for any antibiotics used in treatment
control.notes: The acute form is dramatic and easily recognised. The subacute form is the economically larger problem and is invisible without deliberate monitoring — milk fat depression and unexplained laminitis are the practical clues.

diseases.prognosis: Good with early intervention in mild cases. Guarded to poor in acute grain overload, where mortality can be high without aggressive treatment. Survivors often suffer permanent consequences, including laminitis and reduced production.

diseases.name: Selenium deficiency

agents.name: Selenium
agents.notes: An essential trace element incorporated into the selenoproteins, including glutathione peroxidase, which protects cell membranes from oxidative damage. Its functions are intimately linked to vitamin E, and the two deficiencies produce overlapping syndromes.

agents.name: Low-selenium soils and pasture
agents.notes: Selenium deficiency is a property of the soil and is common on acidic, sandy or heavily leached soils, and in areas with low selenium in the parent geological material. Vitamin E deficiency from poor-quality conserved forage often coexists.

hosts.notes: Young, rapidly growing animals are most susceptible to white muscle disease. Adult animals show reproductive failure and ill-thrift. Sheep are particularly sensitive to selenium toxicity, so supplementation must be dosed carefully.

notifiable.note: A nutritional deficiency with no public health significance directly, although the narrow margin between selenium requirement and toxicity makes supplementation a regulated practice in many countries.

diseases.distribution: Widespread in livestock-rearing areas worldwide, particularly where soils are derived from selenium-poor parent material or where rainfall leaching has depleted the element. In southern Africa, selenium-responsive disease is recognised in several areas, and the combination of selenium and vitamin E deficiency is a common cause of neonatal mortality in lambs and calves.

aetiology.summary: Selenium deficiency impairs the antioxidant defences of cells, making them vulnerable to oxidative damage. Rapidly growing muscle and cardiac tissue are the most affected, producing nutritional muscular dystrophy. The deficiency frequently coexists with vitamin E deficiency, and the two should be considered together.
determinants: Low selenium concentration in soil and therefore in pasture
Low vitamin E intake from conserved forage, particularly hay and silage that has lost tocopherol during storage
Rapid growth in young animals, which increases the oxidative demand on muscle
The narrow margin between requirement and toxicity, which constrains supplementation
The transfer of selenium from dam to fetus and neonate, which depends on maternal status
risk_factors: Grazing on selenium-deficient soils
Feeding conserved forage that has lost vitamin E
Neonatal and rapidly growing young stock
High-grain diets that are low in vitamin E
Pregnancy and lactation, when demand increases
Multiple births in sheep, which increase the demand on the ewe
aetiology.epidemiology: The deficiency is a property of the land and recurs in the same areas. The most visible form is white muscle disease in newborn or rapidly growing lambs and calves, which can cause substantial neonatal mortality. Adult cows may show reduced fertility and increased retained placenta, and the deficiency can be subclinical for years.

pathophysiology.summary: Selenium is a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase, which detoxifies lipid peroxides; vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant in membranes. Together they protect cell membranes from oxidative damage. When either is deficient, peroxidation of membrane lipids proceeds unchecked, particularly in tissues with high oxidative metabolism — skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and the vascular endothelium.

cascade.title: Antioxidant deficit
cascade.detail: Inadequate selenium limits glutathione peroxidase activity, and inadequate vitamin E removes the membrane antioxidant. The two defences are interrelated, and deficiency of either compromises the total antioxidant capacity.

cascade.title: Lipid peroxidation of membranes
cascade.detail: Reactive oxygen species peroxidise the polyunsaturated fatty acids of cell membranes, damaging membrane integrity and function. This is particularly damaging in tissues with high energy turnover and abundant mitochondria, such as skeletal and cardiac muscle.

cascade.title: Myodegeneration
cascade.detail: Muscle fibres undergo hyaline degeneration and necrosis. The affected muscle is pale and streaked with white fibrous tissue — hence 'white muscle disease' — and the damage impairs locomotion and, when the heart is involved, cardiac function.

cascade.title: Cardiac involvement
cascade.detail: Lesions in the myocardium are the most dangerous because they are irreversible. The heart may be pale and flabby, and affected newborns may die suddenly or be weak and unable to suckle.

cascade.title: Clinical expression in the neonate or growing animal
cascade.detail: Newborn animals born with lesions may be stillborn, die in the first days of life or show stiffness and weakness. Rapidly growing older animals develop progressive stiffness and a characteristic stilted gait.

lesions: Pale, streaked, chalky-white muscle, particularly in the thigh, shoulder and lumbar muscles
Bilateral, symmetrical distribution of muscle lesions
Pale, flabby heart muscle with white streaking
Myocardial necrosis and fibrosis on histology
Possible pulmonary oedema from cardiac failure
Low blood or liver selenium and vitamin E concentrations
clinical_signs: Weakness and inability to stand in newborn lambs and calves
Stiffness and a stilted gait in growing animals
Reluctance to move and muscle tremors
Sudden death in neonates from cardiac involvement
Poor growth and ill-thrift
Reduced fertility and increased retained placenta in adult cattle
In severe cases, aspiration pneumonia from recumbency

antemortem: Serum selenium and vitamin E measurement
Whole-blood glutathione peroxidase activity as a functional indicator of selenium status
Liver or kidney selenium concentration for a more definitive assessment
Consider the herd history and the presence of other deficient animals
postmortem: Pale, streaked muscle lesions in a symmetric distribution
Examine the myocardium for pallor and fibrosis
Measure liver selenium to confirm the deficiency
laboratory: Serum selenium and vitamin E
Whole-blood glutathione peroxidase activity
Liver selenium concentration by dry-weight analysis
Histopathology of muscle showing hyaline degeneration and necrosis (Zenker's degeneration)
differentials: Copper deficiency — similar weakness and ill-thrift, but without the specific white muscle lesions
Cobalt deficiency — ill-thrift without muscle lesions
White muscle disease must be distinguished from other causes of neonatal weakness: prematurity, dystocia, hypothermia and septicaemia
Toxaemic and septic conditions causing sudden death in neonates
Rumen acidosis and other metabolic causes of lameness in older animals

prevention: Supplement selenium and vitamin E in deficient areas, particularly in late pregnancy
Use selenium-containing mineral licks, injectable products or slow-release boluses
Ensure adequate vitamin E intake by providing good-quality conserved forage or supplementary vitamin E
Monitor selenium status of herds on known-deficient soils
Avoid over-supplementation — selenium has a narrow margin of safety and can be toxic
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional deficiency.
treatment: Injectable selenium and vitamin E (sodium selenite plus alpha-tocopherol) is the standard treatment and is rapidly effective
Oral selenium supplementation is used for follow-up and prevention
Supportive care for weak neonates: warmth, colostrum and assisted feeding
Treat the whole group on deficient land, not only the clinically affected animals
Note that selenium toxicity can occur with over-supplementation — follow product guidance exactly
outbreak: Confirm the diagnosis with blood or tissue selenium measurement
Implement supplementation of the at-risk group, particularly pregnant females and neonates
Analyse forage and soil to characterise the deficiency
Review the mineral supplementation programme and the vitamin E intake
Monitor the response in the following lambing or calving season
public_health: Selenium deficiency in livestock has no direct public health significance
Selenium is a recognised essential trace element for humans, and supplementation is regulated in food and feed
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for injectable products
control.notes: The selenium and vitamin E pair should always be considered together. Treating selenium deficiency while overlooking vitamin E deficiency, or vice versa, explains many treatment failures.

diseases.prognosis: Good for growing animals with mild deficiency if treated promptly. Poor for neonates with established cardiac lesions. At herd level, prevention through supplementation in late pregnancy is highly effective.

diseases.name: Zinc deficiency

agents.name: Zinc
agents.notes: An essential trace element required as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes and for the transcription factors that regulate gene expression. It is central to keratinisation of the skin, wound healing and immune function, which is why its deficiency presents predominantly as a skin disease.

agents.name: Dietary antagonists and excess calcium
agents.notes: Excess calcium and phosphorus, particularly from high-calcium diets and legume forage, form insoluble complexes with zinc and reduce its absorption. Phytates in cereal grains have the same effect. The problem is usually not a lack of zinc in the diet but a lack of available zinc.

hosts.notes: Pigs are classically susceptible — parakeratosis in weaner pigs is the textbook presentation. Calves and goats also show a characteristic zinc-responsive dermatitis, particularly around the muzzle, eyes and hooves.

notifiable.note: A nutritional deficiency with no public health significance, though it is an important differential in skin disease and one of the most commonly missed diagnoses.

diseases.distribution: Worldwide, particularly where soils are low in zinc or where animals are fed high-calcium or high-phytate rations. In southern Africa, zinc-responsive dermatitis is recognised in calves and goats and is a regular consideration in the differential diagnosis of crusting skin disease.

aetiology.summary: Zinc deficiency is usually a problem of reduced availability rather than absolute absence. High dietary calcium and phytate bind zinc in the gut, and the resulting deficiency impairs the keratinisation of the epidermis, producing a crusting dermatitis that is often mistaken for infectious or parasitic skin disease.
determinants: Low zinc concentration in the diet
Excess calcium and phosphorus intake, particularly from high-legume forage
High phytate intake from cereal grains
The presence of other divalent cations (copper, iron) competing for absorption
High zinc demand during rapid growth, pregnancy and lactation
risk_factors: High-calcium diets, particularly in pigs and in cattle on legume pasture
Cereal-based rations with high phytate content
Rapidly growing weaner pigs
Calves and goats on limited-diversity diets
Grazing on zinc-poor soils
Feeding a diet with excessive supplemental calcium for growth or milk production
aetiology.epidemiology: Zinc deficiency is a herd or group problem related to the ration or the land. In pigs, it is most common in weaners after the change from sow's milk to a cereal-based ration. In calves and goats, it appears in animals on marginal diets or with excessive calcium supplementation. Cases respond rapidly to zinc supplementation, which is itself diagnostic.

pathophysiology.summary: Zinc is required for the synthesis of keratin and for the normal maturation of the epidermis. When zinc is deficient, keratinocytes proliferate but fail to mature and keratinise normally — a state called parakeratosis — producing retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, thickened skin, crusting and impaired wound healing.

cascade.title: Reduced zinc absorption
cascade.detail: Zinc is absorbed in the small intestine, where it competes with calcium, iron and phytate. High dietary calcium and phytate form insoluble complexes and reduce the proportion of zinc that reaches the circulation.

cascade.title: Impaired keratinocyte function
cascade.detail: Zinc is required for the DNA-binding proteins that regulate epidermal differentiation, particularly the zinc-finger transcription factors. Without adequate zinc, keratinocytes fail to progress to normal cornification.

cascade.title: Parakeratosis
cascade.detail: Keratinocytes retain their nuclei into the stratum corneum and the normal basket-weave of keratin is replaced by thickened, disorganised layers. The stratum corneum becomes cracked and crusted, and the skin loses its barrier function.

cascade.title: Crusting dermatitis and secondary infection
cascade.detail: The abnormal epidermis produces the characteristic thick, adherent crusts, particularly on the muzzle, eyes, ears, scrotum and lower limbs. The compromised barrier allows secondary bacterial and fungal colonisation, which can dominate the clinical picture.

cascade.title: Impaired immunity and growth
cascade.detail: Zinc is required for T-lymphocyte function and for wound healing, so deficiency produces increased susceptibility to infection and delayed healing, alongside reduced growth and feed efficiency.

lesions: Thick, adherent, greyish crusts resembling elephant skin
Alopecia and crusting around the muzzle, eyes, ears and on the scrotum
Hyperkeratosis with retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis) on histology
Cracking and fissuring of the skin of the lower limbs
Poor hoof growth on the coronary band and heel
Secondary bacterial infection with purulent exudate
clinical_signs: Thick, crusty skin lesions around the muzzle, eyes and ears
Generalised dry, scaly skin with hair loss
Poor growth and reduced feed efficiency
Cracked and crusted hooves, sometimes with lameness
Reduced wound healing
Increased susceptibility to infections
In pigs, the classic parakeratosis on the back, flanks and limbs of weaners

antemortem: Serum zinc measurement — useful but can be a poor reflection of body status because serum zinc is tightly regulated
Skin biopsy showing parakeratosis, which is a strong diagnostic clue
A therapeutic trial of zinc supplementation, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Dietary analysis for zinc, calcium and phytate content
postmortem: Skin lesions are the principal finding; no systemic lesion is characteristic
Histopathology of skin biopsy is the definitive test
laboratory: Serum or plasma zinc, interpreted with caution
Liver zinc concentration, though it is not a sensitive indicator
Skin biopsy with histology showing parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis
Forage and feed analysis for zinc, calcium and phytate
differentials: Dermatophilosis — crusting lesions with a different distribution and Gram-positive filaments on smear
Mange — pruritic lesions with mites on skin scraping
Ringworm — circular lesions with fungal elements
Selenium deficiency — can cause similar skin and hoof changes, often coexists
Photosensitisation — dermatitis restricted to unpigmented skin
Bovine viral diarrhoea and other viral skin disease

prevention: Provide adequate zinc in the ration, particularly during rapid growth and reproduction
Correct excessive calcium and phytate intake rather than simply adding more zinc
Use a balanced mineral supplement appropriate to the species
Check the zinc status of pasture and soil on deficient land
Avoid over-supplementing calcium, which is a common cause of the problem
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional deficiency.
treatment: Oral zinc supplementation — zinc sulphate or zinc oxide in the feed or as a drench
In severe cases, injectable zinc is available in some countries
Correct the dietary imbalance, particularly excess calcium
Many animals respond within 2-4 weeks, with the skin lesions resolving
Note that zinc toxicity can occur with over-supplementation, and copper status should be monitored as high zinc can induce copper deficiency
outbreak: Confirm the diagnosis, ideally with a skin biopsy and dietary analysis
Review and correct the ration, particularly the calcium and zinc ratio
Supplement zinc in the affected group
Monitor the response and reassess the ration if the lesions recur
Consider concurrent deficiencies, particularly copper and selenium
public_health: Zinc deficiency in livestock has no direct public health significance
Zinc is an essential human nutrient and is regulated in animal feed
Observe withdrawal periods for any veterinary products used
control.notes: This is one of the most commonly missed diagnoses in skin disease. Zinc deficiency is over-diagnosed in textbooks and under-diagnosed in practice, and a skin biopsy is the quickest way to settle the question.

diseases.prognosis: Excellent with supplementation — the skin lesions resolve within weeks and growth resumes. Poor if the underlying dietary imbalance persists, because the condition will recur after the supplementation stops.
